items.passage:
Dear Ms. Alvarez,

As a resident of Building C in the Linden Court apartment complex, I have greatly enjoyed the community garden behind our parking lot since it opened two years ago. It has become a place where neighbors who once passed each other in silence now trade seedlings and advice. However, I would like to bring a growing problem to your attention. The single water faucet that serves the garden is located at the far end of the plot, and the hose attached to it no longer reaches the beds along the eastern fence. As a result, several elderly gardeners have been carrying heavy watering cans back and forth during the hottest part of the day, and two of them have already complained of back pain. I understand that the management office has a limited budget for repairs. Still, I believe that installing a second faucet near the eastern beds would be a relatively inexpensive solution that would benefit many residents. I would sincerely appreciate it if you could consider this request at the next maintenance review.

Respectfully,
Jonah Whitfield
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 공동 정원의 운영 시간 연장을 건의하려고
정원 관리 비용의 분담 방식을 문의하려고
노인 주민을 위한 원예 강좌 개설을 제안하려고
공동 정원에 수도꼭지 추가 설치를 요청하려고
주차장 확장 공사로 인한 불편을 항의하려고
items.exp: 호스가 동쪽 화단까지 닿지 않아 노인들이 물뿌리개를 나르느라 힘들다며, 동쪽 화단 근처에 수도꼭지를 하나 더 설치해 달라고 요청하고 있어요. 그래서 ④가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Leo had rehearsed his talk on river restoration at least twenty times, yet as he waited backstage at the city science festival, the words seemed to drain out of his head one by one. Through the curtain he could hear the murmur of nearly three hundred people. His palms were damp, and he kept checking that the remote for his slides was still in his pocket. When the host called his name, he walked out into a glare of light so bright that the audience disappeared into darkness. His first sentence came out thin and shaky. Then, on the second slide, a photograph of children wading in the once-polluted stream behind his old school appeared on the screen, and someone in the front row let out a small, delighted gasp. Leo glanced at the picture and remembered why he had wanted to give this talk in the first place. His voice steadied. By the time he reached his final slide, he was smiling, and when the applause rose out of the darkness, he felt a warm glow spreading through him, as if he could have gone on talking for another hour.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Leo의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 무대 뒤에서 손에 땀이 나고 첫 문장이 떨려 나올 만큼 긴장했지만, 발표를 마치고 박수 속에서 따뜻한 기쁨을 느꼈어요. 그래서 nervous → satisfied가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Automation is usually praised for removing routine tasks from human hands, and in many respects the praise is deserved. Autopilot systems fly aircraft more smoothly than most pilots, and software flags errors in financial records faster than any accountant. But automation creates a subtle problem that becomes visible only when something goes wrong. Skills that are rarely practiced fade. A pilot who has spent thousands of hours monitoring an autopilot may find that the manual handling skills needed in an emergency have quietly weakened. The system works so well, so much of the time, that the human operator is left with little to do except watch, and watching is a poor way to stay sharp. Then, at the rare moment when the machine reaches the limits of its programming, control is suddenly handed back to a person who is both out of practice and taken by surprise. In this sense, highly reliable automation can [leave us strongest where we least need strength], making the easy cases effortless while making the hardest cases harder than ever.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [leave us strongest where we least need strength]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: force human operators to train more intensively than before
allow machines to take over emergency situations entirely
make routine work smooth while weakening our ability to handle rare crises
help experts focus on difficult tasks by removing simple ones
reduce the total number of accidents caused by human error
items.exp: 자동화 덕분에 평소 쉬운 상황은 매끄럽지만, 연습하지 않은 기술이 약해져 기계가 한계에 이르는 드문 위기 상황에서는 사람이 더 어려움을 겪는다고 했어요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. ④는 자동화의 장점처럼 보이지만 글은 어려운 일에서 오히려 약해진다고 했어요.

items.passage: Moral philosophy has traditionally focused on dramatic dilemmas: whether to lie to save a life, whether to sacrifice one person for many. These cases are useful for testing principles, but they can leave the impression that ethics is mainly a matter of rare and agonizing decisions. In practice, most of our moral life unfolds in moments too small to feel like choices at all. Whether we listen fully when a colleague is speaking, whether we hold back a cutting remark, whether we notice the stranger struggling with a heavy door: these acts are seldom deliberated, yet they shape the people around us far more often than any heroic sacrifice. They also shape us. Each small act of attention or neglect strengthens a habit, and habits, accumulated over years, become character. A person who has never faced a great dilemma may still be deeply good or quietly cruel, depending on thousands of ordinary moments. If we want to understand what it means to live ethically, then, we should look less at the extraordinary crisis and more at the texture of everyday conduct.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 도덕적 원칙은 극단적인 딜레마를 통해서만 검증될 수 있다.
윤리적 삶은 극적인 결정보다 일상의 사소한 행동에서 드러난다.
타인의 말을 경청하는 습관은 직장 생활의 성공을 좌우한다.
선한 성품은 타고나는 것이라 습관으로 바꾸기 어렵다.
영웅적 희생은 주변 사람에게 오랫동안 영향을 미친다.
items.exp: 도덕적 삶의 대부분은 선택이라 느끼지도 못할 만큼 작은 순간에 펼쳐지고, 그것이 습관과 성품이 된다고 했어요. 마지막 문장에서도 극적인 위기보다 일상의 행동을 보라고 하므로 ②가 요지예요. ①은 글이 한계를 지적한 전통적 관점이에요.

items.passage: A lichen growing on a bare rock looks like a single, rather dull organism, a crust of gray or orange that seems to do nothing at all. In fact it is a partnership. Each lichen consists of a fungus living together with algae or bacteria that can photosynthesize. The fungus provides a sheltered structure, holds water, and draws minerals from the surface beneath it; the partners, protected inside, use sunlight to produce sugars that feed both. Neither could survive alone in the places where lichens thrive. On sun-baked cliffs, frozen tundra, and even old gravestones, the combination succeeds where each member would fail. This cooperation has consequences far beyond the lichen itself. By slowly dissolving rock with weak acids, lichens begin the formation of soil, preparing the ground for mosses and later for larger plants. For this reason biologists sometimes call them pioneers. Their story challenges the familiar picture of nature as a contest in which each organism stands alone, showing instead how partnership can open environments that no single species could occupy.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the competition between fungi and mosses for bare rock
the partnership that allows lichens to survive in harsh places
the reasons lichens grow more slowly than other plants
the damage lichens cause to stone buildings and monuments
the chemical methods scientists use to classify lichens
items.exp: 지의류는 균류와 광합성을 하는 조류·세균이 서로 돕는 공생체이고, 그 협력 덕분에 혹독한 환경에서도 살아남아 토양 형성까지 시작한다는 글이에요. 그래서 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 글이 반박한 '경쟁' 그림을 빌린 보기이고, ④는 바위를 녹인다는 내용을 잘못 비튼 것이에요.

items.passage: Curiosity is often imagined as a steady trait, something a person either has or lacks. Research suggests instead that it behaves more like a response to a particular situation: a feeling that arises when we become aware of a gap between what we know and what we want to know. Interestingly, curiosity is weakest at both extremes. When we know nothing about a subject, there is no gap to notice, because we cannot even form a question. When we already know a great deal, the gap seems too small to bother with. Curiosity peaks in between, when we know just enough to sense that something important is missing. This has practical consequences for teachers and writers. Simply presenting facts, however fascinating, may fail to spark interest if the audience has no frame in which to place them. A better approach is to first give people a little knowledge and then reveal a puzzle that their knowledge cannot yet solve. A mystery novel works the same way: it supplies enough clues to make the reader feel close to an answer, while carefully holding the final piece back.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Some People Are Born Curious
The More You Know, the Less You Wonder
Facts First: The Secret of Effective Teaching
The Sweet Spot of Curiosity: Knowing Just Enough
How Mystery Novels Changed Modern Education
items.exp: 호기심은 아는 것이 전혀 없거나 너무 많을 때는 약하고, 무언가 빠져 있다고 느낄 만큼만 알 때 가장 강하다는 내용이에요. 그래서 ④가 알맞아요. ②는 한쪽 극단만 말하고, ③은 사실만 제시하면 흥미를 못 끈다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: The octopus presents a puzzle for anyone who links intelligence to a long life. These animals solve mazes, open jars, and recognize individual human keepers, yet most species live only one or two years. Intelligence in other animals, such as apes, elephants, and crows, ①[tends] to develop alongside long lifespans and complex social groups, in which knowledge can be passed from older to younger members. The octopus has neither. It lives mostly alone, and its young hatch long after their mother has died, ②[leaving] them with no one to learn from. One explanation focuses on the animal's history. Ancestors of the octopus once carried protective shells, but at some point their descendants lost them, gaining flexibility at the cost of ③[becoming] extremely vulnerable to predators. A soft-bodied animal ④[that] must hide, hunt, and escape in a complex reef environment benefits enormously from the ability to learn quickly. In other words, the octopus may have become clever not because it had time to accumulate knowledge, but because, lacking a shell, it ⑤[having] to figure things out quickly in order to survive.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: because절의 주어 it 뒤에 정동사가 필요하므로 having이 아니라 had가 되어야 해요. ①은 주어 Intelligence에 맞는 단수 동사, ②는 결과의 분사구문, ③은 전치사 of 뒤 동명사, ④는 주격 관계대명사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Teachers have long assumed that feedback is most useful when it arrives quickly, ideally while a student's work is still fresh in memory. For simple tasks, such as checking arithmetic, this is often true: immediate correction ①[prevents] errors from becoming habits. For more complex learning, however, research suggests that a short delay can sometimes be ②[beneficial]. When students receive feedback the moment they finish a problem, they may focus only on whether the answer was right or wrong and move on without reflecting. A delay of a day or so forces them to ③[retrieve] their earlier reasoning before comparing it with the correction, and this effort of recalling strengthens memory. Immediate feedback can also make learners overly ④[dependent], since they come to expect that someone will catch every mistake for them rather than checking their own work. None of this means that feedback should be withheld indefinitely; a delay that is too long leaves students unable to connect the comments with what they did. The goal is to find a timing that ⑤[discourages] students to think again before they are told the answer.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 피드백 시점의 목표는 답을 듣기 전에 학생이 다시 생각하게 만드는 것이므로 discourages가 아니라 encourages가 되어야 해요. 나머지는 즉각적 교정의 효과, 지연의 이점, 이전 추론의 인출, 남에게 의존하게 되는 문제라는 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage: Rules are often thought to work through punishment: people obey because they fear the consequences of breaking them. Yet a striking amount of social order depends on something less visible. Consider the experience of standing in line at a bakery or waiting at a red light on an empty street at midnight. No police officer is watching, and the chance of being punished for stepping ahead is close to zero. Most people wait anyway. They do so partly because they expect others to do the same, and partly because breaking the rule would feel embarrassing even with no one around to see it. Researchers who study cooperation have found that once such expectations are widely shared, they become remarkably stable and can sustain fair behavior far more cheaply than any system of fines. But the same research shows a weakness. When people begin to see others openly ignoring a norm, their own commitment can collapse quickly, because the norm was never held up by force in the first place. Social order of this kind is therefore both powerful and ___, resting on a belief that everyone else is playing along.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 공유된 기대에 의한 질서는 강력하지만, 다른 사람들이 규범을 어기는 것을 보면 빠르게 무너진다고 했어요. 그래서 강력하면서도 깨지기 쉽다는 fragile이 알맞아요. 벌금보다 값싸게 유지된다고 했으므로 expensive는 반대예요.

items.passage: It is often said that certain words cannot be translated, and lists of such words circulate widely: a term in one language for the particular sadness of a rainy Sunday, another for the urge to squeeze something unbearably cute. Such lists are charming, but they can encourage a misleading picture of language as a set of sealed containers, each holding feelings that its speakers alone can experience. In reality, a speaker of any language can grasp the meaning of these words once it is explained in a sentence or two, and many will recognize the feeling at once. What is missing in translation is not the experience itself but the convenience of a single, ready-made label for it. That convenience matters, since a word that exists makes a feeling easier to notice, discuss, and remember. But the absence of a word does not mark the boundary of what can be felt or understood. Translation, from this perspective, rarely confronts true impossibility; its usual task is ___, unpacking into several words what another language has packed into one.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: inventing new emotions that one culture has never experienced
preserving the exact sound and rhythm of the original word
replacing a compact expression with a longer description of the same idea
proving that some feelings belong only to native speakers
selecting the single most popular word from a list of synonyms
items.exp: 번역에서 사라지는 것은 경험 자체가 아니라 그것을 한 단어로 부르는 편리함이라고 했고, 빈칸 뒤에서 한 단어에 담긴 것을 여러 단어로 풀어낸다고 했어요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. ④는 글이 부정하는 '봉인된 그릇' 관점이에요.

items.passage: Artificial light at night is so familiar that we rarely think of it as pollution, yet its effects on wildlife can be profound. Over millions of years, living things evolved under a steady rhythm of bright days and dark nights, and many depend on that rhythm. ① Many insects are drawn to streetlights, where they circle until exhaustion or are easily caught by predators, removing vast numbers from the food webs they support. ② Young sea turtles, which hatch on beaches at night and instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, often head inland toward roads and buildings instead of toward the moonlit sea. ③ Migrating birds, many of which navigate partly by the stars, can become disoriented by brightly lit towers and collide with them by the thousands. ④ Modern LED bulbs, which use far less electricity than older lamps, have helped many cities reduce their energy costs significantly. ⑤ Even plants are affected, as trees growing beside lamps may keep their leaves later into autumn, leaving them exposed to early frost.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 야간 인공조명이 곤충, 바다거북, 철새, 식물에 미치는 해로운 영향을 다뤄요. ④는 LED 전구의 에너지 절감을 말해 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
In hot, dry regions, traditional houses were often built around an open courtyard, a design that served as a kind of natural air conditioner long before electric cooling existed.

(A) As this cool air settled, it flowed into the surrounding rooms through doors and windows that opened onto the courtyard rather than the street. By midday, when the sun was high, the high walls shaded much of the courtyard floor, slowing the rate at which it warmed up again.

(B) The process began at night. Because the desert sky is usually clear, the ground and walls lose heat rapidly after sunset, and the air in the enclosed courtyard, being cooler and heavier than the air above, sank and collected there like water in a bowl.

(C) Many families added a small pool or fountain to strengthen this effect, as the evaporation of water absorbed additional heat. Together, these features allowed the inner rooms to remain comfortable even when temperatures outside became extreme.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 안뜰이 천연 냉방기 역할을 했다는 주어진 글 뒤에 그 과정이 밤에 시작된다는 (B)가 와요. (A)의 this cool air가 (B)에서 모인 찬 공기를 받고, (C)의 this effect가 (A)까지의 냉각 효과를 받아 마무리해요.

items.passage: A popular claim holds that glass is actually a very slow liquid, and that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because the glass has gradually flowed downward over the centuries. ( ① ) The idea is appealing, but it does not survive close examination. ( ② ) Calculations based on the measured viscosity of glass at room temperature show that noticeable flow would take far longer than the age of the universe. ( ③ ) Moreover, medieval windows are not consistently thicker at the bottom; some are thicker at the top or along one side. ( ④ ) The real explanation lies in how the glass was made. Early glassmakers spun molten glass into large discs, a method that inevitably produced panes of uneven thickness, and builders often chose to set the heavier edge at the bottom of the frame for stability. ( ⑤ ) Glass is better described as an amorphous solid: its atoms lack the orderly arrangement of a crystal, yet they are effectively locked in place.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Such variation would be hard to explain if the glass had truly been flowing, since gravity pulls in only one direction.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 Such variation은 위쪽이나 한쪽 옆이 더 두꺼운 창문도 있다는 바로 앞 문장을 가리키므로 ④에 들어가야 해요. 그 뒤에 The real explanation이 이어져 자연스러워요. ③ 앞에는 아직 두께의 차이가 나오지 않았어요.

items.passage: Many subscription services charge a small amount each month rather than a single larger annual fee, and this pricing choice has effects that go beyond simple convenience. When a cost is broken into small, regular payments, each individual charge seems minor and is easily overlooked in a bank statement. Studies of consumer behavior show that people who pay monthly are considerably less likely to review whether they still use a service than those who pay once a year. An annual bill, by contrast, arrives as a noticeable lump sum that forces a moment of reflection: is this still worth it? In one experiment, gym members who paid yearly attended more regularly in the weeks right after each payment and were more likely to cancel when their attendance dropped, while monthly payers often kept paying for months after they had stopped going. The smaller and more frequent the payment, it seems, the less attention it receives, allowing unused subscriptions to continue quietly in the background.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Splitting a cost into small, frequent payments makes each payment less (A) ___, which reduces the chance that consumers will (B) ___ whether the service is still worth paying for.
items.exp: 작고 잦은 결제는 눈에 잘 띄지 않아 서비스를 계속 쓸 가치가 있는지 다시 검토할 가능성을 낮춘다고 했어요. 그래서 (A) noticeable, (B) reconsider가 알맞아요. forget을 넣으면 '잊을 가능성을 줄인다'가 되어 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: Public health campaigns have traditionally relied on information. If people knew that washing their hands prevented disease, the reasoning went, they would wash their hands; if they understood the risks of a sugary diet, they would eat differently. Decades of experience have shown that this assumption is far too (a)[optimistic]. Most people already know that handwashing protects them, yet observational studies in hospitals, schools, and public restrooms repeatedly find that a large share of people skip it or rush through it. The gap between knowledge and action is not mainly a failure of understanding; it is a failure of (b)[habit] and environment. Recognizing this, many health programs have begun to focus less on persuading individuals and more on redesigning the settings in which choices are made. In one village program, for example, organizers found that families rarely washed their hands before meals, not because they doubted its value, but because soap and water were kept in a separate shed far from the kitchen. Placing a simple washing station beside the cooking area, with soap fixed at eye level, (c)[increased] handwashing far more than months of posters and lectures had done. Similar thinking has shaped efforts to reduce injuries and improve nutrition: placing fruit at the front of school cafeteria lines, or setting healthier options as the default on menus, changes behavior without requiring anyone to make a deliberate decision. Critics sometimes worry that such approaches treat people as objects to be steered rather than as citizens to be informed. The concern deserves attention, since design choices are never neutral. Yet information and design need not be (d)[rivals]. The most effective programs tend to combine them, explaining why a behavior matters while also making it the (e)[hardest] thing to do.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Knowledge Alone Is Enough to Change Health Behavior
Why Posters Remain the Best Tool for Health Campaigns
Beyond Information: Designing Settings for Healthier Choices
The Hidden Dangers of Sugary Diets in Schools
How Villages Built the First Modern Hospitals
items.exp: 건강 행동은 정보만으로 바뀌지 않으므로 선택이 이루어지는 환경을 설계하는 쪽으로 관심이 옮겨가고 있다는 내용이에요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. ①은 글이 지나치게 낙관적이라고 비판한 가정이에요.

items.passage:
(A)
For thirty-one years, Mr. Okafor's bakery on Fenwick Street had opened at six every morning, and for most of those years, Tessa had stopped by on her way to school for a cinnamon roll. Now she was nineteen and home from university for the summer, and the first thing she noticed was the handwritten sign in the window: Closing at the end of August. Inside, the baker looked tired. "My hands are not what they were," (a)[he] told her, flexing his fingers. "And nobody wants to get up at three to knead dough anymore."

(B)
On the last day of August, Mr. Okafor did not take down the sign. Instead, he crossed out the words and wrote beneath them in careful letters: Under new management, same recipes. Tessa had decided to take a year off from university to run the bakery, with the old baker coming in three mornings a week to supervise. When (b)[she] pulled the first tray of rolls from the oven, the old baker nodded and said that they smelled exactly the way they should.

(C)
The next morning, Tessa knocked on the bakery door at three. Mr. Okafor opened it in his flour-covered apron, plainly surprised. "I just want to learn how you make them," (c)[she] said. "Even if it is only for a few weeks." He hesitated, then handed her an apron. Her first batch of dough was too dry, and her second rose unevenly, but he corrected her gently, guiding her wrists through the motion of folding and pressing until (d)[she] began to feel the rhythm.

(D)
By the third week, regular customers had begun to recognize Tessa behind the counter, and several told Mr. Okafor that the rolls tasted just as they always had. One morning, an elderly woman pressed a folded letter into Tessa's hand. It was signed by more than eighty neighbors asking that the bakery stay open. Tessa read it twice, then looked across the kitchen at the old man, who was pretending to be busy with the ovens. That night, (e)[she] lay awake for hours, thinking about what she might be willing to give up.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 폐업 소식을 들은 (A) 뒤에 다음 날 새벽 세 시에 빵 만드는 법을 배우러 간 (C)가 와요. 셋째 주에 이웃들의 편지를 받고 고민하는 (D)가 이어지고, 8월 마지막 날 새 운영자가 된 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Whitfield,

I am writing on behalf of the residents of Building C at Linden Court, where you serve as property manager. Since the recycling station was moved to the far end of the parking lot last month, many of us have noticed a troubling change. Elderly residents, in particular, find it difficult to carry heavy bags of glass and paper across a poorly lit lot, especially after dark. As a result, recyclables are increasingly being left beside the main entrance or thrown into general waste bins, which defeats the very purpose of the station. We understand that the move was intended to reduce noise near the ground-floor units, and we respect that concern. However, we believe a compromise is possible. We would therefore like to ask that the station be returned to a location closer to the building, perhaps near the bicycle shelter, where it would remain accessible without disturbing anyone. We would be happy to meet with you to discuss this further.

Sincerely,
Daniel Okafor
Residents' Committee, Building C
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 주차장에 야간 조명을 설치해 달라고 건의하려고
재활용 수거장을 건물 가까운 곳으로 다시 옮겨 달라고 요청하려고
재활용 분리배출 규칙을 지켜 달라고 당부하려고
items.exp: 필자는 수거장이 멀어져 생긴 문제를 설명한 뒤 'We would therefore like to ask that the station be returned to a location closer to the building'이라고 요청하고 있어요. 조명이 어둡다는 내용은 문제 상황의 일부일 뿐, 조명 설치를 건의하는 글은 아니에요.

items.passage: Mira tied on her green apron and stared at the line of customers stretching to the door. It was her first Saturday at the café, and the manager had been called away, leaving her alone at the counter with a coworker who was busy at the espresso machine. Orders came faster than she could write them down: an oat-milk latte, two iced teas with no sugar, a blueberry muffin warmed but not too hot. Her fingers fumbled with the register, and when a man sighed loudly at her mistake, her face burned. She wanted to disappear into the storage room. But she forced herself to slow down, repeat each order aloud, and smile. Gradually the line shrank. By noon, a regular customer leaned over the counter and told her she was faster than the last new hire. Mira wiped the counter, straightened her apron, and caught herself humming. She had survived the rush, and she had handled it well.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Mira의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 문 앞까지 늘어선 줄과 쏟아지는 주문에 손이 헛돌고 창고로 숨고 싶어 한 모습에서 감당하기 벅찬 마음이 드러나요. 차분히 주문을 처리해 줄을 줄이고 칭찬을 들은 뒤 콧노래를 부르며 잘 해냈다고 느꼈으므로 만족스러운 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 overwhelmed → satisfied가 알맞아요.

items.passage: When a government agency announces that a new traffic policy has reduced accidents by twenty percent, most citizens have no choice but to take the claim on trust. The report that accompanies such an announcement typically presents conclusions, a few charts, and a summary of methods, while the underlying records remain locked inside the agency. This arrangement may once have been justified by the cost of printing and distributing large data sets, but that excuse no longer holds. Today, raw figures can be shared at almost no cost, with personal information removed. Public institutions should therefore release the data on which their conclusions rest, along with a clear account of how those data were analyzed. Doing so would not weaken trust in government; it would place trust on firmer ground. Independent researchers could confirm sound findings, catch honest errors before they shape further policy, and propose alternative interpretations. An agency that refuses to open its evidence to examination asks citizens to believe rather than to understand, and in a democracy that is too much to ask.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 공공 기관은 결론의 근거가 되는 원자료와 분석 방법을 공개해야 한다.
정부는 교통 정책의 효과를 정기적으로 평가해야 한다.
공공 데이터를 공개할 때는 개인 정보 보호를 최우선으로 해야 한다.
시민들은 정부의 발표를 비판적으로 받아들여야 한다.
독립 연구자들에게 정책 수립 권한을 부여해야 한다.
items.exp: 'Public institutions should therefore release the data on which their conclusions rest, along with a clear account of how those data were analyzed.'가 필자의 주장이에요. 개인 정보 삭제는 공개의 조건으로 잠깐 언급될 뿐이고, 연구자는 검증하는 역할이지 정책 권한을 갖는 것이 아니에요.

items.passage: Modern news organizations are extraordinarily good at telling us what happened in the last sixty minutes. Alerts arrive on our phones within seconds of a court ruling, a market drop, or a political resignation, and each story is updated as fresh details emerge. Yet many of the forces that most profoundly shape our lives do not happen in any particular hour. The gradual thinning of groundwater, the slow rise in the average age of farmers, the quiet shift in how young people form friendships—such changes unfold over years, and no single day offers a dramatic moment that demands a headline. Because the machinery of journalism is built around events, it struggles to notice processes. A story with no clear beginning offers no obvious reason to publish it today rather than tomorrow, so it is postponed again and again. The result is a curious distortion: [the news of the hour crowds out the news of the decade]. Readers who follow every update may end up well informed about what is loud and poorly informed about what is large.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the news of the hour crowds out the news of the decade]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: news outlets exaggerate minor events to attract more readers
rapid reporting often spreads errors that are later corrected
past historical events are forgotten as new ones are reported
readers prefer long investigative stories to short breaking news
focus on immediate events leaves slow but significant changes underreported
items.exp: 언론은 사건 중심으로 움직여 몇 년에 걸쳐 일어나는 느린 변화(processes)를 잘 다루지 못한다고 했어요. 즉 '지금 이 시간의 소식'이 '십 년 단위의 중요한 변화'를 밀어낸다는 뜻이에요. 과거 사건이 잊힌다는 ③은 '느리게 진행 중인 변화'라는 핵심을 놓쳤어요.

items.passage: In many desert annual plants, a puzzling pattern appears: even when conditions are ideal, only a fraction of the seeds produced in a given year will germinate the following season. The rest remain dormant in the soil, some for a decade or more. At first glance this seems wasteful, since a seed that refuses to sprout under favorable conditions gives up a chance to reproduce. But the desert does not keep its promises. A heavy early rain may be followed by months of drought that kills every seedling before it can flower. A plant whose seeds all germinated at once would be staking its entire lineage on a single season's weather. By spreading germination across many years, the parent ensures that no single catastrophe can wipe out all of its offspring. Biologists call this strategy bet-hedging: it lowers the average success in good years in exchange for reducing the chance of total failure in bad ones. In unpredictable environments, survival over the long run depends less on maximizing gains than on avoiding ruin.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of heavy rainfall in triggering seed germination
competition among desert plants for scarce water
delayed germination as a strategy for coping with environmental uncertainty
the high cost of seed production in harsh climates
how desert seeds resist damage from extreme heat
items.exp: 사막 식물이 씨앗의 발아를 여러 해에 나누어 예측할 수 없는 환경에서 전멸을 피한다는 '위험 분산(bet-hedging)' 전략을 설명하는 글이에요. 큰비는 위험한 예시로 나올 뿐, 발아를 일으키는 역할이 주제가 아니에요.

items.passage: A century ago, a broken toaster would almost certainly have been taken to a repair shop. Today it is far more likely to be thrown away and replaced. It is tempting to blame this shift on a culture of carelessness, but the real explanation lies largely in relative prices. Over the past several decades, automated factories and global supply chains have steadily lowered the cost of producing new goods, while the cost of skilled labor in wealthy countries has risen along with wages in general. Repair, however, remains stubbornly labor-intensive: a technician must still diagnose the fault, open the casing, and replace the part by hand. As a result, fixing a toaster can now cost more than buying a new one, and a consumer who chooses replacement is behaving quite rationally. The trouble is that this individual logic ignores costs that no price tag reflects, such as the resources consumed in manufacturing and the waste piling up in landfills. What is cheap for each household may be expensive for everyone.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Fixing Things Stopped Making Economic Sense
Careless Consumers Are Filling Our Landfills
How Automation Made Products Last Longer
Global Supply Chains Raise the Price of Goods
items.exp: 새 제품 생산비는 내려가고 수리에 드는 인건비는 올라서 고치는 것보다 사는 것이 경제적으로 합리적이 되었다는 내용이에요. 글은 소비자의 부주의(carelessness) 탓이 아니라고 했으므로 ③은 맞지 않고, 공급망은 가격을 낮췄으므로 ⑤도 반대예요.

items.passage: Edvina Sorlund (1868–1941) was a Swedish astronomer best known for her catalog of variable stars. Born in a small fishing village, she taught herself mathematics from her uncle's old navigation manuals. Because universities in her region did not yet admit women to science programs, she began her career as a paid assistant at a private observatory, where her job was to measure star positions on photographic plates. Over eighteen years, she examined more than forty thousand plates and identified some 1,200 stars whose brightness changed over time. Her careful notes later helped astronomers estimate distances to nearby star clusters. In 1912, she became the first woman elected to her country's astronomical society, though she declined an invitation to lecture abroad, saying her work required her presence at the telescope. After her death, a scholarship for young women in astronomy was established in her name.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 삼촌의 낡은 항해 교범으로 수학을 독학했다.
사설 천문대에서 유급 조수로 경력을 시작했다.
18년 동안 4만 장이 넘는 사진 건판을 조사했다.
해외 강연 초청을 받아들여 여러 나라를 방문했다.
사후에 그녀의 이름을 딴 장학금이 만들어졌다.
items.exp: 'she declined an invitation to lecture abroad'라고 했으므로 해외 강연 초청을 거절했어요. 나머지는 각각 navigation manuals, paid assistant, forty thousand plates, scholarship 부분과 일치해요.

items.passage: When a person points at one of two upturned cups, a pet dog will usually go straight to the cup indicated, even if it has never been trained to do so. This ability, ①[which] seems trivial to us, is surprisingly rare in the animal world. Chimpanzees, despite ②[being] our closest living relatives and skilled problem-solvers in many other tasks, tend to perform poorly on the same test. More striking still, wolves raised by humans from birth generally fail to follow a pointing finger unless they receive extensive training. Puppies, by contrast, succeed at the task within weeks of birth, often before they have had much contact with people at all. Such findings suggest that sensitivity to human gestures is not simply learned through experience but ③[has been] shaped by thousands of years of domestication, during which dogs that understood their human companions were more likely to be fed and kept. Some researchers go further, arguing that dogs ④[are] better at reading our communicative intentions than any other species, a claim that, if correct, ⑤[make] the familiar household dog a valuable subject for studying the origins of social intelligence.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 관계대명사 that의 선행사 a claim이 단수이므로 make를 makes(또는 would make)로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 앞의 This ability를 받는 계속적 용법 관계대명사, ②는 전치사 despite 뒤의 동명사, ③은 is not simply learned와 병렬을 이루는 현재완료 수동태, ④는 복수 주어 dogs에 맞는 동사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: When a language borrows a word from another, the word rarely arrives unchanged. Its pronunciation is typically ①[adjusted] to fit the sound system of the borrowing language, so that combinations of consonants that speakers find difficult are broken up or simplified. Its meaning, too, often shifts. A borrowed term may ②[narrow] to refer to only one specific version of what it originally named, or it may acquire connotations of prestige or novelty that it never carried at home. Over time, many loanwords become so thoroughly integrated that ordinary speakers are ③[unaware] of their foreign origin, and they begin to take native grammatical endings like any other word. This process shows that borrowing is not a passive act of copying but an active act of ④[reshaping]. Far from ⑤[expressing] the borrowing language's identity, then, the loanwords it absorbs often reveal it most clearly, since the changes they undergo display the habits and preferences of the speakers who adopted them.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 차용어는 받아들인 언어의 습관에 맞게 바뀌므로 오히려 그 언어의 정체성을 잘 드러낸다는 흐름이에요. 'Far from ~, ... reveal it most clearly'라는 대조가 성립하려면 ⑤ expressing을 threatening(위협하는) 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Nostalgia has long had a poor reputation. For centuries it was treated as a kind of illness, and even today it is often dismissed as a sentimental retreat from the demands of the present. Recent research in psychology, however, paints a different picture. When people are asked to recall a cherished memory from their past, they tend to report feeling more connected to others, more confident that their lives have meaning, and more optimistic about what lies ahead. Strikingly, nostalgic reflection appears most often when people are lonely, anxious, or facing an uncertain transition, such as moving to a new city. Rather than trapping them in what has been lost, the memory seems to remind them that they have been loved and have overcome difficulties before—evidence that they can do so again. In several studies, participants who had just written about a nostalgic event were more willing to pursue challenging goals than those who had written about an ordinary one. Nostalgia, in short, functions less as an escape from the present than as a ___ for facing the future.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 향수는 소속감·삶의 의미·낙관을 높이고, 어려운 목표에 도전할 의지까지 키워 준다고 했어요. 따라서 미래를 마주하기 위한 '자원(resource)'으로 기능한다는 말이 알맞아요. 'distraction'은 글이 부정한 '현재로부터의 도피'와 같은 의미라 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Organizations that wish to remove human discretion from decisions often respond to disputed cases by writing more detailed rules. If a guideline on 'reasonable expenses' produces disagreement, a list of permitted items is added; if the list proves ambiguous, definitions of each item follow. Each step seems to narrow the space in which anyone must exercise judgment. Yet a familiar philosophical argument suggests that this hope is misplaced. A rule does not apply itself. To follow 'meals under thirty dollars are reimbursable,' someone must still decide whether a snack bought at an airport counts as a meal, whether tax is included, and what to do when a receipt is lost. Any further rule written to settle these questions will, in turn, require someone to interpret its terms, and so on without end. Judgment, in other words, cannot be eliminated from the application of rules, because it is presupposed by the very act of applying them. Every attempt to banish it by adding rules merely ___. This is not an argument against rules, which coordinate behavior and limit arbitrary choices, but it is a reason to invest in the good sense of the people who apply them.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: relocates the need for it to the interpretation of the new rules
reduces the number of cases that call for interpretation
shows that ordinary people rarely need guidance at all
allows experts to agree on a single correct application
makes the original rule unnecessary for future decisions
items.exp: 규칙은 스스로 적용되지 않으며, 질문을 정리하려고 만든 새 규칙도 다시 누군가의 해석을 필요로 해 끝이 없다고 했어요. 그러므로 규칙을 덧붙여 판단을 없애려는 시도는 판단의 필요를 새 규칙의 해석으로 '옮겨 놓을' 뿐이에요. ②는 글이 '그럴 것 같지만 틀린 희망'으로 제시한 내용이에요.

items.passage: The risk that loud sound poses to hearing depends not only on how intense the sound is but also on how long a person is exposed to it. ① Safety guidelines reflect this by allowing shorter listening times as volume increases, so that a level considered safe for eight hours may be harmful after only fifteen minutes when it is raised substantially. ② This is because the delicate hair cells of the inner ear can recover from brief stress but are permanently damaged when overworked without rest. ③ Unlike many other cells in the body, these hair cells do not regenerate in humans once they are destroyed, which makes the damage irreversible. ④ Modern hearing aids, by contrast, have become small enough to fit almost invisibly inside the ear canal and can connect wirelessly to phones. ⑤ For this reason, someone who spends a long commute with earphones at moderate volume may accumulate more harm than a concertgoer who endures a single loud evening.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 소음의 세기와 노출 시간이 함께 청력 손상을 결정한다는 내용이에요. ④는 보청기의 소형화와 무선 연결 기술을 다루어 흐름에서 벗어나요. ⑤의 For this reason은 ①~③에서 말한 '노출 시간과 회복 불가능한 손상'을 이어받아요.

items.passage:
Software engineers working under tight deadlines often face a choice between building a feature properly and building it quickly with shortcuts they know they will regret.

(A) Over time, the cost becomes impossible to ignore. Every change takes longer, because developers must work around earlier compromises, and fixing one problem quietly creates two more. Eventually, teams may spend more effort managing old shortcuts than building anything new.

(B) Such paralysis is the strongest argument for taking the metaphor seriously. It reminds managers that shortcuts are borrowed time, and that, like any loan, they must eventually be repaid—preferably on a schedule chosen by the team rather than by a crisis.

(C) The quick path is often the right one in the short run, and the industry has a name for the gap it leaves: 'technical debt.' Like a financial loan, it lets a team get something now in exchange for paying more later, and the longer the shortcuts remain, the more 'interest' accumulates.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 빠른 길(shortcuts)을 (C)가 The quick path로 받아 'technical debt'라는 이름과 이자 개념을 소개해요. (A)는 이자가 쌓여 커지는 비용(the cost)을 설명하고, (B)의 Such paralysis는 (A) 끝의 '새로운 것을 만들지 못하는 상태'를 가리키므로 (C)–(A)–(B)예요.

items.passage: In the early seventeenth century, European maps began to show California not as part of the North American mainland but as a large island separated from it by a narrow sea. ( ① ) The idea seems to have originated in a mistaken report from an expedition, and once a few respected mapmakers adopted it, others followed. ( ② ) The reason lay in how printing changed the life of a mistake: one copied by hand might have stayed in a single library, whereas a printed one could be reproduced in thousands of copies across several countries within a few years. ( ③ ) The working habits of mapmakers made matters worse. Because they rarely traveled to the regions they drew, they relied heavily on earlier maps, and the more often a feature appeared, the more trustworthy it seemed. ( ④ ) Explorers who later reported that California was in fact connected to the mainland were sometimes doubted, since their accounts contradicted dozens of published maps. ( ⑤ ) The island persisted on many maps for well over a century, a reminder that repetition can be mistaken for confirmation.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Ironically, the very speed with which printed maps spread made the error harder to correct.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 인쇄 지도가 빠르게 퍼졌기 때문에 오류를 고치기가 더 어려웠다는 내용이에요. ② 뒤의 The reason lay in how printing changed the life of a mistake는 주어진 문장이 말한 '오류 수정이 어려워진 이유'를 설명하므로 ②에 들어가야 해요. ① 앞에는 아직 인쇄 이야기가 나오지 않아요.

items.passage: Museum labels often describe ancient tools in modest terms: a "simple" stone blade, a "crude" dugout canoe, a "basic" bone needle. Experimental archaeologists, who try to make and use such objects with only the materials and techniques available at the time, have repeatedly found that these descriptions underestimate their makers. Volunteers attempting to shape a flint blade usually produce nothing but shattered fragments for weeks before they manage a usable edge, because the stone must be struck at precise angles that depend on its hidden internal structure. Replica canoes carved with stone axes turn out to require careful choices about which tree to fell, how thick to leave the hull, and when to use fire to soften the wood. In each case, an object that looks primitive in a display case proves to contain a long chain of decisions and a level of skill that can take years to acquire. Such findings cannot be obtained by measuring or photographing artifacts alone; they emerge only when modern hands attempt to repeat the ancient work.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

By (A) ___ ancient techniques with their own hands, experimental archaeologists have shown that objects described as simple actually reflect considerable (B) ___.
items.exp: 실험 고고학자들은 당시의 재료와 기술로 직접 도구를 만들어 보며(make and use, repeat the ancient work) 알아냈으므로 (A)는 reproducing이에요. 단순해 보이는 물건에 긴 결정 과정과 오랜 숙련(skill)이 담겨 있다고 했으므로 (B)는 expertise예요. 측정·촬영만으로는 알 수 없다고 했으니 documenting은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Parents who want their young children to develop self-control often reach for structured activities: worksheets, rule-based games, and lessons in which an adult directs every step. Yet developmental research suggests that one of the most (a)[effective] training grounds for self-regulation is something far less organized—elaborate pretend play among children themselves.

Consider what happens when four-year-olds decide to play 'restaurant.' One child becomes the cook, another the waiter, a third the customer. To keep the game going, each must remember the role, suppress actions that do not fit it, and adjust when a partner changes the plot. A child who would gladly grab a toy in ordinary circumstances may (b)[wait] patiently to be 'served,' because grabbing would break the fiction everyone is maintaining. In this sense, the rules of pretend play are not imposed from outside but (c)[generated] by the children, and they are enforced by peers who are surprisingly strict about how a waiter or a doctor ought to behave.

Studies have found that children who regularly engage in such sustained, cooperative make-believe tend to perform better on later tests of attention and impulse control than peers whose play is mostly solitary or directed by adults. One explanation is that pretend play offers (d)[repeated] practice in exactly the skills that self-regulation requires, in a setting children find intrinsically motivating. No adult has to persuade them to keep trying; the desire to continue the game does the work.

None of this means that adults have no role. They can provide time, space, and simple props, and they can help a game get started. But when grown-ups take over the plot or turn play into a lesson, they may (e)[strengthen] the very feature that makes it valuable: the children's own effort to sustain a shared imaginary world.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Structured Lessons Build Better Attention
Solitary Play: The Hidden Key to Creativity
Make-Believe as a Child-Led School of Self-Control
How Adults Can Teach Children Social Roles
Strict Peers: A Threat to Young Imaginations
items.exp: 아이들이 스스로 규칙을 만들고 지키는 협동적 역할 놀이가 자기 조절 능력을 기르는 훈련장이 된다는 글이에요. 구조화된 수업보다 덜 조직된 놀이를 강조하므로 ①은 반대이고, 혼자 하는 놀이는 오히려 효과가 덜하다고 했으므로 ②도 틀려요.

items.exp: 어른이 줄거리를 가져가거나 놀이를 수업으로 바꾸면 아이들이 스스로 놀이 세계를 유지하려는 노력, 즉 놀이의 가치를 오히려 약화시키게 돼요. 따라서 (e) strengthen은 undermine(약화시키다) 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
The call came just after four in the afternoon, as the first clouds of a forecast storm were gathering over Granite Ridge. A sixteen-year-old named Theo had set out alone on the ridge trail that morning and had not returned. For Hana, who had joined the volunteer rescue team only three months earlier, it was her first real search. She packed her gear with trembling hands while Marcus, the team leader with twenty years on the mountain, studied the map in silence. Within half an hour, the four-person team was climbing toward the trailhead, headlamps ready for the dark.

(B)
The snow began before they reached the first switchback. Hana, thinking of a boy alone in the cold, kept pulling ahead, and twice Marcus called her back. At a fork in the trail (a)[he] stopped completely, knelt, and swept the fresh powder aside with a gloved hand. 'We're not just looking for Theo,' he said quietly. 'We're looking for the mistake he made.' Hana bit back her impatience. Every minute felt precious, yet Marcus was moving at a pace she would have found slow on a summer afternoon.

(C)
Carrying Theo down took nearly three hours. At the trailhead, wrapped in a blanket and sipping hot tea, the boy thanked each of them in turn, and when he reached Marcus, his voice broke. Later, as the team loaded the vehicle, Hana admitted that she had wanted to run the whole way up. Marcus smiled. 'So did I, on my first search,' (b)[he] said. 'But the mountain punishes people who hurry. Tonight, being slow is what found him.' Hana looked up at the dark ridge and realized that (c)[he] had been teaching her the whole time.

(D)
The mistake turned out to be visible to anyone patient enough to look. Beneath the new snow, Marcus found a partial boot print heading not along the main trail but down a narrow gully that, in poor light, resembled the path. Following it, (d)[he] led the team for another forty minutes until a faint whistle answered their calls. They found Theo curled inside a hollow beneath an overhanging rock, cold and frightened but unhurt. Remembering advice from a safety class, (e)[he] had stopped moving once he realized he was lost, which made him far easier to find.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 출동한 뒤 (B)에서 눈 속을 오르며 Marcus가 'Theo가 저지른 실수'를 찾는다고 말해요. (D)는 The mistake turned out to be ...로 그 실수를 받아 Theo를 찾는 장면이고, (C)는 Theo를 데리고 하산한 뒤의 대화이므로 (B)–(D)–(C)예요.

'But the mountain punishes people who hurry. Tonight, being slow is what found him.' Hana looked up at the dark ridge and realized that (c)[he] had been teaching her the whole time.

(D)
The mistake turned out to be visible to anyone patient enough to look. Beneath the new snow, Marcus found a partial boot print heading not along the main trail but down a narrow gully that, in poor light, resembled the path. Following it, (d)[he] led the team for another forty minutes until a faint whistle answered their calls. They found Theo curled inside a hollow beneath an overhanging rock, cold and frightened but unhurt. Remembering advice from a safety class, (e)[he] had stopped moving once he realized he was lost, which made him far easier to find.
items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Theo는 아침에 혼자 능선 등산로로 출발했다.
Hana는 구조대에 합류한 지 석 달밖에 되지 않았다.
Marcus는 갈림길에서 무릎을 꿇고 눈을 걷어 냈다.
Theo는 주 등산로를 따라 내려가다 길을 잃었다.
Theo는 바위 아래 움푹한 곳에서 발견되었다.
items.exp: (D)에서 발자국은 주 등산로가 아니라 길처럼 보이는 좁은 협곡(gully) 아래쪽으로 나 있었다고 했으므로 ④가 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 (A)의 set out alone, only three months earlier, (B)의 knelt, (D)의 hollow beneath an overhanging rock과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Hartley,

Thank you for the warm welcome you and your staff have given our volunteer guides at the Eastbrook Maritime Museum over the past two years. As coordinator of the guide program, I have watched our volunteers grow in confidence and knowledge, and visitor feedback on their tours has been consistently positive. However, our current schedule allows guides to lead tours only on weekend afternoons, which means that school groups visiting on weekdays receive no guided tour at all. Several teachers have told us that their students wandered through the galleries without understanding what they were seeing. Fifteen of our guides have indicated that they are available on weekday mornings, and they have already prepared a shorter tour designed for students aged ten to fourteen. I am therefore writing to ask your permission to begin offering weekday morning tours for school groups from next semester. I would be glad to provide a detailed schedule and a list of the volunteers involved.

Kind regards,
Priya Nandakumar
Volunteer Guide Coordinator
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 주말 오후 투어 일정 변경을 안내하려고
평일 오전 학생 단체 대상 해설 투어 운영을 허락해 달라고 요청하려고
학생용 짧은 투어 프로그램 개발을 제안하려고
items.exp: 'I am therefore writing to ask your permission to begin offering weekday morning tours for school groups'에서 목적이 드러나요. 학생용 짧은 투어는 이미 준비되었다고 했으므로 개발을 제안하는 ⑤는 목적이 아니에요.

items.passage: The judges had already tasted four dishes when they reached Jun's station, and their faces had given nothing away. Jun had trained for this regional cooking final for half a year, yet he felt strangely at ease. His braised short ribs had come out exactly as he had practiced them, glossy and tender, and he arranged the plate with steady hands, humming under his breath. The head judge cut into the meat, chewed slowly, and then set down her fork. 'Did you taste the sauce before plating?' she asked. Jun's smile faded. In the rush of the final minutes, he had added a second spoonful of soy sauce to deepen the color and had not tasted it again. He dipped a clean spoon into the leftover sauce. It was harsh with salt, nothing like the balanced flavor he had served a hundred times at home. His face grew hot, and he stared at the plate as the judges moved on to the next station, unable to hear a word of what they were saying.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jun의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에 Jun은 연습한 대로 요리가 나와 콧노래를 부를 만큼 자신 있었어요(confident). 그러나 마지막에 넣은 간장 때문에 소스가 너무 짜다는 것을 알고 얼굴이 달아오르며 낙담했어요(dismayed). 'nervous → relieved'는 반대 흐름이에요.

items.passage: When audiences leave a film saying that it was beautifully edited, editors are often less pleased than one might expect. For most of cinema's history, the dominant goal of film editing has been to keep viewers from noticing it at all. A typical scene may contain dozens of cuts, yet an audience absorbed in the story experiences it as a single, continuous flow of events. Editors achieve this by hiding each change of shot inside a natural movement: cutting as an actor turns a head, opens a door, or reaches for a glass, so that the eye follows the action across the cut instead of registering the jump. They match the direction of a glance in one shot with the position of the object in the next, and they let sound from the following scene begin a moment early to carry the viewer over the gap. When these techniques succeed, the audience believes it has simply watched what happened, unaware of the hundreds of decisions that shaped where its attention went. In this sense, [an editor's finest work leaves no fingerprints]. Its very success lies in being mistaken for the absence of any work at all.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [an editor's finest work leaves no fingerprints]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: editors rarely receive public credit for the films they shape
the best editing guides viewers without their noticing it
skilled editors avoid cutting scenes as much as possible
audiences prefer films with fewer visible special effects
editors should leave decisions about scenes to the actors
items.exp: 편집의 목표는 관객이 편집을 알아차리지 못하게 하는 것이고, 관객은 수백 가지 결정이 주의를 이끈 줄 모르고 그냥 사건을 본다고 믿는다고 했어요. 그러니 최고의 편집은 흔적 없이 관객을 이끈다는 뜻이에요. 컷을 피한다는 ③은 한 장면에도 수십 개의 컷이 있다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: We usually read a nineteenth-century novel as a single, finished object, bound between two covers. Many of these works, however, first reached readers in monthly or weekly installments, sold cheaply in magazines or in separate parts over a year or more. This mode of publication left deep marks on the stories themselves. Authors had to end each installment at a point that would make readers eager to buy the next, which encouraged dramatic turns and unresolved suspense at regular intervals. Because readers might forget details across a gap of several weeks, writers gave characters memorable habits and phrases and repeated key information more often than a modern editor would allow. Some even adjusted their plots in response to sales or letters from readers, expanding a popular character or changing a story's direction midway. Features that modern critics sometimes dismiss as clumsy, such as crowded plots or exaggerated personalities, make more sense once we remember the conditions under which they were produced. To understand a literary work fully, then, we need to consider not only what its author intended but also the form in which it was delivered to its first readers.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 19세기 소설은 오늘날의 기준에 맞게 다시 편집해서 읽어야 한다.
연재 소설은 단행본 소설보다 문학적 완성도가 떨어진다.
문학 작품을 제대로 이해하려면 처음 독자에게 전달된 출판 형식도 고려해야 한다.
작가는 독자의 반응에 흔들리지 말고 자신의 의도를 지켜야 한다.
독자의 기억을 돕기 위해 소설 속 인물의 수를 줄여야 한다.
items.exp: 연재라는 출판 방식이 극적인 끊기, 반복, 독자 반응에 따른 줄거리 변경 등 작품 자체에 흔적을 남겼다고 하고, 마지막 문장에서 작품이 처음 전달된 형식도 고려해야 한다고 정리했어요. 그래서 ③이 요지예요. ②는 비평가들이 서툴다고 보는 특징을 오히려 이해할 수 있다고 한 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: In some cultures, a pause of more than a second or two in conversation creates discomfort, and speakers rush to fill it with a comment, a question, or a polite laugh. In others, silence of several seconds is not only tolerated but expected, particularly after someone has said something important. To a listener from the first group, a long pause may signal disagreement, boredom, or confusion; to a listener from the second, a quick reply may seem thoughtless, as if the speaker had not bothered to consider what was said. These differences can quietly damage relationships in international business and education, because neither side recognizes that the other is following a different rule. Each instead concludes that the other is rude, evasive, or shallow. What is at stake is not the content of what is said but the meaning assigned to the gaps between words—a layer of communication so familiar to its users that they rarely notice it exists until it is violated.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the benefits of thinking carefully before speaking
why international business meetings often fail
the decline of polite conversation in modern society
how body language replaces words in communication
cultural differences in how silence in conversation is interpreted
items.exp: 대화 중 침묵을 어떤 문화는 불편하게, 어떤 문화는 자연스럽게 여겨 서로 오해가 생긴다는 내용이므로 '대화 속 침묵 해석의 문화적 차이'가 주제예요. ②는 결과의 일부만 다루고, ①은 한쪽 문화의 관점에 불과해요.

items.passage: Most engineering materials begin to fail the moment they are put into use. Tiny cracks form in concrete as it dries and expands with changing temperatures, and over years these cracks let in water that corrodes the steel inside. Repairing such damage is costly, and much of it is discovered only after it has become serious. Researchers have recently developed concrete that addresses this problem in an unexpected way: by keeping living bacteria inside it. Dormant spores of certain bacteria, mixed into the concrete along with a source of nutrients, can survive for years in a sealed state. When a crack opens and water seeps in, the spores awaken, consume the nutrients, and produce limestone, which gradually fills the gap. In laboratory tests, cracks up to nearly a millimeter wide have closed within weeks. The material does not prevent damage, but it allows a structure to respond to damage on its own, much as skin closes over a cut.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Concrete That Mends Itself with the Help of Bacteria
Steel Versus Concrete: Which Lasts Longer?
How to Detect Cracks Before They Spread
items.exp: 콘크리트 속에 잠든 박테리아가 균열에 물이 스며들면 깨어나 석회석을 만들어 틈을 메운다는 내용이에요. 박테리아는 건물을 약하게 하는 것이 아니라 고치는 역할이므로 ②는 반대예요.

items.passage:

items.q: Harborview Kite Festival 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 연 만들기 워크숍은 토요일과 일요일에 모두 열린다.
연날리기 대회 참가 신청은 현장에서 받지 않는다.
금속 프레임이 있는 연은 사용할 수 없다.
items.exp: 'Kite-Making Workshop: $8 per person (materials included), Saturday only'라고 했으므로 워크숍은 토요일에만 열려요. 나머지는 일정, Free for spectators, on-site registration is not available, metal frames 안내와 일치해요.

items.passage: Before coins were widely minted, many societies used objects such as shells, salt, or cloth as money. What made a particular object suitable was not its usefulness in daily life but a combination of qualities ①[that] allowed it to circulate easily. It had to be durable enough to survive repeated exchange, divisible into smaller units, and difficult to counterfeit or ②[produce] in large quantities. Certain shells from the Indian Ocean met these requirements remarkably well, ③[which] explains why they were accepted as payment across a vast region of Africa and Asia for centuries. Problems arose, however, when outsiders discovered sources of the shells far richer than any previously known. Ships began carrying them by the ton, and the value of shells that local traders had accumulated over a lifetime ④[falling] sharply. The episode illustrates a principle that still applies to modern currencies: money works only as long as its supply remains limited, and anything that suddenly ⑤[makes] it abundant undermines the trust on which its value depends.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④는 주어 the value에 대한 술어 동사가 와야 하는 자리이므로 falling을 fell로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 qualities를 받는 주격 관계대명사, ②는 to counterfeit와 병렬인 동사원형, ③은 앞 절 전체를 받는 계속적 용법 which, ⑤는 단수 주어 anything에 맞춘 makes로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: In many ant colonies, no individual directs the work of others, yet tasks such as foraging, nest repair, and caring for larvae are distributed with remarkable efficiency. Each ant responds to simple local cues: the rate at which it encounters nestmates returning with food, for instance, or the smell of a damaged chamber. When foragers return quickly, signaling that food is ①[plentiful], more ants leave the nest to collect it; when returns slow, fewer ants go out. Through such cues, the colony adjusts its workforce to changing conditions without any ant ②[possessing] an overview of the whole situation. This decentralized system has an important advantage: because no single member is ③[essential], the loss of individuals rarely disrupts the colony's operation. It also has limits. Since each ant reacts only to what it senses nearby, the colony can be slow to ④[detect] distant opportunities or threats. Still, for creatures with tiny brains, the arrangement is strikingly ⑤[inefficient], producing coordinated behavior that no individual could plan.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 글 전체가 지휘자 없이도 일을 놀라울 만큼 효율적으로 나누는 개미 집단을 설명하고, Still 뒤에서 한계에도 불구하고 개인이 계획할 수 없는 협동을 만들어 낸다고 칭찬하고 있어요. 따라서 ⑤ inefficient는 effective(효과적인) 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Sports statistics have traditionally rewarded what can be counted: goals, assists, tackles, and saves. For attackers, this works reasonably well, since their contributions usually take the form of visible actions. Defenders pose a deeper problem. The finest defensive play often consists of being in exactly the right position, so that an opponent never attempts the pass or the shot at all. A defender who reads the game well may complete fewer tackles than a weaker teammate, precisely because opponents avoid challenging him, while the teammate is forced into dramatic last-second interventions that look impressive in highlights. Judged by the numbers, the second player appears more valuable, yet coaches who watch closely know the opposite is true. Newer tracking systems try to address this by measuring how much space a player denies to opponents rather than how many actions he performs. They are, in effect, attempting to measure the ___, giving value to the events that a skilled defender quietly prevents from happening.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 뛰어난 수비는 상대가 아예 패스나 슛을 시도하지 못하게 하는 것이라 기록에 남지 않는다고 했어요. 새 추적 시스템은 이렇게 '일어나지 않은 일'을 측정하려 하므로 보이지 않는 것(invisible)이 알맞아요. spectacular는 오히려 하이라이트에 잡히는 화려한 수비를 가리켜 반대예요.

items.passage: Historians are trained to build their accounts on evidence, and the most abundant evidence for most past societies is written: tax registers, court records, letters, chronicles. Yet the documents that survive are not a random sample of what once happened. They were produced by people who could write, preserved by institutions that judged them worth keeping, and protected from fire, damp, and war by those with the resources to do so. A peasant community that settled its disputes through oral agreements may leave almost no trace, while a single wealthy family may leave thousands of pages describing its estates. A historian who reasons only from what the archive contains may therefore conclude that disputes were rare in the countryside, or that the wealthy family was central to regional life, when both impressions are partly artifacts of record-keeping. The careful scholar must learn to read the archive as a product of past decisions, asking not only what a document says but why it exists at all. In short, she must recognize that ___. Only then can the absences in the record become evidence in their own right rather than mere blanks.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: written records are more reliable than oral traditions in every case
the wealthy were in fact the main actors in historical change
documents lose their value once their authors are unknown
rural communities were more peaceful than surviving records suggest
the silence of the sources does not necessarily reflect a silence in the past
items.exp: 남아 있는 문서는 쓰고 보존할 수 있던 사람들이 남긴 것이라 기록이 없는 것이 곧 그 일이 없었다는 뜻은 아니라고 했어요. 마지막 문장도 기록의 '부재'를 증거로 읽어야 한다고 하므로 '사료의 침묵이 반드시 과거의 침묵을 반영하지는 않는다'가 알맞아요. ⑤는 농촌이 실제로 더 평화로웠다고 단정해 글의 신중한 태도와 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: A typeface that looks elegant in a book can become nearly useless on a highway sign, where a driver moving at a hundred kilometers per hour may have only a second or two to read it. ① Designers of road lettering therefore favor wide, open letter shapes, because narrow letters tend to blur into one another when seen from a distance. ② Many countries have also moved away from words written entirely in capitals toward a mix of upper- and lowercase letters, since the varied outlines of lowercase words help drivers recognize place names as whole shapes. ③ At night, light reflected from a sign can make bright letters appear to spread into the dark background, so some newer typefaces leave extra space inside letters such as 'e' and 'a' to keep them from filling in. ④ Tests in which volunteers try to read signs from increasing distances have shown that such small adjustments can noticeably extend the distance at which a name becomes readable. ⑤ Old enamel signs from the early decades of motoring, with their hand-painted lettering, have meanwhile become valued by collectors as charming examples of folk design.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 글은 고속으로 달리는 운전자가 빨리 읽을 수 있도록 도로 표지판 글자를 설계하는 방법(넓은 글자, 대소문자 혼용, 글자 속 여유 공간)과 그 효과를 다뤄요. ⑤는 옛 법랑 표지판이 수집품으로 인기라는 내용으로 가독성이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요. ④는 앞의 조정들이 실제로 효과가 있음을 보여 주어 흐름에 맞아요.

items.passage:
Philosophers have long relied on thought experiments—imagined scenarios designed to test a principle by applying it to a carefully constructed case.

(A) Critics reply that this strength is also a weakness. Because the scenarios are often so far removed from ordinary life, involving teleporters, perfect duplicates, or runaway trains, the intuitions they provoke may reflect nothing more than confusion about an unfamiliar situation, and a principle should not be discarded on such shaky grounds.

(B) Defenders of the method, in turn, point out that physics has used imagined cases in much the same way, and that removing real-world clutter is exactly what allows a hidden assumption to come into view. On this view, strangeness is not a defect but the price of clarity.

(C) Their power lies in isolation. By stripping away the distracting details of real situations, a thought experiment can show that a principle which seemed obviously correct leads to a conclusion almost everyone rejects.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 thought experiments를 (C)가 Their power로 받아 장점(세부를 제거해 원리를 시험함)을 설명해요. (A)는 this strength로 그 장점을 가리키며 비판을 소개하고, (B)는 in turn으로 비판에 대한 옹호론의 반박을 제시하므로 (C)–(A)–(B)예요.

items.passage: For decades, high blood pressure was diagnosed mainly from readings taken in a doctor's office. ( ① ) Researchers eventually noticed, however, that a substantial number of patients showed elevated readings only in clinical settings, apparently because the stress of the visit itself raised their pressure. ( ② ) Treating these patients with medication on the basis of office readings alone risked giving them drugs they did not need. ( ③ ) Some people have normal readings in the clinic but high pressure during their daily routines, perhaps because of work stress or poor sleep, and because their office measurements look reassuring, the problem may go unnoticed for years. ( ④ ) To catch both groups, many guidelines now recommend that diagnosis be confirmed with measurements taken at home or with a portable device worn over a full day. ( ⑤ ) These readings capture blood pressure as it is actually experienced over hours of ordinary life, not as it appears during a brief and unusual moment in a clinic.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The opposite pattern also exists, and it is arguably more dangerous.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 The opposite pattern은 ①·② 뒤에서 설명한 '병원에서만 혈압이 높게 나오는' 경우의 반대를 가리켜요. ③ 뒤 문장이 '병원에서는 정상이지만 일상에서는 높은' 경우를 설명하고 더 위험한 이유(오랫동안 발견되지 않음)를 제시하므로 ③에 들어가야 해요. ④ 뒤의 both groups도 두 유형이 모두 나온 다음이어야 자연스러워요.

items.passage: When people estimate how long it will take them to finish a project, they are notoriously optimistic, routinely underestimating the time required even when they have failed to meet similar deadlines before. Curiously, the same people are much more accurate when they predict how long a task will take someone else. In one study, students asked to forecast the completion date of their own assignments missed by several days on average, while observers given the same information about those students produced estimates that came considerably closer to the actual dates. The difference appears to arise from where attention is directed. When thinking about our own work, we picture a detailed plan for how the task will unfold and focus on the future, ignoring the interruptions that have derailed us in the past. When thinking about others, we lack access to their plans and therefore rely on what we know of their general behavior, which naturally includes their past delays.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

People forecast others' task completion more (A) ___ than their own, because when judging themselves they concentrate on future plans, while for others they draw on (B) ___ patterns.
items.exp: 다른 사람의 완료 시점은 실제 날짜에 더 가깝게 예측했으므로 (A)는 realistically(현실적으로)예요. 다른 사람을 판단할 때는 과거의 지연을 포함한 일반적 행동, 즉 이전(previous)의 패턴에 의존한다고 했으므로 (B)는 previous예요. optimistically는 자기 자신에 대한 예측의 특징이에요.

items.passage:
Negotiators facing a complex deal often try to make it manageable by settling one issue at a time. A company and a supplier might agree on price first, then move on to delivery dates, then to payment terms. The approach feels orderly, and it seems to (a)[increase] the risk of confusion. Yet research on bargaining suggests that it frequently leaves both sides worse off than they could have been.

The reason is that parties rarely care equally about every issue. The supplier may be desperate for early payment to ease its cash flow, while the buyer may care far more about a fast delivery schedule than about a small difference in price. When each issue is negotiated (b)[separately], neither side has a way to express these differences in priority. Each point becomes a tug-of-war in which any gain for one party is a loss for the other, and the usual outcome is a compromise somewhere in the middle.

When several issues are placed on the table together, by contrast, a different kind of bargain becomes possible. The buyer can (c)[concede] on payment terms, which costs it relatively little, in exchange for the delivery schedule it values highly, and the supplier can do the reverse. Each side gives up what matters less to it in order to gain what matters more, and the total value of the agreement (d)[grows] rather than merely being divided.

Taking advantage of this possibility, however, requires a degree of openness that many negotiators find uncomfortable. Parties must reveal at least something about their priorities, and they must resist the instinct to treat every issue as a contest to be won. Those who manage this often discover that the most (e)[valuable] question in a negotiation is not 'How much can I get?' but 'What do you care about most?'
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Splitting the Difference Is the Fairest Solution
Bundle the Issues: How Trading Priorities Expands the Deal
Settle Price First, and the Rest Will Follow
The Hidden Dangers of Revealing Your Priorities
Winning Every Point: The Key to a Strong Agreement
items.exp: 여러 쟁점을 한꺼번에 협상하면 각자 덜 중요한 것을 양보하고 더 중요한 것을 얻어 합의의 전체 가치가 커진다는 글이에요. 중간에서 타협하는 것은 쟁점을 따로 다룰 때의 평범한 결과로 소개되었고, 우선순위를 드러내는 것은 위험이 아니라 필요한 일로 제시되었어요.

items.exp: 쟁점을 하나씩 처리하는 방식은 질서 있게 느껴지고 혼란의 위험을 줄여 주는 것처럼 보인다는 흐름이므로 (a) increase는 reduce(줄이다)로 바꿔야 해요. 뒤의 Yet이 '그럴듯해 보이지만 실제로는 손해'라는 대조를 이끌어요.

items.passage:
(A)
Two weeks before the spring concert, Ms. Alvarez, the conductor of the Westfield High School orchestra, announced that the principal cellist, a senior, had broken his wrist in a cycling accident. The solo passage in the second movement would have to be played by someone else. Every eye in the room turned toward Nadia, a sophomore who had joined the cello section only that year. Nadia stared at her music stand. She could play the passage in an empty practice room, but the thought of playing it alone before six hundred people made her stomach turn.

(B)
On the night of the concert, Nadia's hands were cold as she took her seat. When the solo arrived, she looked up for a moment and saw Ms. Alvarez give a small nod. Nadia closed her eyes and played the passage as if (a)[she] were back in the empty music room with Grace beside her. The hall was silent when (b)[she] finished, and then, from somewhere near the back of the hall, someone began to clap before the movement had even ended. Ms. Alvarez only smiled and kept the orchestra going, but Nadia could see that her eyes were shining.

(C)
For the first week, Nadia practiced the solo every lunch period, and every day she stumbled in the same place, a quick climb into the upper register. Her stand partner, Grace, a junior who had wanted the solo herself, noticed Nadia's frustration. Instead of keeping her distance, Grace began appearing in the music room at lunch. 'Breathe before the climb,' (c)[she] suggested one afternoon, 'not during it.' It sounded too simple, but the next time Nadia tried it, the notes came out clean.

(D)
With Grace's help, the climb improved, yet at the dress rehearsal Nadia froze halfway through the solo, and the orchestra stumbled to a halt. Afterward, Ms. Alvarez found (d)[her] sitting alone backstage. Instead of offering advice, the conductor told the girl about her own first solo, when she had forgotten an entire page of music. 'Nobody remembers the mistakes,' Ms. Alvarez said. 'They remember that you kept going.' Nadia walked home that evening repeating the words to herself until (e)[she] could almost believe them.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Nadia가 독주를 맡게 된 뒤 (C)는 For the first week로 첫 주의 연습과 Grace의 도움을 그려요. (D)는 With Grace's help로 이어져 총연습에서의 실수와 지휘자의 격려를 보여 주고, (B)는 공연 당일 밤이므로 (C)–(D)–(B)예요.

choices: 첼로 수석 연주자는 자전거 사고로 손목이 부러졌다.
Nadia는 공연 날 밤 독주 중에 Ms. Alvarez의 끄덕임을 보았다.
Grace는 원래 그 독주를 맡고 싶어 했다.
