items.exp: (D)에서 Nadia는 총연습 때 독주 중간에 얼어붙어 오케스트라가 멈추었다고 했으므로 ④는 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 (A)의 cycling accident, (B)의 small nod, (C)의 had wanted the solo herself, (D)의 her own first solo와 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Director Morales,

I am writing on behalf of the residents of the Eastbrook district, many of whom work evening shifts at the hospital and the distribution center along Harlow Road. Until last spring, Route 14 ran until 1 a.m., giving these workers a safe and affordable way home. Since the schedule was cut back to end at 10 p.m., many of them have had to rely on expensive taxis or walk nearly forty minutes along poorly lit roads. Several have told me that they are now considering leaving jobs they otherwise value. We understand that ridership after ten was lower than on daytime routes, and that the authority faces real budget limits. However, we believe that even two additional late departures, at 11:30 p.m. and 12:45 a.m., would meet most of the need at a modest cost. We would be glad to help collect data on demand if that would support a review. I sincerely ask you to consider restoring these late-night services to Route 14.

Sincerely,
Teresa Huang
Eastbrook Residents' Council
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 버스 노선의 낮 시간 배차 간격을 줄여 달라고 요청하려고
14번 노선의 심야 운행 일부를 복원해 달라고 요청하려고
야간 근무자를 위한 택시 요금 지원을 제안하려고
어두운 도로에 가로등을 설치해 달라고 건의하려고
심야 승객 수요 조사 결과를 보고하려고
items.exp: 필자는 10시로 단축된 14번 버스 운행 때문에 야간 근무자들이 겪는 어려움을 설명한 뒤, 마지막에 심야 운행을 복원해 달라고 요청하고 있어요. 수요 조사는 도울 수 있다고 제안한 것일 뿐 결과를 보고하는 글이 아니에요.

items.passage: For seven weeks Yuna had helped feed the fox cub that a farmer had found beside a highway, too weak even to lift its head. Now the cub was healthy, and today it was going home. As the rescue center's van bumped along the forest road, she kept glancing at the carrier on her lap. What if it had grown too used to people? What if it simply sat in the grass, waiting for a bowl of food that would never come? Her stomach tightened when Dr. Ahn stopped the van at the edge of a meadow and handed her the carrier. 'You open it,' he said. Her fingers trembled on the latch. The door swung wide, and for a long moment nothing happened. Then a narrow red face appeared, sniffed the air, and the cub shot out across the meadow, leaping over a fallen log as if it had never been ill. At the tree line it paused, glanced back once, and vanished. Yuna laughed out loud, tears running down her cheeks, and Dr. Ahn grinned beside her.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Yuna의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: Yuna는 여우 새끼가 사람에게 길들어 야생으로 돌아가지 못할까 봐 속이 조이고 손이 떨렸지만, 새끼가 힘차게 숲으로 달려가자 소리 내어 웃으며 눈물을 흘려요. 따라서 걱정하다가 기뻐하는 ④가 알맞아요. 결말이 기쁜 장면이므로 ③은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Many students treat revision as the final cleanup of a finished draft: they fix spelling, smooth a few awkward phrases, and hand the paper in. This habit is understandable, because it is how revision is often presented, as the polishing stage that follows the real work of writing. Yet this view misses what revision can do. A first draft is rarely a record of what a writer already thinks; more often it is the process by which the writer discovers what she thinks. The clearest idea in an essay may appear only in its final paragraph, after the writer has fumbled through the earlier ones. Real revision, then, means returning to the beginning with that late discovery in hand and rebuilding the essay around it, even if that requires deleting pages that took hours to write. Teachers should therefore ask students to rethink their arguments, not merely to correct their sentences, and should grade drafts in a way that rewards bold restructuring rather than penalizing the temporary mess it creates.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 학생들이 글을 고칠 때 문장 교정보다 논지 자체를 다시 생각하도록 지도해야 한다.
초고를 쓸 때부터 맞춤법과 문장 표현에 신경 써야 한다.
글의 핵심 생각은 반드시 첫 문단에 분명히 제시해야 한다.
오랜 시간을 들여 쓴 부분은 수정 과정에서 삭제하지 말아야 한다.
교사는 학생 초고의 오류를 직접 고쳐 주어야 한다.
items.exp: 마지막 문장에서 교사는 학생들에게 문장만 고치게 하지 말고 논지를 다시 생각하게 해야 한다고 주장해요. 오랜 시간 쓴 페이지라도 지울 수 있어야 한다고 했으므로 ④는 반대 내용이에요.

items.passage: Every few years a headline announces that most car accidents happen within a few kilometers of the driver's home, and readers are advised to take special care on familiar streets. The advice may be harmless, but the reasoning behind it is not. Most accidents occur near home for the simple reason that most driving occurs near home; a statistic about where crashes happen tells us nothing about danger until it is set against how much time people actually spend in each place. The same error appears whenever a raw count is presented as if it spoke for itself. The claim that most injured cyclists were wearing helmets, or that more household injuries occur in the kitchen than in any other room, sounds alarming or reassuring only because we forget to ask how many people were in those situations to begin with. A figure of this kind is [a numerator in search of its denominator]: until it is matched with the larger total it should be divided by, it can be made to support almost any conclusion, and the careful reader withholds judgment until that total is supplied.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a numerator in search of its denominator]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a statistic that has been deliberately altered to mislead the public
a count that cannot be judged until it is compared with how often the situation occurs
a danger that grows smaller as a place becomes more familiar
a figure that becomes more accurate as more cases are collected
a number that reports accidents while ignoring safe journeys home
items.exp: 집 근처 사고가 많은 것은 운전 자체가 집 근처에서 많이 이루어지기 때문이라며, 단순한 건수는 그 상황에 놓인 전체 규모와 비교하기 전까지는 판단할 수 없다고 했어요. 그래서 나눌 전체(분모)를 찾지 못한 분자라는 표현은 ②의 뜻이에요. 의도적인 조작을 말한 글이 아니므로 ①은 틀리고, ⑤는 지문 낱말을 빌린 부분적 진술이에요.

items.passage: In temperate forests, a tree that opens its leaves too early risks losing them to a late frost, while one that waits too long gives up weeks of sunlight to its neighbors. Trees solve this dilemma not with a single signal but by combining several. Many species require a certain amount of accumulated cold during winter before their buds will respond to warmth at all, which prevents a brief mild spell in January from triggering growth. Once this chilling requirement is met, buds begin to track rising temperatures, and some species further check day length, refusing to open until nights have become sufficiently short. Because day length changes on the same calendar every year, it acts as a safety lock that temperature alone cannot provide. Species differ in how heavily they weight each cue: cautious ones depend more on day length, while opportunistic ones respond mostly to warmth. This variety explains why, on the same hillside, some trees burst into green while others still stand bare.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the damage that late frosts cause to forest ecosystems
competition among trees for sunlight in dense forests
the influence of climate change on the timing of spring
reasons why day length is a less reliable cue than temperature
how trees combine multiple environmental cues to time leaf growth
items.exp: 나무는 겨울 추위 누적, 기온 상승, 낮의 길이 같은 여러 신호를 결합해 잎을 낼 시기를 정한다는 내용이에요. 글에서는 낮의 길이가 기온보다 더 안정적인 안전장치라고 했으므로 ④는 반대예요.

items.passage: When the potato first arrived in Europe from South America in the sixteenth century, it was greeted with suspicion rather than enthusiasm. Many people regarded it as food fit only for animals or the very poor, and some feared it caused disease because it belonged to the same plant family as several poisonous species. For generations it was grown mainly as a botanical curiosity or as fodder. What eventually changed minds was not persuasion so much as hardship. In years when grain harvests failed, families who had planted potatoes still had something to eat, and the lesson spread from village to village. The crop also had a quiet military advantage: because its edible part grew underground, it was far harder for passing armies to destroy or seize than a field of ripe wheat. Some rulers began actively encouraging its cultivation. By the nineteenth century, the once-despised tuber had become a staple on which millions of Europeans depended every day.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Europeans Preferred Wheat to Every Other Crop
From Suspicion to Staple: The Potato's Slow Victory in Europe
The Poisonous Relatives of Everyday Vegetables
How Armies Spread New Crops Across Continents
The Scientists Who Proved the Potato Was Safe
items.exp: 처음에 의심받던 감자가 흉년과 전쟁 같은 어려움 속에서 가치를 인정받아 결국 유럽의 주식이 되었다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. 사람들의 생각을 바꾼 것은 설득보다 고난이었다고 했으므로 과학자의 증명을 내세운 ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Teodora Marin (1879–1958) was a Romanian naturalist known for her studies of honeybee behavior. The daughter of a village schoolteacher, she kept her first hive at the age of twelve and filled notebooks with observations of the bees' daily routines. Unable to enter university because of the cost, she worked as a pharmacist's assistant in Cluj while continuing her research in her spare time. In 1911 she designed a glass-walled observation hive that allowed her to watch the colony without disturbing it, and the design was soon copied by beekeepers across Eastern Europe. Her careful records of how foragers shared information about flowers attracted the attention of the national academy, which awarded her a research grant in 1924. Marin never married and spent her later years running a small school for village beekeepers. Her collected notebooks, donated to a museum in Bucharest after her death, are still consulted by researchers today.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 그녀의 노트는 사후에 부쿠레슈티의 박물관에 기증되었다.
items.exp: 1924년에 국립 학술원은 그녀에게 연구 보조금을 주었다고 했지(awarded her a research grant), 정식 연구원으로 임용했다는 내용은 없어요. 따라서 ④가 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 모두 글과 일치해요.

items.passage: Interoception, the sense of the body's internal state, tells us when we are hungry, tired, or anxious long before we can explain why. Researchers have found that people ①[differ] widely in how accurately they detect these signals; some can count their own heartbeats almost perfectly, while others miss more than half. Low accuracy is not simply a curiosity. People who struggle to read their internal cues often find it harder ②[to regulate] their emotions, because they notice distress only after it has grown intense. Encouragingly, interoceptive awareness appears to be trainable. Practices that ask people to pay quiet attention to their breathing or muscle tension ③[has] been shown, in several studies, to improve accuracy over a few weeks. The goal is not to monitor the body constantly, ④[which] could itself increase anxiety, but to restore a channel of information that modern routines, full of screens and schedules, tend to drown out. A body that is listened to ⑤[gives] earlier and gentler warnings.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③의 주어는 복수 명사 Practices이므로 has를 have로 고쳐야 해요. ②는 find it harder 뒤의 진주어 to부정사, ④는 앞 내용을 받는 계속적 용법 관계대명사, ⑤는 단수 주어 A body에 맞는 동사라서 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: After harvest, many farm fields are left bare through the winter, and bare soil is ①[vulnerable]. Rain strikes the surface directly, breaking apart the clumps that hold soil together, and wind carries away the finest, most fertile particles. Cover crops, such as rye or clover planted between main growing seasons, offer a simple ②[defense]. Their leaves soften the impact of rain, and their roots bind the soil in place while feeding the microorganisms that build its structure. Some cover crops, particularly legumes, also ③[add] nitrogen to the soil, reducing the need for chemical fertilizer in the following season. Despite these benefits, adoption has been slow. Farmers must pay for seed and labor in the present, while the rewards, such as richer soil and higher yields, appear only gradually over several years. For a farmer operating on thin margins, this ④[delay] can make the practice seem like a luxury. Programs that share the early costs can therefore make a difference, because they ⑤[increase] the burden that farmers must carry while they wait for the benefits to arrive.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 초기 비용을 나눠 주는 프로그램은 이익이 올 때까지 농부가 져야 하는 부담을 덜어 주는 것이므로, ⑤ increase는 reduce(줄이다)나 ease 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. ④ delay는 이익이 늦게 온다는 앞 내용과 맞아요.

items.passage: When a gazelle spots a cheetah approaching across the open plain, it sometimes does something that seems almost suicidal. Instead of fleeing at once, it leaps high into the air with its legs held stiff, bouncing several times in plain view of the predator. This behavior, called stotting, wastes energy and time that could be spent running, so biologists long wondered why natural selection had not eliminated it. One explanation is that the leap is a message aimed at the predator itself. Only a gazelle in excellent condition can afford to spend effort on such a display and still escape, so the height and vigor of the jumps tell the cheetah how hard this particular animal would be to catch. Field observations support the idea: cheetahs are less likely to chase gazelles that stot vigorously, and when they do chase, they rarely succeed. A sick or weak gazelle could not produce the same performance even if it tried. The display works precisely because it is costly; a signal that any animal could give would carry no information, but this one cannot easily be ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 병들거나 약한 가젤은 애써도 같은 도약을 해낼 수 없고, 아무나 보낼 수 있는 신호는 정보가 없다고 했어요. 따라서 이 신호는 쉽게 '속일(흉내 낼)' 수 없다는 faked가 알맞아요. 치타가 바로 보는 앞에서 하는 행동이므로 noticed는 반대 의미가 돼요.

items.passage: A map drawn at a scale of one to one would contain every road, every tree, every stone, and it would be useless, since consulting it would be no easier than walking the land itself. Scientific models face a similar paradox. A model of the atmosphere that included every molecule could not be run on any computer, and even if it could, its output would be as bewildering as the weather it imitated. What makes a model valuable is precisely that its builders have decided which features of the system can be safely set aside for the question at hand. An economist modeling price changes may treat consumers as identical; an ecologist may ignore the age structure of a population. Critics sometimes treat such simplifications as admissions of failure, as if a better model would simply be a more complete one. But completeness is not the goal. A model earns its explanatory power ___, and the art of modeling lies in choosing what can be left out without losing what matters.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: by approaching the full complexity of the real system
only when it is confirmed by independent experiments
through the precision of its numerical predictions
by deliberately ignoring much of what is true about its subject
when its assumptions are accepted by experts in other fields
items.exp: 실물 크기 지도처럼 모든 것을 담은 모형은 쓸모가 없고, 모형의 가치는 어떤 특징을 제쳐 둘지 정했다는 데서 나온다고 했어요. 따라서 대상에 관한 많은 사실을 의도적으로 무시함으로써 설명력을 얻는다는 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 완전성이 목표가 아니라는 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: The white marble statues of ancient Greece have long been admired as models of pure, colorless beauty, yet their whiteness is largely an accident of time. ① Under ultraviolet light and with chemical analysis, researchers have found faint traces of pigment on many sculptures, revealing patterned clothing, colored eyes, and tinted skin. ② These traces show that the original works were painted, often brightly, and would have looked strikingly different to ancient viewers from how they look in museums today. ③ Much of the marble used by Greek sculptors came from quarries on the island of Paros, whose stone was prized for its fine grain and its ability to let light pass a short way beneath the surface. ④ The colors faded over centuries of burial and weathering, and some were even scrubbed away by later collectors who assumed the stains were dirt. ⑤ When Renaissance and later artists imitated what they believed to be classical sculpture, they therefore copied the bare stone, and a misunderstanding hardened into an ideal of white perfection.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 고대 그리스 조각상이 원래는 채색되어 있었는데 색이 바래거나 지워져 '흰 대리석'이라는 이상이 생겼다는 흐름이에요. ③은 조각에 쓰인 파로스섬 대리석의 품질을 설명해 채색과 그 오해라는 흐름에서 벗어나요. ④는 ②의 원래 색이 어떻게 사라졌는지 이어 주는 문장이에요.

items.passage:
At first glance, traditional woodblock printing seems a simple craft: an artist carves a design into a flat piece of wood, covers the raised surface with ink, and presses a sheet of paper against it.

(A) Color adds a second and far greater problem. Because each color usually requires its own block, a print with seven colors may demand seven separately carved pieces of wood, each holding only the areas where that single color should appear on the finished sheet.

(B) The first difficulty is that everything must be carved in reverse. A tree meant to stand on the left side of the print has to be cut on the right side of the block, and any written characters must be formed backward, a habit that takes apprentices years to master.

(C) All of these blocks must then print onto the same sheet in perfect alignment, or the colors will spill past their outlines. To achieve this, printers cut small guide marks into a corner and an edge of every block, so the paper can be laid down in exactly the same position each time.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 단순해 보인다는 주어진 글 뒤에 첫 번째 어려움(The first difficulty)인 반대로 새기기를 다룬 (B)가 오고, 두 번째 문제(a second problem)인 색깔별 판목을 다룬 (A)가 이어져요. (A)의 여러 판목을 These blocks로 받아 정렬 방법을 설명한 (C)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: For centuries, many scholars believed that light traveled instantly from one place to another. ( ① ) In the 1670s, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer, working at the Paris Observatory, was studying Io, one of Jupiter's moons, which disappears into the planet's shadow at very regular intervals. ( ② ) Over many months, however, he noticed that these eclipses came several minutes later than predicted when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and several minutes earlier when Earth was approaching it. ( ③ ) When Earth was farther from Jupiter, that journey was longer, so each eclipse appeared to be delayed. ( ④ ) Using the best estimates of the size of Earth's orbit available at the time, his colleagues calculated a speed of roughly 220,000 kilometers per second, lower than the modern figure but astonishingly close for a first attempt. ( ⑤ ) More important than the exact number was the conclusion itself: light, however fast, has a finite speed, a fact that would later become central to modern physics.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Rømer realized that the timetable itself was not wrong; the light carrying the news of each eclipse simply needed time to reach Earth.
items.exp: 지구가 목성에서 멀어질 때 식이 늦게 나타난다는 관찰 뒤에, 주어진 문장이 그 이유를 빛이 지구에 닿는 데 시간이 걸리기 때문이라고 밝혀요. ③ 뒤의 that journey는 주어진 문장 속 빛이 오는 여정을 가리키므로 ③이 알맞아요.

items.passage: Traffic engineers have traditionally tried to make streets safer by adding more control: signs, painted lanes, barriers, and signals that tell every driver and pedestrian exactly where to go. In some European towns, planners have experimented with the opposite approach. They removed curbs, traffic lights, and most signs from busy town centers, leaving a single shared surface on which cars, cyclists, and people on foot must work out their movements among themselves. To many observers this looked like an invitation to chaos. Yet in a number of these towns, average speeds dropped and serious accidents did not rise; in some cases they fell. The explanation lies in how people respond to uncertainty. When the rules clearly assign a driver the right of way, he tends to focus on the signals and drive faster, trusting the system to protect him. When no such guarantee exists, drivers slow down, make eye contact with pedestrians, and pay attention to what is actually happening around them. The design does not remove responsibility; it hands it back to the people using the street.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Removing signs and signals from streets can make them safer, because (A) ___ about who has priority leads road users to behave more (B) ___.
items.exp: 통행 우선권이 정해져 있지 않은 불확실한 상황(ambiguity)에서 운전자들이 속도를 줄이고 보행자와 눈을 맞추며 주변에 주의를 기울인다고 했어요. 그래서 (A)는 ambiguity, (B)는 attentively가 알맞아요. clarity는 오히려 운전자가 신호만 보고 빨리 달리게 만드는 조건이에요.

items.passage:
When people hand over physical cash, they experience something researchers call the pain of paying: a small but real discomfort at watching money leave their hands. This sensation is often treated as an irrational quirk, yet it performs a useful function. It acts as a brake at the moment of purchase, forcing a brief, almost bodily comparison between the pleasure of the item and the loss of the money. Because the feeling is (a)[immediate], it does its work before the purchase is complete rather than weeks later when a statement arrives.

Modern payment methods have steadily (b)[weakened] this brake. A credit card separates the purchase from the payment in time; a phone tap removes even the physical gesture of handing over a card; a stored account on a shopping site reduces buying to a single click. Each step makes spending smoother, and studies consistently find that people tend to spend more, and remember their spending less (c)[accurately], when the payment is less visible. None of this means people are fooled in any simple sense; they know, if asked, that the money is real. But knowing is different from feeling, and decisions in the moment are often guided by feeling.

The lesson is not that we should return to paying for everything in coins. Frictionless payment has genuine advantages in safety and convenience. Rather, people who want to control their spending may benefit from deliberately (d)[removing] some friction: checking a balance before a purchase, using a separate account for discretionary spending, or waiting a day before confirming an online order. Such strategies work not because they provide new information, but because they restore the (e)[moment] of felt cost that convenience has quietly erased.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: When Paying Stops Hurting: The Hidden Cost of Convenience
Why Cash Will Soon Disappear from Our Wallets
Credit Cards: A Safer Way to Manage Money
How Knowing Prices Changes What We Buy
The Myth of the Irrational Shopper
items.exp: 현금을 낼 때 느끼는 지불의 고통이 소비를 억제하는 브레이크 역할을 하는데, 편리한 결제 수단이 이 고통을 없애 소비를 늘린다는 내용이에요. 따라서 지불이 더 이상 아프지 않을 때 생기는 편리함의 숨은 대가라는 제목이 알맞아요. 필자는 현금으로 돌아가자는 것이 아니라고 했으므로 ②는 맞지 않아요.

items.exp: 잔액 확인, 별도 계좌 사용, 하루 기다리기는 모두 결제에 마찰을 더하는 방법이에요. 따라서 (d) removing은 adding이나 reintroducing으로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Rafael had agreed to tutor his neighbor's son only because his school required forty hours of community service before graduation, and Mrs. Duarte had offered to sign his form. Teddy was ten, small for his age, and absolutely certain of one thing: he was bad at math. At their first session, he pushed the worksheet of fractions across the kitchen table without even glancing at it. "I just don't have a math brain," (a)[he] announced, as calmly as if he were reporting the weather, and spent the rest of the hour drawing robots in the margins.

(B)
Three weeks later, Mrs. Duarte met Rafael at the door holding a test paper with a large red B+ at the top. Teddy hovered behind her, trying not to smile and failing completely. "He says the cards did it," she said, clearly puzzled. Before Rafael left that evening, Teddy pressed a card into his hand: the silver dragon that (b)[he] had sworn never to give up. It was, Teddy insisted, payment. Walking home under the streetlights, (c)[he] realized that he had stopped counting his service hours days ago.

(C)
The next week, Rafael arrived early and found Teddy at the table with a shoebox full of trading cards, sorting them into piles with the speed of a bank clerk. A boy from down the street was bargaining with him. "Your dragon's worth three of my knights," the boy said. "Then two dragons are six knights, and you've only got five," Teddy shot back, "so you'll have to add a wizard." The boy left grumbling, but he paid. Teddy, Rafael soon learned, ran the busiest card exchange in his school, and (d)[he] carried every price in his head, though he had never once traded away his own silver dragon.

(D)
At the following session, Rafael left the worksheet in his bag. Instead, he spread a dozen of Teddy's cards across the table and began asking questions. If one dragon was worth three knights, what fraction of a dragon was a single knight? If Teddy traded away a quarter of his twelve knights, how many would he have left? Teddy answered each question before Rafael had finished asking it, rolling (e)[his] eyes at how easy they were. Only when Rafael wrote the same problems on paper, with numbers instead of cards, did Teddy fall silent. "Wait," he said slowly. "This is the stuff on the worksheet."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 수학을 싫어하는 Teddy를 처음 만난 뒤, 다음 주(The next week) 카드 교환을 하는 Teddy를 발견하는 (C)가 와요. 이어서 그다음 수업(At the following session)에 카드로 분수 문제를 내는 (D)가 오고, 3주 뒤 B+ 시험지를 받고 카드 덕분이라고 말하는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Okafor,

My name is Hannah Byrne, and I teach biology to second-year students at Westfield High School. This semester our class has been studying soil, pollination, and the life cycles of crops, but most of what my students know about farming comes from textbooks and short videos. Several of them have told me they have never seen a vegetable growing in the ground. A colleague mentioned that your family farm on Millbrook Lane welcomed a group of younger children last year, and that the visit left a lasting impression on them. I was wondering whether you might be willing to host my class of twenty-four students for a morning in early May. We would follow any safety rules you set, bring our own lunches, and of course be happy to help with simple tasks such as weeding or planting if that would be useful to you. Please let me know whether such a visit might be possible and which dates would suit you best.

Warm regards,
Hannah Byrne
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 농장에서 쓸 학교 텃밭 도구를 빌려 달라고 부탁하려고
지난해 어린이 방문에 대해 감사를 전하려고
학생들의 농장 견학을 받아 줄 수 있는지 문의하려고
생물 수업에 쓸 농작물 영상을 요청하려고
items.exp: 필자는 학생들이 실제 농작물을 본 적이 없다고 설명한 뒤, 5월 초에 24명의 학생이 농장을 방문할 수 있는지와 가능한 날짜를 묻고 있어요. 지난해 방문은 동료에게 들은 이야기일 뿐 감사 인사가 목적이 아니에요.

items.passage: Jiwoo had agreed to spend Saturday at her uncle's watch-repair shop only because her mother insisted. The shop was a narrow room that smelled of oil and old paper, and the only sound was the uneven ticking of dozens of clocks on the walls. For the first hour she sat on a stool by the window, scrolling through her phone and sighing every few minutes, wondering how anyone could spend a whole life in such a quiet place. Then her uncle called her over and handed her a magnifying lens. "Look," he said, lifting the back off an old pocket watch. Beneath the glass lay a tiny city of gears, each one turning the next, and a spring no thicker than a hair breathing in and out with every second. Jiwoo leaned closer. She asked what each part did, then asked again when she did not understand. Her uncle showed her how a single bent tooth on one wheel could make a watch lose ten minutes a day. By the time the shop closed, her phone lay forgotten on the stool, and she was already asking whether she could come back the following Saturday.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jiwoo의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음에는 억지로 와서 휴대폰만 보며 한숨을 쉬고 이런 조용한 곳에서 어떻게 평생을 보내나 생각했지만, 시계 속 톱니를 본 뒤 계속 질문하고 다음 주에도 오고 싶어 해요. 그래서 bored → fascinated가 알맞아요. 실망하거나 죄책감을 느끼는 장면은 없어요.

items.passage: On a clear night, the sky seems to present a single, shared moment: every star appears to shine at the same instant, side by side on the same dark surface. Yet this impression is misleading. Light travels at a finite speed, and the distances between us and the stars are so vast that their light takes years, centuries, or even many thousands of years to arrive. The faint point above the horizon may show a star as it was when the pyramids were built, while its neighbor in the sky shows another as it was only a decade ago. Some of the stars we admire may have already collapsed or exploded, and we will not learn of it until the news, carried by light, finally reaches us. To look up at the night sky, then, is to be [reading letters from writers long gone]: each message is genuine, but each describes a situation that may no longer exist, and no two were sent at the same time.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [reading letters from writers long gone]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: learning the ancient stories that people told about the stars
trying to predict the future positions of distant stars
observing many stars that all exist at the same moment
recognizing that most stars visible tonight have disappeared
receiving true information that reflects different points in the past
items.exp: 별빛은 저마다 다른 시간 동안 이동해 오므로, 밤하늘의 별들은 각기 다른 과거의 모습을 보여 줘요. 각 메시지는 진짜지만 지금은 존재하지 않을 수도 있는 상황을 서로 다른 시점에 담고 있다는 뜻이에요. 일부 별이 이미 사라졌을 수도 있다고 했을 뿐 대부분이 사라졌다고 하지 않았으므로 ④는 틀려요.

items.passage: Groups that make important decisions often value harmony, and members who raise objections may be seen as difficult or disloyal. Over time, people learn to keep their doubts to themselves, and a plan that no one fully trusts can move forward simply because no one wants to be the first to question it. One remedy is surprisingly simple: assign someone the formal role of arguing against the proposal. When dissent becomes a duty rather than a personal stance, it loses much of its social cost. The person playing critic is not attacking colleagues; they are doing the job the group asked them to do. Others, too, find it easier to voice reservations once the first objection has been made legitimate. Studies of teams using this approach suggest that their final decisions are not necessarily slower, but they are more likely to anticipate risks and to include backup plans. The point is not to create conflict for its own sake, but to make sure that disagreement which already exists is finally heard.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 집단의 결정은 구성원 간의 조화를 최우선으로 해야 한다.
반대 의견을 공식적인 역할로 두면 집단 결정의 질이 높아진다.
중요한 결정은 소수의 전문가에게 맡기는 것이 효율적이다.
반대 의견을 자주 내는 구성원은 집단의 결속을 해친다.
의도적인 갈등을 만들면 결정이 지나치게 느려진다.
items.exp: 반대하는 역할을 공식적으로 맡기면 반대 의견의 사회적 부담이 줄고, 위험을 예상하고 대비책을 세우는 더 나은 결정이 나온다는 것이 요지예요. 결정이 반드시 느려지는 것은 아니라고 했으므로 ⑤는 틀려요.

items.passage: Most people believe that bread goes stale because it dries out, but the main cause lies elsewhere. When dough is baked, the heat causes starch granules in the flour to absorb water and swell, losing their orderly internal structure. This disordered starch is what gives fresh bread its soft, springy texture. As the loaf cools and sits, however, the starch molecules gradually realign into tight, crystal-like arrangements, pushing water out of their structure and making the crumb firm and crumbly. Remarkably, this happens even when the bread is tightly wrapped and loses almost no moisture to the air. The process also explains two familiar kitchen observations. Bread stored in a refrigerator goes stale faster than bread kept at room temperature, because cool temperatures speed up the realignment of starch. And a stale loaf briefly reheated in an oven softens again, since the heat breaks the crystals apart once more, at least until the bread cools down.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the best method of wrapping bread to keep it moist
changes in starch structure as the real cause of stale bread
the role of water in making dough rise during baking
why refrigerators are the best place to store baked goods
differences between fresh bread and bread from factories
items.exp: 빵이 딱딱해지는 주된 원인은 수분 손실이 아니라 녹말 분자가 다시 결정처럼 배열되는 변화라는 내용이에요. 냉장 보관하면 오히려 더 빨리 굳는다고 했으므로 ④는 반대예요.

items.passage: Today we take it for granted that a serious book will end with an index, an alphabetical list of topics with the pages on which they appear. Yet for most of the history of writing, no such tool existed, and none was needed. Early books were scrolls, which had no fixed pages to point to, and readers were expected to move through a text from beginning to end, often memorizing large portions of it. The index became possible only after the bound book with numbered pages replaced the scroll, and it became useful only when a new kind of reader appeared. In the growing universities of medieval Europe, scholars and preachers needed to find particular passages quickly, to compare authorities or to prepare a sermon on a given theme. For them, a book was less a journey to be completed than a store of material to be searched. The index answered that need, and in doing so it quietly encouraged a new way of reading, one that jumps directly to the relevant part rather than following the author's path.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Medieval Scholars Memorized Entire Books
The Index: A Tool That Changed How We Read
The Lost Habit of Reading from Beginning to End
Scrolls Versus Books: Which Lasted Longer?
How Universities Spread Literacy Across Europe
items.exp: 색인은 쪽 번호가 있는 책과 특정 부분을 빨리 찾으려는 새로운 독자가 등장하면서 생겨났고, 필요한 부분으로 곧장 가는 새로운 읽기 방식을 낳았다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. ③은 글의 일부만 다룬 제목이에요.

items.passage:
Harbor Lantern Kayak Tour 2027

Paddle through the calm waters of Gull Bay as the sun sets and the harbor lights come on! No experience is needed.

items.q: Harbor Lantern Kayak Tour 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 십 대 참가비에는 구명조끼 대여가 포함되지 않는다.
items.exp: 참가비에 카약, 노, 구명조끼가 포함되어 있다고 했으므로 ③이 안내문과 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 모두 안내문 내용과 같아요.

items.passage: The moon does not simply pull the ocean toward itself on one side of the Earth. If ①[it] did, there would be only one high tide each day, yet most coasts experience two. The explanation lies in the fact that the moon's gravity weakens with distance. Water on the side facing the moon ②[is pulled] more strongly than the Earth's center, while the Earth's center, in turn, is pulled more strongly than the water on the far side. As a result, the oceans bulge outward in two directions at once, and the planet rotates beneath both bulges, ③[producing] two high tides roughly twelve hours apart. The sun creates similar but smaller bulges. When sun and moon line up, their effects combine, and the difference between high and low water ④[becomes] unusually large. When they pull at right angles, the tides are much weaker. Local geography then shapes these patterns further, ⑤[what] is why some narrow bays see tides of more than ten meters.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 앞 절 전체를 받아 이유를 덧붙이는 자리이므로 what을 계속적 용법 관계대명사 which로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 the moon을 받는 대명사, ②는 물이 당겨지는 수동태, ③은 결과를 나타내는 분사구문, ④는 단수 주어 the difference에 맞는 동사라서 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support roughly a quarter of all marine species. Their richness depends on a delicate partnership. Inside the tissues of reef-building corals live tiny algae that ①[supply] the coral with most of its food through photosynthesis, while the coral provides the algae with shelter and nutrients. This arrangement works well within a narrow range of conditions. When water temperatures rise even one or two degrees above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership ②[breaks] down. The stressed coral expels its algae, and because the algae give coral much of its color, the animal turns pale, an event known as bleaching. Bleached coral is not yet dead, and if temperatures return to normal quickly, it can ③[recover] its algae. Prolonged heat, however, leaves it starving and ④[resistant] to disease. As marine heatwaves become more frequent, reefs have less time to recover between events, and scientists warn that repeated bleaching may ⑤[transform] once-colorful reefs into stretches of bare rock.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 오랜 고온이 산호를 굶주리게 한다는 흐름이므로 질병에도 약해진다는 뜻이 되어야 해요. 따라서 ④ resistant는 vulnerable 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: A joke that delights one audience may fall completely flat with another, even when everyone understands the words. The reason is that humor rarely lies in what is said; it lies in the gap between what is said and what the listener already expects. A punchline works by leading the mind down one path and then suddenly revealing that a second, unexpected meaning was hidden there all along. For this surprise to happen, the listener must already hold the first expectation firmly, and that expectation is built from knowledge about a particular workplace, a local politician, a famous film, or a habit everyone in the room recognizes. Without that background, the second meaning has nothing to collide with, and the joke becomes merely a strange statement. This is why humor is one of the hardest things to translate and why newcomers to a culture often report that understanding jokes is among the last skills they acquire. Laughter, in the end, is a sign of ___ understanding.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 유머는 듣는 사람이 이미 가진 기대와 배경지식에 달려 있으며, 그 배경이 없으면 농담이 통하지 않는다고 했어요. 따라서 웃음은 공유된 이해의 표시라는 shared가 알맞아요. 말 자체가 아니라 그 틈에 유머가 있다고 했으므로 literal은 반대예요.

items.passage: Feathers are so closely associated with flight that it is natural to assume they evolved for that purpose. The fossil record tells a different story. Simple, hair-like feathers appear on many small dinosaurs that could not possibly have flown, and more complex feathers seem to have served first for insulation, for display, or for shielding eggs in the nest. Only much later, in certain lineages, did feathers become shaped into the stiff, asymmetrical structures that make powered flight possible. Biologists use the term exaptation for a trait that comes to serve a function different from the one that originally favored it. The lesson extends well beyond birds. The small bones of the mammalian middle ear, which transmit sound, are descended from bones that once formed part of the jaw in ancestral animals. In each case, asking what a trait does today is a poor guide to its past, because ___. Evolution does not design toward goals; it reuses whatever happens to be available.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: every trait is gradually perfected for the role it first played
the fossil record rarely preserves soft tissues such as feathers
the function that keeps a trait useful now need not be the one that produced it
animals that lack flight cannot develop complex structures
biologists disagree about which traits should count as useful
items.exp: 깃털은 처음에 보온이나 과시용으로 생겼다가 나중에 비행에 쓰였고, 귀뼈도 원래 턱뼈였다고 했어요. 따라서 지금 형질을 쓸모 있게 하는 기능이 그 형질을 만들어 낸 기능일 필요는 없다는 ③이 알맞아요. ①은 형질이 처음 역할에 맞게 완성된다는 뜻이라 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: Open-plan offices were promoted as a way to break down walls between colleagues and encourage spontaneous conversation among people who might otherwise never meet. Several studies, however, have found that when companies remove private offices and cubicles, face-to-face interaction often decreases rather than increases. ① Surrounded by others and constantly visible, employees tend to protect their concentration by wearing headphones and avoiding eye contact. ② Many also shift their conversations to email and messaging apps, which feel more private than talking across a crowded room. ③ The very openness meant to bring people together thus pushes them into a kind of polite withdrawal. ④ Open layouts are also cheaper to build, since they fit more desks into the same floor area and require fewer interior walls. ⑤ This does not mean that walls are always better, but it suggests that people need some control over when they are available to others before they are willing to engage with them freely.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 개방형 사무실이 오히려 직접 대화를 줄이는 이유와 그 의미를 설명하는 글이에요. ④는 개방형 사무실의 건축 비용에 관한 내용이라 대화가 줄어든다는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
Limestone caves can stretch for kilometers beneath the ground, yet they are carved not by rushing rivers or grinding ice but by something far gentler: ordinary rainwater.

(A) Over thousands of years, this slow chemical attack widens the cracks into passages, and the passages into chambers large enough to hold a cathedral. The process can also run in reverse. Where water drips from a cave ceiling and loses its dissolved gas to the air, the rock it carried is deposited again, forming stalactites.

(B) Those formations grow at a pace of only a few centimeters per century, so a single broken tip can represent the work of many human lifetimes. For this reason, many caves now limit the number of visitors and forbid touching the walls.

(C) As rain falls through the air and seeps through soil, it absorbs carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid. When this slightly acidic water trickles into tiny cracks in limestone, it slowly dissolves the rock, carrying it away particle by particle.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 빗물이 동굴을 만든다는 주어진 글 뒤에, 빗물이 약산성이 되어 석회암을 녹인다는 (C)가 와요. 이 느린 화학 작용(this slow chemical attack)이 동굴을 넓히고 종유석을 만든다는 (A)가 이어지고, 그 생성물(Those formations)이 느리게 자라 보호가 필요하다는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Before an orchestra begins to play, the musicians perform a brief ritual that audiences often mistake for a warm-up. ( ① ) A single note, an A, sounds from the oboe, and the other instruments adjust their tuning to match it. ( ② ) The choice of the oboe is not arbitrary. Its tone is penetrating and rich in overtones, so it cuts clearly through the sound of string players testing their instruments, and its pitch is relatively stable once the reed is warm. ( ③ ) String instruments, by contrast, drift out of tune as their strings stretch and as the temperature of the hall changes under the stage lights. ( ④ ) The oboe, however, offers no such option. Because its pitch depends largely on the reed and the player's breath, it cannot be retuned as easily, so it makes sense for the rest of the orchestra to come to the oboe rather than the other way around. ( ⑤ ) The ritual, in other words, reflects a practical judgment about which instrument should serve as the reference for all the others.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Their players, however, can correct this drift easily by turning the pegs that tighten or loosen each string.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 Their players와 this drift는 ④ 앞 문장의 현악기와 음이 틀어지는 현상을 가리켜요. 또 ④ 뒤의 no such option은 주어진 문장의 '쉽게 조율을 바로잡는 방법'을 받으므로 ④에 들어가야 해요.

items.passage: When a medical treatment goes wrong, many hospitals have traditionally advised doctors to say as little as possible, fearing that any expression of regret would be used against them in court. Several hospitals that abandoned this approach have reported unexpected results. Under their new policies, doctors meet with patients and families soon after an error, explain clearly what happened, take responsibility, and describe the steps being taken to prevent a repeat. Rather than increasing legal claims, these programs were followed by fewer lawsuits and lower settlement costs. Interviews with patients help explain why. Many people who sue are not primarily seeking money; they are seeking answers and a sense that their suffering has been taken seriously. When those needs are met directly, the motive to turn to a lawyer weakens. Silence, by contrast, tends to be read as concealment, and it often transforms disappointment into anger that only a courtroom seems able to address.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Openly (A) ___ medical errors to patients tends to (B) ___ legal disputes, because it addresses patients' need for honesty and recognition.
items.exp: 오류 직후 무슨 일이 있었는지 설명하고 책임을 인정하자 소송과 합의 비용이 줄었다고 했으므로 (A)에는 admitting, (B)에는 reduce가 알맞아요. ⑤의 explaining은 (A)로 가능하지만 소송을 늘린다는 prolong은 글과 반대예요.

items.passage:
For years, websites have tried to make passwords stronger by imposing rules: at least eight characters, one capital letter, one number, one symbol, and a new password every ninety days. Each rule seems (a)[reasonable] on its own, since a longer and more varied password should be harder for an attacker to guess. The trouble is that these rules were written as if users would respond by choosing characters at random. Real people do no such thing.

Faced with a demand for a capital letter, most users simply capitalize the first letter of a familiar word; asked for a number and a symbol, they add "1!" to the end. When forced to change their password every few months, they make the (b)[largest] possible change, turning "Summer2026!" into "Autumn2026!" or adding one to the final digit. Attackers know these habits well, and the programs they use to guess passwords try such patterns first. The rules, in other words, produce passwords that look complex to a computer checking boxes but remain (c)[predictable] to anyone who understands human behavior. Worse, people who struggle to remember a growing collection of complicated passwords often write them down or reuse the same one across many sites, so that a single leak can (d)[expose] dozens of accounts.

Security experts have therefore begun to recommend a different approach. Instead of demanding a mix of symbols, many now advise long passphrases made of several unrelated words, which are both easier to remember and harder to guess. They also suggest changing a password only when there is evidence that it has been stolen, rather than on a fixed schedule. The lesson extends well beyond computers: a rule designed without considering how people actually behave can (e)[undermine] the very goal it was meant to serve.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Passphrases: An Old Idea That Nobody Uses
How Computers Measure the Strength of a Password
Changing Passwords Often: The Key to Online Safety
When Strict Password Rules Backfire: Designing for Real Users
items.exp: 복잡한 비밀번호 규칙은 사람들이 뻔한 방식으로 대응하기 때문에 오히려 예측하기 쉬운 비밀번호와 재사용을 낳고, 그래서 실제 사람의 행동을 고려한 방식이 필요하다는 내용이므로 ⑤가 알맞아요. ④는 글이 비판한 주기적 변경을 지지하는 반대 내용이에요.

Instead of demanding a mix of symbols, many now advise long passphrases made of several unrelated words, which are both easier to remember and harder to guess. They also suggest changing a password only when there is evidence that it has been stolen, rather than on a fixed schedule. The lesson extends well beyond computers: a rule designed without considering how people actually behave can (e)[undermine] the very goal it was meant to serve.
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 사용자들은 비밀번호를 바꾸라고 하면 Summer를 Autumn으로 바꾸거나 마지막 숫자에 1을 더하는 식으로 최소한만 바꾼다는 흐름이므로 (b) largest는 smallest로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
Leo had passed the narrow shop on Carver Street a hundred times without going in. Its window was clouded with dust, and the hand-painted sign, Abernathy Books, had faded almost to nothing. But his father's birthday was a week away, and Leo had an idea. His father often spoke of a small book of sea poems he had owned as a teenager and lost when the family moved. It had been out of print for decades. Inside, the shop smelled of paper and pipe smoke, and an old man with half-moon glasses looked up from behind a mountain of books. When Leo described the volume, (a)[he] frowned and shook his head.

(B)
"Not on the shelves," Mr. Abernathy said. "But I have a back room where books go to wait. Some have waited thirty years." He led Leo through a curtain into a space crowded with boxes stacked to the ceiling. For an hour they searched by the light of a single bulb, sneezing at the dust. Leo was about to give up when the old man pulled out a thin blue volume and held it up. (b)[He] was smiling for the first time.

(C)
Leo reached for his wallet, but Mr. Abernathy waved it away. "A book that finds its way home is not for sale," (c)[he] said. A week later, Leo watched his father unwrap the gift. (d)[He] went very still, then opened the cover and touched the faded handwriting with one finger. "Where on earth did you find this?" he whispered. The next Saturday, father and son walked together to Carver Street, and the old bookseller greeted them both like old friends.

(D)
It was the right title, but that was not what made Leo's heart race. On the first page, written in pencil in a careful, boyish hand, was a name: Thomas Reyes, his father's name, and beneath it an address in the town where his father had grown up. Leo stared at it, unable to speak. Mr. Abernathy leaned closer, read the name, and listened as Leo explained. Then (e)[the old man] nodded slowly. "Books travel," he said softly, "but sometimes they come back."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 책을 찾자 고개를 저은 주인이 뒷방으로 데려가 파란 책을 찾아내는 (B)가 오고, 그 책에 아버지의 이름이 적혀 있었다는 (D)가 이어져요. 주인이 돈을 받지 않고 아버지가 선물을 받는 (C)가 마지막이에요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Leo는 그 가게 앞을 여러 번 지나갔지만 들어간 적이 없었다.
Leo와 주인은 뒷방에서 한 시간 동안 책을 찾았다.
책의 첫 장에는 아버지의 이름이 연필로 적혀 있었다.
책에 적힌 주소는 Leo가 자란 동네의 것이었다.
items.exp: (D)에서 책에 적힌 주소는 아버지가 자란 동네의 것이라고 했어요. 따라서 Leo가 자란 동네라는 ⑤가 글의 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Lindqvist,

I live at 42 Corwin Street, directly across from the site where your company is building the new medical center, and I am writing on behalf of several neighbors as well as myself. We understand that the project will bring valuable services to our district, and we have no wish to delay it. However, for the past three weeks, heavy machinery has started operating at 6:30 every morning, including Saturdays. The city's guidelines permit construction noise only after 7:30 on weekdays and 9:00 on weekends. Many residents on this street are night-shift nurses and factory workers who sleep during the early morning, and several families have small children who are now waking well before dawn. We would be grateful if your crews could begin work no earlier than the times the guidelines allow. If an earlier start is truly unavoidable on particular days, advance notice would help us plan accordingly.

Respectfully,
Elena Barros
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 의료 센터 건설 계획에 대한 반대 의견을 밝히려고
공사 작업을 규정에 맞는 시간 이후에 시작해 달라고 요청하려고
야간 근무자를 위한 소음 방지 시설 설치를 건의하려고
주말 공사를 완전히 중단해 달라고 요구하려고
공사 일정에 관한 주민 설명회 개최를 제안하려고
items.exp: 매일 오전 6시 30분부터 중장비가 작동해 주민들이 잠을 설친다고 설명한 뒤, 규정이 허용하는 시간 이전에는 작업을 시작하지 말아 달라(begin work no earlier than the times the guidelines allow)고 요청하고 있어요. 그래서 ②가 알맞아요. 공사를 늦추고 싶지 않다고 했으므로 ①은 틀려요.

items.passage: Grandpa and I had spent the whole winter in his garage bringing the old bicycle back to life. It had belonged to him when he was my age, and when we pulled it out from behind a stack of boxes in November, it was little more than a rusted frame with two flat tires. Every Saturday we sanded, oiled, and replaced one part after another, and by March it gleamed under a fresh coat of deep green paint. The first warm Sunday of spring was supposed to be its big day. I wheeled it to the end of the driveway while Grandpa stood by the door with his camera, grinning as widely as I was. I pushed off, pedaled hard down the gentle slope, and felt the wind rush past my ears. Then, with a sharp metallic snap, the pedals suddenly spun freely under my feet. The chain lay in the road behind me, broken in two. I coasted to a stop and looked back at Grandpa, who slowly lowered his camera. All those months of work, and the ride had lasted less than a minute.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 할아버지와 겨울 내내 고친 자전거를 처음 타는 날 활짝 웃으며 신나게 출발했지만, 체인이 끊어져 1분도 안 되어 멈추고 말았어요. 그래서 excited → disappointed가 알맞아요. 처음에 긴장하거나 의심한 것이 아니므로 ②, ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: When something goes wrong in an organization, the instinctive response is to find out who was responsible and make sure it never happens again. The logic seems sound: if mistakes carry consequences, people will be more careful. Yet in practice, punishment rarely reduces errors; it mainly reduces the reporting of errors. Employees who fear blame learn to conceal small slips, quietly patch problems, and hope no one notices. The organization then loses precisely the information it most needs, such as early warnings that a procedure is confusing, a tool is poorly designed, or a deadline is unrealistic. Small, visible mistakes are cheap lessons; hidden ones accumulate until they surface as costly disasters. Leaders who genuinely want fewer failures must therefore make it safe, and even rewarding, to speak up. A manager who thanks an employee for admitting an error, and then fixes the system that made the error likely, is not being soft. She is buying, at a low price, knowledge that her competitors will eventually pay for in a crisis.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 조직은 실수를 처벌하기보다 보고를 장려하여 실수에 관한 정보를 얻어야 한다.
관리자는 실수가 생기면 책임 소재를 분명히 밝혀야 한다.
작은 실수라도 반복되면 엄격하게 제재해야 한다.
비현실적인 마감 기한은 업무 효율을 떨어뜨리므로 피해야 한다.
조직은 경쟁사의 위기 사례를 분석하여 교훈을 얻어야 한다.
items.exp: 처벌은 실수가 아니라 실수 보고를 줄일 뿐이므로, 리더는 실수를 말하는 것을 안전하고 보람 있게 만들어야 한다고 주장해요. 책임자를 찾는 것은 필자가 비판하는 본능적 반응이고, 마감 기한은 숨겨진 정보의 예시일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Poker players have a habit that outsiders find strange: after a hand, they rarely ask whether they won. They ask whether they played it well. The distinction matters because in any activity involving chance, a good decision can lead to a bad result, and a reckless one can be rewarded. A driver who speeds home without incident has not made a wise choice; he has merely been lucky. Yet in ordinary life we constantly evaluate choices by how they turned out. We praise the investor whose risky bet paid off and blame the doctor whose careful treatment failed, as though the outcome revealed the quality of the reasoning behind it. Over time, this habit teaches the wrong lessons. We repeat lucky mistakes and abandon sound strategies after a single unfortunate result. Learning from experience requires separating what we controlled from what we did not, and that means resisting the temptation of [judging the bet by the card that fell]. Only by examining the decision itself, including the information available and the alternatives considered, can we improve the next one.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [judging the bet by the card that fell]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: trusting experts' advice over one's own judgment
avoiding all risks in order to guarantee a good result
blaming others for mistakes we made ourselves
relying on past experience when facing a new situation
evaluating a choice by its chance-driven outcome rather than its reasoning
items.exp: bet은 우리가 통제한 결정, the card that fell은 운으로 정해진 결과를 가리켜요. 즉 결정의 질이 아니라 우연한 결과로 선택을 평가하는 것을 뜻해요. 위험을 피하라는 내용은 글에 없고, 필자는 결정 과정 자체를 살펴보라고 말해요.

items.passage: When a fire alarm sounds in an office building, one might expect people to head for the exits at once. Studies of real evacuations tell a different story. In many cases, occupants spend several minutes, sometimes far longer, doing things that seem puzzling in hindsight: saving files, finishing phone calls, gathering belongings, or simply looking around to see what others are doing. This delay is rarely a matter of panic or carelessness. Alarms are ambiguous signals; most people have experienced far more false alarms and drills than genuine emergencies, so the default interpretation is that nothing serious is happening. Before acting, people therefore seek confirmation, and the most readily available source is the behavior of those around them. If colleagues remain seated, each person reads their calm as evidence that there is no danger, while those same colleagues are drawing an identical conclusion in return. A group can thus reassure itself into inaction. For this reason, safety specialists argue that clear, specific information about the threat often does more to speed an evacuation than a louder alarm.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the psychological causes of panic during building fires
technical improvements that make fire alarms more reliable
why people often delay leaving buildings when alarms sound
the importance of regular fire drills in the workplace
how leaders should take charge during emergencies
items.exp: 경보가 울려도 사람들이 바로 대피하지 않고, 경보를 모호한 신호로 받아들여 주변 사람의 행동으로 확인하려다 서로를 안심시키며 늦어지는 이유를 설명하고 있어요. 지연은 공황 때문이 아니라고 했으므로 ①은 맞지 않고, 잦은 훈련은 오히려 경보를 가볍게 여기게 하는 배경으로 언급되었을 뿐이에요.

items.passage: In the crowded markets of medieval Europe, a buyer had few ways to judge the quality of a knife, a barrel, or a bolt of cloth before using it. Defects often appeared only weeks later, by which time the seller might have disappeared. Craft guilds addressed this problem in a way that resembles modern branding. Members were required to stamp their goods with a mark identifying both the guild and the individual maker. If a buyer discovered a flaw, the mark led directly back to its source, and the guild could fine the offender or even expel him. Because one member's shoddy work damaged the reputation of all, guilds had strong reasons to inspect products and enforce standards. The mark thus transformed an anonymous object into a promise backed by an entire community of craftsmen. Historians have often criticized guilds for restricting competition and keeping prices high, and those criticisms have merit. Yet the humble maker's mark reveals another side of the institution: it allowed strangers to trust one another in a world without warranties or consumer protection laws.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Guilds Kept Prices High in Medieval Markets
Stamped Promises: Guild Marks as an Early Basis of Trust
The Decline of Craftsmanship in Medieval Europe
Why Medieval Buyers Preferred Local Sellers
Competition Among Guilds and the Birth of Free Markets
items.exp: 길드의 제작자 표식이 익명의 물건을 공동체가 보증하는 약속으로 바꾸어 낯선 사람끼리도 믿고 거래하게 했다는 내용이에요. 가격을 높게 유지했다는 비판은 필자가 인정하되 글의 초점은 아니므로 ①은 오답이에요.

items.passage: Lucinda Farrow (1872–1949) was an Irish pharmacist who brought medicine to some of the most isolated villages in the west of Ireland. The daughter of a schoolteacher in County Galway, she was trained by her town's only chemist, who took her on as an apprentice after she had helped him through a winter epidemic. In 1898 she passed the national pharmacy examination, becoming one of the first women in the province to do so. Troubled that many farming families lived a full day's journey from any shop selling medicine, she converted a covered cart into a traveling dispensary in 1903 and drove it along a fixed route each month. For nearly thirty years she made the circuit in all weathers, accepting eggs or vegetables from families who could not pay. Her handwritten records of the illnesses she encountered were later used by public health officials to plan the region's first rural clinics. A replica of her cart now stands outside the county museum.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 겨울 전염병 때 약사를 도운 뒤 견습생이 되었다.
1903년부터 정해진 경로 없이 필요한 마을을 찾아다녔다.
그녀의 기록은 지역 최초의 농촌 진료소 계획에 쓰였다.
items.exp: 마차를 이동 약국으로 개조해 매달 정해진 경로를 따라 다녔다고 했으므로 ④가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 교사의 딸, 겨울 전염병 뒤 견습생, 1898년 시험 합격, 기록이 농촌 진료소 계획에 쓰인 것과 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: Medieval manuscripts were expensive objects, ①[copying] by hand onto prepared animal skin over months or even years. It is surprising, then, that so many of them contain images that seem to have nothing to do with the sacred texts they surround. In the margins of prayer books, knights fight giant snails, rabbits chase hunters, and monkeys play musical instruments ②[while] dressed as bishops. For a long time, scholars treated these drawings as idle doodles, the private jokes of bored scribes. More recent research suggests that many were planned as carefully as the main illustrations and ③[that] they served several purposes. Some helped readers find their place in a long text, ④[acting] as visual bookmarks that were easier to remember than page numbers, which many manuscripts lacked. Others commented on the text in a playful way, inviting the reader to consider its meaning from an unexpected angle. And some simply reflected the pleasure that wealthy owners took in possessing a book full of surprises. Whatever their purpose, these strange margins remind us that medieval readers did not always approach serious books with the unbroken solemnity we might expect, and that humor and devotion could share the same page ⑤[without] any sense of contradiction.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ①은 manuscripts가 손으로 '베껴 쓰인' 것이므로 수동 의미의 과거분사 copied가 되어야 해요. ②는 while (they were) dressed의 생략 구문, ③은 suggests의 두 번째 목적어절을 이끄는 that, ④는 분사구문, ⑤는 전치사 without으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: People tend to place a surprisingly high value on things they have helped create. In one series of studies, participants who assembled simple storage boxes themselves were willing to pay considerably more for them than for identical boxes that came ①[pre-assembled]. The effect appeared even when the self-built boxes were slightly crooked. Researchers suggest that labor ②[enhances] our sense of ownership: the time and energy we invest become part of the object's meaning, making it feel like an extension of ourselves. Importantly, the effect depends on completion. When participants were made to ③[dismantle] their creations or were stopped before finishing, the extra valuation largely disappeared. This helps explain why companies that give customers a small role in production, such as mixing their own cake batter or customizing a product online, often see greater ④[satisfaction] than those that deliver everything ready-made. However, the same tendency can mislead us. Because we ⑤[underestimate] what we have built, we may cling to flawed projects or ideas simply because they are ours, failing to notice that others see them far less generously.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 자기가 만든 것을 지나치게 높이 평가하기 때문에 결함 있는 계획에 매달린다는 흐름이므로 ⑤ underestimate는 overestimate(과대평가하다)로 바꿔야 해요. 완성하지 못하면 효과가 사라진다는 ③ dismantle과 고객 참여로 만족이 커진다는 ④는 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: When deaf children who share no common language are brought together, something remarkable often happens: a new sign language begins to form. The first generation typically communicates with a rich but inconsistent collection of gestures. Each signer may express the same idea differently, and the order of signs varies from one conversation to the next. The transformation comes when younger children enter the community. Exposed to this loose system, they do not simply copy it. Instead, they impose regularities that their older peers never used: consistent word order, markers that show who did what to whom, and ways of breaking a single complex movement into separate units that can be recombined. Within a few cohorts, the system acquires the structure linguists recognize as grammar. What makes these cases so striking is that the grammar is not taught by anyone; it appears to be ___ by the learners themselves. Language, in this view, is not merely passed down from one generation to the next but rebuilt and sharpened each time it moves through young minds.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 어린 학습자들이 윗세대가 쓰지 않던 규칙을 스스로 덧붙여 문법이 생겨난다는 내용이므로 created가 알맞아요. 문법은 누가 가르친 것도, 단순히 물려받은 것도 아니라고 했으므로 inherited는 반대이고, 구조가 더해지므로 simplified도 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Engineers and managers are trained to see redundancy as waste. A second pump that sits idle, a warehouse stocked beyond current demand, a hospital ward kept partly empty: each looks, on a balance sheet, like money doing nothing. In a stable world, eliminating such slack is a straightforward route to efficiency, and organizations that trim it aggressively often outperform their rivals for years. The difficulty is that efficiency and robustness are measured on different timescales. Efficiency is judged by average performance under expected conditions; robustness is revealed only in rare moments when conditions are anything but expected. A supply chain stripped down to a single supplier works beautifully until that supplier's factory floods. Ecosystems offer a useful comparison. A forest often contains several species that perform roughly the same role, such as fixing nitrogen or pollinating flowers. To an observer counting only present functions, the duplication seems unnecessary, yet when disease strikes one species, another quietly takes its place. In both cases, ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the most efficient systems turn out to be the best prepared for sudden shocks
what appears to be idle excess in normal times is what keeps the system working when shocks arrive
duplicated parts should be removed once their present function has been identified
stability depends on finding the single species or supplier that performs best
long-term planning matters less than responding quickly to current demand
items.exp: 평소에는 낭비처럼 보이는 여분의 펌프·창고·병상, 같은 역할을 하는 여러 종이 위기 때 시스템을 지탱한다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 효율과 견고함이 다르다는 글의 논지와 반대이고, ③④는 필자가 위험하다고 보는 여유 제거와 단일 공급처 의존을 지지해요.

items.passage: The films of the so-called silent era were rarely watched in silence. ① In large city theaters, orchestras of thirty or more musicians performed alongside the screen, while smaller cinemas relied on a single pianist or organist who often improvised to match the action. ② To help these musicians, publishers produced collections of short pieces sorted by mood, with headings such as 'chase,' 'storm,' or 'sad farewell,' that could be combined to fit almost any scene. ③ Some studios went further, sending detailed cue sheets or even complete scores along with their films so that audiences in different towns would hear roughly the same music. ④ The length of feature films also grew steadily during this period, from a single reel lasting a few minutes to programs of well over an hour. ⑤ When synchronized sound arrived in the late 1920s, thousands of theater musicians lost their jobs almost overnight, and a living tradition of performance largely disappeared. Ironically, the era we call silent was one of the most musically busy periods in the history of cinema.

items.passage:
Economists have long used the lighthouse as a textbook example of a public good. Its light benefits every ship that passes, and there is no practical way to prevent a captain who refuses to pay from seeing it.

(A) These fees worked because a ship's use of the port could be observed and charged, even if its use of the light could not. The lesson is not that public goods are a myth, but that clever institutions can sometimes attach payment to something that can be measured, making private provision possible after all.

(B) Because of this, the argument went, no private business could ever profit from building one. Lighthouses would therefore have to be provided by governments and funded through taxes, since voluntary payments would never cover the cost.

(C) Historical research, however, has complicated this neat story. In nineteenth-century Britain, many lighthouses were built and operated by private individuals, who collected fees from ships when they docked at nearby ports.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?

items.passage: In a nineteenth-century city apartment building, the floor on which people lived said a great deal about their social position. ( ① ) The most desirable apartments were on the second floor, high enough to escape the noise and dust of the street but low enough to be reached without effort. ( ② ) Each additional flight of stairs reduced the rent, so that the upper stories housed clerks, students, and struggling artists. ( ③ ) At the very top, under the roof, were small rooms for servants, cold in winter and stifling in summer. ( ④ ) A visitor climbing the staircase could therefore read the building almost like a social map, with wealth thinning out as the steps went on. ( ⑤ ) Once the climb to the top floor required no more effort than pressing a button, height came to mean light, quiet, and a view rather than exhaustion. Apartments on the upper floors began to command the highest prices, and the rooftop rooms once given to servants were transformed into the luxurious penthouses that now crown city towers. A single machine had quietly rearranged the social geography of the building.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The arrival of the elevator turned this order upside down.
items.exp: ④ 뒤까지는 층이 높을수록 가난한 사람이 산다는 '사회 지도'를 설명하고, ⑤ 뒤에는 버튼만 누르면 꼭대기에 오르게 되어 높은 층이 비싸졌다는 정반대 상황이 나와요. this order가 앞의 층별 질서를 가리키고, 엘리베이터 등장이 버튼을 누르는 내용을 이끌므로 ⑤가 알맞아요.

items.passage: When shoppers scan online reviews, they face a problem: anyone can write anything, and the reviewer is usually a stranger. How, then, do readers decide which opinions to take seriously? Studies of review platforms suggest that people rely heavily on particulars. A review stating that a backpack's left zipper jammed after two weeks of daily commuting is judged far more believable than one declaring simply that the backpack is terrible, even when both carry the same one-star rating. Mentions of particular circumstances, such as when the product was used, by whom, and for what purpose, signal that the writer actually had the experience being described. Interestingly, this preference holds for positive reviews as well: vague enthusiasm is discounted, while praise tied to precise observations is taken to heart. Readers seem to treat detail as evidence of genuine experience, and they reward it with their confidence, regardless of whether the opinion itself is favorable or harsh.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Readers of online reviews tend to (A) ___ a review more when it contains (B) ___ information about how the product was actually used.
items.exp: 지퍼가 2주 만에 고장 났다는 식의 구체적 세부 사항이 있는 리뷰를 더 믿는다고 했으므로 (A) credit(믿다), (B) concrete(구체적인)가 알맞아요. 막연한 열광은 오히려 낮게 평가되므로 general이나 emotional은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
On coral reefs, small fish called cleaner wrasses run what looks like a service station. Larger fish visit their cleaning stations and hold still while the wrasses pick parasites from their skin, gills, and even mouths. The arrangement seems to be a textbook case of mutual benefit: the client gets rid of pests, and the cleaner gets a meal. Closer observation, however, reveals a more (a)[harmonious] relationship. Cleaners actually prefer to eat the protective mucus that coats their clients' skin, which is more nutritious than parasites but costly for the client to lose. Each time a cleaner bites into mucus rather than removing a parasite, it is, in effect, cheating.

Clients are not defenseless against this. When bitten, a client often jolts, and it may chase the cleaner or simply swim off to another station, (b)[depriving] the cheater of future meals. More remarkably, cleaners appear to manage their (c)[reputations]. Researchers have found that cleaners behave more cooperatively when other potential clients are watching, as though aware that onlookers might choose to go elsewhere after witnessing bad service. They also treat clients differently according to the clients' options: fish that can easily switch to another station receive better service than those with access to only one. Predatory clients, which could respond to a bite by (d)[swallowing] the cleaner, are rarely cheated at all.

These findings suggest that cooperation in nature need not depend on pure goodwill. It can be (e)[sustained] by a balance of temptation and control, in which partners have both the ability to exploit and the power to punish exploitation. The reef, in this sense, resembles a marketplace in which honesty is less a virtue than a strategy shaped by the presence of competitors and witnesses.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Coral Reefs Depend on Cleaner Fish for Survival
Parasites: The Hidden Threat to Reef Fish
Honesty as Strategy: How Cleaner Fish Balance Cheating and Cooperation
Predators and Prey: A Never-Ending Battle on the Reef
Mucus: The Secret Ingredient of Fish Health
items.exp: 청소놀래기가 점액을 먹는 속임수의 유혹과, 고객의 처벌·평판 관리 사이에서 협력이 유지된다는 내용이므로 ③이 알맞아요. 기생충이나 포식자는 글의 일부 소재일 뿐 중심 내용이 아니에요.

items.passage:
(A)
Jonas had run the Harborview Marathon eleven times, but this year he was not racing for himself. As an official pacer, he would carry a small orange flag marked "4:00" and lead anyone who wanted to finish in under four hours. Pacing demanded discipline rather than speed: every kilometer had to be covered in almost exactly the same time, regardless of hills, wind, or how good (a)[he] felt. At the starting line, a lean, gray-haired man introduced himself as Samuel Okafor. He was seventy-one, he explained, and this would be his final marathon. Thirty years earlier he had broken four hours, and he hoped to do it once more before retiring his running shoes.

(B)
They crossed the finish line together as the clock turned to 3:59:41. Samuel's knees buckled, and Jonas caught him before he fell. Samuel's granddaughter slipped under the barrier to hug him, and (b)[he] laughed and wept at the same time, repeating that he had not felt so young in years. Later that afternoon, Clara found Jonas in the recovery tent and reported that most of the group had finished just under four hours. "You lost your flag," she said with a grin, "but I think you found a better job."

(C)
"Don't look at your watch," Jonas told Samuel. "Just follow my feet." He shortened his own stride to match Samuel's and talked him through each kilometer, pointing out the next water table, the next corner, the next small goal. When Samuel's breathing grew ragged, Jonas slowed them both for twenty seconds and then gradually built the pace back up. With two kilometers left, the race clock in the distance read 3:47. Samuel shook his head, convinced it was hopeless, but (c)[the younger man] refused to let him stop.

(D)
For thirty kilometers, Samuel stayed close to the orange flag. Then, on the long climb past the old shipyard, his stride began to shorten, and the gap between him and the group widened with every step. Jonas faced a dilemma. Dozens of runners were depending on him to hold a steady pace, yet he could not bear the thought of Samuel's last race slipping away. A woman running beside (d)[him], an experienced marathoner named Clara, noticed his backward glances. "Give me the flag," she said. "I know the pace. Go." After a moment's hesitation, Jonas handed it over and dropped back until (e)[he] was shoulder to shoulder with the old man.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Samuel을 처음 만난 뒤, 30킬로미터 이후 Samuel이 뒤처지자 Clara에게 깃발을 넘기는 (D)가 오고, 뒤로 물러나 Samuel 곁에서 달리며 격려하는 (C)가 이어져요. 마지막으로 함께 결승선을 통과하고 Clara가 결과를 전하는 (B)가 와요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Callahan,

My name is Robert Tan, and I have been a member of the Ashford Public Library for more than twenty years. Because I am blind, I rely on screen-reading software, which reads the text of a web page aloud to me. Until last month, I could reserve books and study rooms through the library's website without any difficulty. Since the website was redesigned in September, however, the reservation page has become almost impossible for me to use. Its buttons carry no text labels, so my software announces only the word "button," and the calendar for choosing a date cannot be operated with a keyboard at all. Several other members of our local association for the visually impaired have reported the same problem. I understand that launching a new website involves a great many changes, but I would be grateful if your team could make the reservation page compatible with screen readers as soon as possible. I would also be glad to help test any changes before they are released.

Sincerely,
Robert Tan
