choices: 예약 페이지를 화면 낭독 프로그램으로 쓸 수 있게 고쳐 달라고 요청하려고
items.exp: 웹사이트 개편 뒤 예약 페이지의 버튼에 이름이 없고 달력을 키보드로 조작할 수 없어 화면 낭독 프로그램을 쓰는 사람이 이용할 수 없다며, 서둘러 호환되게 고쳐 달라고 부탁하는 글이에요. 변경 사항 테스트를 돕겠다는 말은 덧붙인 제안일 뿐 목적이 아니에요.

items.passage: My uncle had promised that the sea would be calm, but twenty minutes after we left the harbor, the little fishing boat began to rise and fall like an elevator that could not decide where to stop. I gripped the rail with both hands. My stomach rolled with every wave, the smell of diesel and bait filled my nose, and I wondered why I had ever agreed to spend my only free Saturday out here. My uncle handed me a dry cracker and told me to keep my eyes on the horizon. I tried, though the gray line kept tilting. Then, just off the bow, the water broke open. A dark curved back slid out of the sea, then another, and another, until a whole group of dolphins was racing beside us, leaping so close that I could hear the puff of their breath. I forgot about the cracker. I forgot about my stomach. Leaning over the rail, I laughed out loud and shouted for my uncle to look, my hands no longer clutching but waving.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 배멀미로 난간을 붙잡고 왜 왔나 후회할 만큼 괴로워하다가, 돌고래 떼가 배 옆을 달리자 소리 내어 웃고 손을 흔들어요. 그래서 miserable → thrilled가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Beginners in almost any craft are handed rules. A new writer is told to avoid the passive voice; a chess novice learns never to move the same piece twice in the opening; a cooking student is taught exact measurements. These rules are not perfectly true. Skilled writers use the passive voice when it serves them, grandmasters break opening principles for good reasons, and experienced cooks adjust by taste rather than by teaspoon. Why, then, teach rules at all? Because a beginner lacks the judgment to recognize when an exception is justified. Without simple guidelines, the novice faces countless choices with no way to sort the sensible ones from the disastrous. The rules narrow the field and allow practice to begin. Over time, through repeated success and failure, the learner gradually absorbs the reasons behind them and develops a feel for the situations in which they no longer apply. Rules of this kind are best understood as [a ladder meant to be left behind]: indispensable for reaching a certain height, but an obstacle if one insists on standing on them forever.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a ladder meant to be left behind]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a temporary guide that learners rely on until their own judgment matures
a strict standard that experts must follow throughout their careers
a shortcut that allows beginners to skip years of practice
a set of errors that teachers deliberately introduce to confuse students
a tradition that prevents experts from developing new techniques
items.exp: 규칙은 판단력이 없는 초보자가 연습을 시작하게 돕지만, 실력이 쌓이면 벗어나야 할 것이라고 했어요. 그러니 판단력이 성숙할 때까지 의지하는 임시 안내라는 ①이 알맞아요. ②는 전문가도 규칙을 깬다는 내용과 반대이고, 연습을 건너뛴다는 ③은 글에 없어요.

items.passage: Mathematics classes reward exact answers, and students quickly learn that a result off by a single digit earns no credit. Yet much of the quantitative thinking that adults actually need involves no exact answer at all. How many people might attend a festival in the park? Roughly how much water does a household use in a year? Is a newspaper's claim that a city produces a million tons of trash a day even plausible? Questions like these call for estimation: breaking a problem into parts, making reasonable assumptions, and arriving at a figure that is approximately right. Such skill is not a weaker version of calculation but a distinct ability, one that lets people judge whether a number makes sense before trusting it and catch errors that a calculator would never flag. Students who can estimate are less easily fooled by impressive-sounding statistics and more confident in tackling unfamiliar problems. Schools that devote all their attention to precision therefore leave out a capacity that matters at least as much in everyday life.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 수학 교육은 계산의 정확성을 무엇보다 중시해야 한다.
어림하여 판단하는 능력은 정확한 계산만큼 중요하므로 학교에서 길러야 한다.
통계 수치를 믿기 전에 출처를 반드시 확인해야 한다.
낯선 문제는 여러 부분으로 나누어 접근해야 한다.
items.exp: 어른에게 필요한 수량적 사고는 대부분 정확한 답이 아닌 어림셈이며, 어림 능력은 숫자가 말이 되는지 판단하게 해 주므로 정확성만 가르치면 중요한 능력을 빠뜨린다는 글이에요. 그래서 ②가 요지로 알맞아요. ⑤는 어림하는 방법의 하나일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Travelers who cross certain mountain ranges often notice a startling change within a few dozen kilometers: one side is covered in dense forest, while the other is dry grassland or even desert. The difference is created by the mountains themselves. When moist air blowing in from the ocean meets a range, it is forced upward. As it rises, it expands and cools, and because cool air can hold less water vapor, the moisture condenses into clouds and falls as rain or snow on the windward slopes. By the time the air passes over the crest, much of its water has already been removed. Descending the far side, the air is compressed and warms, which makes it even drier, so it tends to absorb moisture from the land rather than deliver it. The result is a zone known as a rain shadow. Some of the driest places on Earth lie in such shadows, only a short distance from some of the wettest, and the pattern shapes everything from the crops farmers can grow to where cities have historically been built.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of oceans in producing violent mountain storms
how mountain ranges create sharply different rainfall on their two sides
why deserts gradually spread into neighboring forests
the effect of farming on rainfall in mountain valleys
reasons why cities are built on the windward side of mountains
items.exp: 습한 공기가 산을 넘으며 바람받이 쪽에 비를 뿌리고, 반대편은 건조해지는 비그늘 현상을 설명하는 글이므로 ②가 주제예요. ⑤는 글 끝에 덧붙인 영향의 한 예일 뿐이고, ③처럼 사막이 숲으로 번진다는 내용은 없어요.

items.passage: If the universe were infinite, unchanging, and filled evenly with stars, every line of sight would eventually end on the surface of a star, and the night sky should blaze as brightly as the sun. This puzzle troubled astronomers for centuries, because the sky is, of course, mostly dark. The solution came not from counting stars more carefully but from discovering facts about the universe itself. First, the universe has a finite age, roughly fourteen billion years. Light from very distant stars has simply not had enough time to reach us, so we see only a limited region of space no matter how far we look. Second, the universe is expanding, and this expansion stretches the light traveling across it. Light from extremely distant sources is shifted toward longer wavelengths, much of it beyond what human eyes can detect. The darkness between the stars, then, is not empty of meaning. It carries evidence that the cosmos had a beginning and has been growing ever since, a profound conclusion hidden in an observation anyone can make on a clear night.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: The Dark Night Sky as a Clue to the Universe's History
How Many Stars Can the Human Eye See?
Why Distant Stars Are Brighter Than We Think
Light Pollution: The Disappearing Night Sky
An Infinite Universe Filled with Unchanging Stars
items.exp: 밤하늘이 어두운 이유가 우주의 유한한 나이와 팽창 때문이며, 그 어둠이 우주에 시작이 있었다는 증거라는 내용이므로 ①이 알맞아요. ⑤는 글에서 틀린 것으로 드러난 가정이에요.

items.passage:
Harbor City Lantern Walk 2027

Celebrate the end of autumn with a guided evening walk along the old harbor, lit by hundreds of handmade paper lanterns.

• When: Saturday, November 13, 2027, 6:00 p.m. - 8:30 p.m.
• Where: Starting point at Pier 3 Plaza (the walk ends at Lighthouse Park)
• Fees: Adults $8, children under 12 free

Program
• 5:00 p.m. - 6:00 p.m.: Lantern-making workshop at Pier 3 Plaza (materials provided)
• 6:00 p.m.: Walk begins, led by local storytellers
• 8:00 p.m.: Live music at Lighthouse Park

Notes
• Registration is required and can be completed only on our website by November 6.
• The event will be postponed to November 14 in case of heavy rain.
• Pets are not allowed on the route.
items.q: Harbor City Lantern Walk 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: Pier 3 Plaza에서 출발하여 Lighthouse Park에서 끝난다.
등불 만들기 재료는 참가자가 직접 준비해야 한다.
items.exp: 등불 만들기 워크숍은 재료가 제공된다(materials provided)고 했으므로 ③이 안내문과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 출발·도착 장소, 어린이 무료, 웹사이트 등록, 폭우 시 연기 안내와 일치해요.

items.passage: The great Gothic cathedrals of medieval Europe seem to defy the limits of stone. Their walls rise to astonishing heights and ①[are pierced] by enormous windows of stained glass, yet they have stood for centuries. The secret lies largely outside the buildings. A tall stone vault pushes not only downward but also outward, and earlier builders had resisted this sideways force with thick walls ②[that] left little room for windows. Gothic architects found a different solution: the flying buttress, an arched support that stands apart from the wall and carries the outward push down to a heavy pier on the ground. Because the buttresses ③[took] over much of the work once done by solid masonry, the walls themselves could become thinner and more open. Light poured into interiors that had previously been dim, ④[transforming] the experience of worship. The builders achieved all this without mathematical theories of structure. They relied instead on rules of proportion passed down through generations of masons and on bold experiments, some of ⑤[them] ended in collapse.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤는 두 절을 잇는 접속사가 없으므로 대명사 them이 아니라 관계대명사 which를 써서 some of which ended in collapse가 되어야 해요. ①은 벽이 뚫린 수동 관계, ②는 thick walls를 꾸미는 관계대명사, ③은 과거 시제 동사, ④는 결과의 분사구문으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: In parts of Scandinavia, harbors built a few centuries ago now stand some distance from the water, and stone rings once used to tie up boats can be found in fields. The sea has not simply ①[retreated]; the land itself is rising. During the last ice age, ice sheets up to three kilometers thick pressed down on the region, pushing the Earth's crust into the softer, slowly flowing rock beneath it. When the ice melted roughly ten thousand years ago, that enormous weight was ②[removed], and the crust began to spring back. Because the rock below behaves like an extremely thick fluid, the recovery is ③[gradual]: in some places the ground still rises by nearly a centimeter each year. Over a human lifetime this ④[reverses] into more than half a meter, enough to turn shallow bays into meadows and to force coastal towns to extend their docks. Scientists use the rate of this rise to ⑤[estimate] how thick the vanished ice once was and how the deep interior of the planet responds to changing loads.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 해마다 조금씩 오른 높이가 평생 동안 쌓여 반 미터 이상이 된다는 흐름이므로 ④ reverses는 adds up 같은 말로 바꿔야 해요. 바다가 물러난 것만은 아니라는 ①, 무게가 사라졌다는 ②, 회복이 느리다는 ③, 얼음 두께를 추정한다는 ⑤는 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: When photography spread through Europe in the mid-nineteenth century, many painters feared for their livelihoods. For centuries, one of painting's central purposes had been to record how people, places, and events actually looked. Wealthy families commissioned portraits to preserve a likeness, and governments hired artists to document battles and ceremonies. A camera could now perform these tasks faster, more cheaply, and with a precision no brush could match. Yet the invention that seemed to threaten painting ended up liberating it. Freed from the obligation to reproduce appearances faithfully, artists began to explore what a camera could not capture: the play of light as the eye experiences it, the emotional force of exaggerated color, the structure of objects seen from several angles at once. Movements from Impressionism to Cubism can be understood partly as responses to this new situation. By taking over the duty of ___, photography pushed painting toward expression, interpretation, and experiment, opening paths that might otherwise have remained unexplored.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 카메라가 사람과 장소의 모습을 정확히 기록하는 일을 대신하자 화가들이 표현과 실험으로 나아갔다는 내용이므로 accurate depiction이 알맞아요. emotional expression은 사진이 오히려 회화 쪽으로 밀어 준 영역이라 반대예요.

items.passage: We tend to imagine memory as a kind of archive. An experience is recorded, filed away, and later retrieved, much as a document is pulled from a drawer, read, and returned unchanged. Research over the past few decades has made this picture increasingly difficult to defend. When a memory is recalled, it appears to enter a fragile state in which it must be stored again, and during this window it can be altered by whatever the person currently knows, feels, or is told. A witness who discusses an event with others may later remember details that only the others reported; a person who recalls a childhood scene while in a sad mood may store it again with a darker tone. Remarkably, the memories we revisit most often are therefore not necessarily the most accurate but sometimes the most revised, since each recollection offers a new opportunity for change. This does not mean that memory is worthless, only that its reliability cannot be judged by vividness or frequency of recall. In this sense, remembering is less like reading an old document than ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: storing a duplicate copy of the file in a safer place
forgetting events that happened long ago
rewriting it slightly each time it is opened
reading it aloud to an audience of strangers
preserving the original in its exact form
items.exp: 기억을 떠올릴 때마다 다시 저장되며 현재의 지식과 감정에 따라 바뀐다고 했으므로, 회상은 문서를 열 때마다 조금씩 고쳐 쓰는 일에 가깝다는 ③이 알맞아요. ⑤는 글이 비판하는 기록 보관소 비유이고, ①은 바뀌지 않는 복사본을 뜻해 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Endurance athletes have long traveled to the mountains to train, hoping that thin air will give them an edge at sea level. ① At high altitude, each breath delivers less oxygen, and the body responds over several weeks by producing more red blood cells to carry what oxygen is available. ② When the athletes return to lower elevations, this enlarged supply of red blood cells can, for a time, deliver more oxygen to working muscles. ③ Training hard at altitude, however, is difficult, because the lack of oxygen forces athletes to run or cycle more slowly than they would at home. ④ Mountain regions have also become popular destinations for tourists, who enjoy the scenery and the cool summer weather. ⑤ For this reason, many coaches now recommend a strategy known as "live high, train low," in which athletes sleep at altitude but descend to lower ground for their most intense workouts. In this way, they gain the blood-building benefits of thin air without sacrificing the quality of their training.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 고지대 훈련이 적혈구를 늘리는 원리와 그 한계를 보완하는 전략을 설명하는 글인데, ④는 산악 지역이 관광지로 인기라는 내용이라 흐름에서 벗어나요. ③의 훈련 강도 문제는 ⑤의 For this reason으로 이어지는 필요한 문장이에요.

items.passage:
Few kitchen tasks bring tears as reliably as chopping an onion. Cooks have tried everything from holding bread in their mouths to cutting under running water. The real reason is a chemical defense system that the plant keeps carefully divided until the moment it is damaged.

(A) Once released into the air, this gas drifts upward and reaches the surface of the eye. There it irritates nerve endings, and the eye responds by producing tears in an effort to wash the irritant away. Chilling the onion before cutting slows the evaporation and reduces the effect.

(B) Inside an intact onion, sulfur-containing compounds and the enzymes that act on them are stored in separate compartments of the cells. A knife blade ruptures these compartments, and the two substances mix for the first time.

(C) The reaction that follows produces a series of compounds, ending with a volatile gas that evaporates easily. Its purpose is to discourage animals from eating the bulb, but it affects human cooks just as well.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 '나뉘어 보관된 방어 체계'를 구체적으로 설명하며 칼이 칸막이를 터뜨린다는 (B)가 먼저 와요. 두 물질이 섞인 뒤의 반응(The reaction that follows)으로 기체가 생기는 (C)가 이어지고, 그 기체(this gas)가 눈에 닿는 (A)가 마지막이에요.

items.passage: Rates of nearsightedness among children have risen sharply in many parts of the world over the past half century. ( ① ) For years, the most common explanation was close work: children who spent long hours reading or staring at screens were thought to strain their eyes into a nearsighted shape. ( ② ) Close work does seem to play some role, but a series of studies has pointed to a stronger factor. ( ③ ) In large studies across several countries, children who spend more time outdoors are considerably less likely to become nearsighted, even if they also read a great deal. ( ④ ) Researchers believe that bright light stimulates the release of dopamine in the retina, which in turn slows the excessive lengthening of the eyeball that causes nearsightedness. ( ⑤ ) Based on these findings, several schools in East Asia have added outdoor class periods to the daily schedule, and early results suggest that the strategy has reduced the number of new cases.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The key appears to be not exercise or fresh air itself but light, since daylight outdoors is many times brighter than typical indoor lighting.
items.exp: ③ 뒤에서 야외 활동을 많이 하는 아이가 근시가 덜하다고 했고, ④ 뒤의 bright light가 망막에 작용한다는 설명은 '핵심은 빛'이라는 주어진 문장이 먼저 나와야 자연스러워요. 따라서 ④가 알맞아요.

items.passage: In a series of experiments, researchers showed participants the same painting or poem, telling some of them that the artist had spent only a few hours on it and others that it had taken several days. Although the works were identical, those who believed more time had been invested rated them as higher in quality, more valuable, and more enjoyable. The effect was strongest among people who knew little about art and therefore found it hard to judge the works on their own merits. When genuine expertise is lacking, it seems, people fall back on a simpler question: how hard did someone work on this? Effort thus becomes a stand-in for quality, a shortcut that often points in the right direction, since careful work does tend to produce better results, but one that can also mislead. A sketch completed in minutes by a master may be finer than a canvas labored over for months by a beginner, yet an untrained viewer, told only the hours involved, will often prefer the canvas. The same tendency appears well beyond the arts, wherever the worth of a product or a service is difficult to assess directly.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When people cannot easily (A) ___ the quality of a work on their own, they tend to rely on the (B) ___ they believe went into it as a substitute measure.
items.exp: 예술을 잘 몰라 작품을 스스로 판단(evaluate)하기 어려운 사람일수록 작품에 들인 시간, 즉 노력(labor)을 품질 대신 기준으로 삼는다고 했어요. 실험에서 바뀐 것은 작업 시간이었으므로 talent는 근거가 없고, express와 improve는 판단의 문제와 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
Why does a song we have heard a hundred times still move us? One influential answer is that musical pleasure arises from the interplay between expectation and its fulfillment or violation. As we listen, the brain continuously predicts what will come next, drawing on patterns absorbed from a lifetime of exposure to a particular musical culture. A chord progression that seems to be heading home creates a sense of tension that is (a)[resolved] when the final chord arrives. When the composer delays that arrival, or substitutes an unexpected chord, the tension is prolonged, and the eventual resolution feels all the more satisfying.

Brain imaging studies support this view. Researchers have observed that regions associated with reward become active not only at the emotional peak of a piece but also in the moments (b)[leading] up to it, as listeners anticipate what is coming. Pleasure, in other words, is built partly from prediction itself. This helps explain a puzzle: a familiar piece remains (c)[enjoyable] even when we know exactly what will happen. Our conscious knowledge of the music does not entirely shut down the automatic expectations formed by general musical patterns, so a deceptive chord can still produce a small thrill on the hundredth hearing.

The theory also accounts for why taste is shaped by culture. A listener raised on one musical tradition may find another tradition's music (d)[confusing] at first, not because it lacks structure but because its patterns do not match the listener's expectations. With repeated exposure, new patterns are learned, predictions become possible, and the music begins to reward attention. Music that is entirely predictable tends to bore us, while music that is wholly unpredictable tends to bewilder us. The richest listening experiences seem to occur somewhere in between, where expectation is (e)[abandoned] and then, at just the right moment, either confirmed or gently overturned.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Prediction and Pleasure: The Role of Expectation in Enjoying Music
Can Music Be Understood Across All Cultures?
The Power of Surprise: Why Unpredictable Music Is Best
How Composers Learn Their Musical Patterns
Brain Regions That Process Sound and Rhythm
items.exp: 음악의 즐거움이 예측과 그 충족·위반 사이의 상호 작용에서 나온다는 내용이므로 ①이 알맞아요. 완전히 예측 불가능한 음악은 당혹스럽다고 했으므로 ②는 글과 반대예요.

items.exp: 가장 풍부한 감상은 기대가 형성된 뒤 적절한 순간에 확인되거나 뒤집힐 때 일어난다는 흐름이므로 (e) abandoned는 built나 established 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요. 긴장이 해소되는 (a), 절정에 이르는 순간의 (b), 익숙해도 즐겁다는 (c), 처음엔 혼란스럽다는 (d)는 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Priya had spent four months preparing for the regional science fair. Her project asked whether a coating made from crushed eggshells could reduce the rate at which iron nails rusted in salt water. Every evening after school she checked twenty jars lined up on a shelf in the garage, photographing each nail and recording its weight. Her younger brother, Arun, often sat on the steps watching. He was only eight and thought the jars looked like a strange museum, and he asked so many questions that (a)[she] finally gave him a notebook of his own.

(B)
When the judges reached her table, Priya took a deep breath and told them everything: her hypothesis, the failed result, and the clue in Arun's notes. One judge, a chemist named Dr. Hollis, leaned closer to the photographs and asked whether (b)[the young scientist] had a plan to test the explanation. Priya described a second experiment in which each jar would sit at the same distance from the window and the heater, with a thermometer placed beside every row. Dr. Hollis smiled. "Most students hide a result like this," she said. "You've turned it into a better question."

(C)
Arun read the notes aloud. On the cloudy days, he had written, the jars near the window felt cold, while the ones by the heater felt warm. Priya stared at him and then at the shelf, slowly realizing what he meant. All of her coated nails had been placed near the heater, and the uncoated ones near the cold window. Temperature, not the coating, might explain her results. Though (c)[she] felt sick at the thought of presenting a flawed project, she rewrote her poster that night, adding a section titled "What Went Wrong and What I Learned."

(D)
Two weeks before the fair, the final measurements were in, and they were not what Priya had hoped. The coated nails had rusted just as quickly as the uncoated ones; a few had rusted even faster. After all those weeks of careful measurement, (d)[she] sat on the garage floor surrounded by charts, wondering whether she should change her topic entirely. Arun sat down beside her and opened his notebook. "I wrote down other things too," (e)[he] said quietly. "Like which jars felt warm."
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Priya가 실험을 하고 Arun이 공책을 받은 뒤, 결과가 실망스럽고 Arun이 다른 것도 적었다며 공책을 여는 (D)가 와요. Arun이 기록을 읽어 주고 Priya가 포스터를 고치는 (C)가 이어지고, 심사위원 앞에서 발표하는 (B)가 마지막이에요.

"Most students hide a result like this," she said. "You've turned it into a better question."

(C)
Arun read the notes aloud. On the cloudy days, he had written, the jars near the window felt cold, while the ones by the heater felt warm. Priya stared at him and then at the shelf, slowly realizing what he meant. All of her coated nails had been placed near the heater, and the uncoated ones near the cold window. Temperature, not the coating, might explain her results. Though (c)[she] felt sick at the thought of presenting a flawed project, she rewrote her poster that night, adding a section titled "What Went Wrong and What I Learned."

(D)
Two weeks before the fair, the final measurements were in, and they were not what Priya had hoped. The coated nails had rusted just as quickly as the uncoated ones; a few had rusted even faster. After all those weeks of careful measurement, (d)[she] sat on the garage floor surrounded by charts, wondering whether she should change her topic entirely. Arun sat down beside her and opened his notebook. "I wrote down other things too," (e)[he] said quietly. "Like which jars felt warm."
items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 가리키는 대상이 나머지 넷과 다른 것은?
items.exp: (e)는 공책을 열며 따뜻한 병에 대해 말한 동생 Arun을 가리키고, 나머지 (a), (b), (c), (d)는 모두 Priya를 가리켜요.

items.passage:
(A)
Priya had spent four months preparing for the regional science fair. Her project asked whether a coating made from crushed eggshells could reduce the rate at which iron nails rusted in salt water. Every evening after school she checked twenty jars lined up on a shelf in the garage, photographing each nail and recording its weight. Her younger brother, Arun, often sat on the steps watching. He was only eight and thought the jars looked like a strange museum, and he asked so many questions that (a)[she] finally gave him a notebook of his own.

(B)
When the judges reached her table, Priya took a deep breath and told them everything: her hypothesis, the failed result, and the clue in Arun's notes. One judge, a chemist named Dr. Hollis, leaned closer to the photographs and asked whether (b)[the young scientist] had a plan to test the explanation. Priya described a second experiment in which each jar would sit at the same distance from the window and the heater, with a thermometer placed beside every row. Dr. Hollis smiled. "Most students hide a result like this," she said. "You've turned it into a better question."

(C)
Arun read the notes aloud. On the cloudy days, he had written, the jars near the window felt cold, while the ones by the heater felt warm. Priya stared at him and then at the shelf, slowly realizing what he meant. All of her coated nails had been placed near the heater, and the uncoated ones near the cold window. Temperature, not the coating, might explain her results. Though (c)[she] felt sick at the thought of presenting a flawed project, she rewrote her poster that night, adding a section titled "What Went Wrong and What I Learned."

(D)
Two weeks before the fair, the final measurements were in, and they were not what Priya had hoped. The coated nails had rusted just as quickly as the uncoated ones; a few had rusted even faster. After all those weeks of careful measurement, (d)[she] sat on the garage floor surrounded by charts, wondering whether she should change her topic entirely. Arun sat down beside her and opened his notebook. "I wrote down other things too," (e)[he] said quietly. "Like which jars felt warm."
items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Priya는 같은 거리에 병을 두는 두 번째 실험을 설명했다.
Priya는 코팅한 못을 모두 창문 근처에 두었다.
Arun은 일부 병이 따뜻하게 느껴졌다고 적어 두었다.
items.exp: 코팅한 못은 모두 난로 근처에, 코팅하지 않은 못은 차가운 창문 근처에 두었다고 했으므로 ④가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 (A), (B), (D)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Whitfield,

On behalf of the English department at Carlton High School, I would like to thank you again for agreeing to visit our school and speak to our students about your novel The Salt Road, which all of our eleventh graders have read this semester. The students have prepared their questions and are very much looking forward to meeting you. Unfortunately, I must now ask a favor. The date we agreed on, Friday, May 14, has just been chosen by the district for a statewide practice exam, and our eleventh graders will be required to spend the entire day in testing rooms. Rather than cancel a visit that means so much to them, we would be grateful if you could come one week later, on Friday, May 21, at the same time. If that date is not convenient, please let me know which days would suit you, and we will gladly arrange our schedule around yours. I apologize for the inconvenience and truly appreciate your understanding.

Sincerely,
Daniel Ortiz
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 작가 초청 강연에 참석해 준 것에 감사하려고
작가의 학교 방문 날짜를 한 주 뒤로 바꿔 달라고 요청하려고
학생들이 준비한 질문 목록을 미리 보내려고
작가의 소설을 수업 교재로 쓰도록 허락을 구하려고
items.exp: 약속한 5월 14일에 모의시험이 잡혀 학생들이 하루 종일 시험을 봐야 하니, 한 주 뒤인 5월 21일에 와 달라고 부탁하는 편지예요. 모의시험 일정은 날짜를 바꿔야 하는 이유일 뿐 글의 목적이 아니므로 ④는 오답이에요.

items.passage: For two years I had followed Mr. Albrecht from house to house, carrying his tool case and watching his hands as he turned the pins and listened. That Thursday, he called me from his bed with a fever. "The grand piano in the Linden School concert hall must be tuned by four," he said. "You'll go alone." I arrived an hour early, my mouth dry. The hall was enormous and silent, and the piano looked less like an instrument than an examination waiting for me to fail it. When I struck the first A, the note wavered, and my hand trembled so badly that I nearly let the tuning hammer slip from the pin. I closed my eyes and recalled what he always told me: listen to the beating between the notes, not to the beating of your own heart. Slowly, string by string, the wavering faded into a clean, steady tone. At four o'clock the young pianist sat down, played a few bars, and looked up with a quiet nod. Walking out into the afternoon light, I felt, for the first time, that the tool case in my hand was truly my own.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 처음 혼자 피아노 조율을 맡은 I는 입이 마르고 손이 떨릴 정도로 불안했어요. 하지만 스승의 조언을 떠올려 조율을 마치고 피아니스트의 인정을 받은 뒤 공구 가방이 진정한 자신의 것이라고 느꼈으므로 ④가 알맞아요. 처음부터 자랑스러웠던 것이 아니므로 ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Modern city planning tends to assign a purpose to every square meter. A plaza is designed for outdoor dining, a strip of grass for dog walking, a corner for bicycle parking, each with its own furniture, signs, and rules. The result is efficient and orderly, but something valuable is lost. Some of the liveliest uses of urban space have always appeared where no one planned them: teenagers practicing dance moves on an empty loading dock, neighbors setting up a weekend market on a vacant lot, children inventing games on a patch of ground that belongs to no particular activity. Such spaces work precisely because they do not tell people what to do. They invite residents to shape the city rather than simply consume it, and they allow new needs to be met before any official has noticed them. Planners should therefore resist the urge to fill every gap. Leaving some places open, undefined, and slightly rough is not a failure of design but a deliberate choice that keeps a city adaptable and alive.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 도시에 특정 용도가 정해지지 않은 여유 공간을 남겨 두어야 한다.
공공 공간은 이용 목적에 맞게 세밀하게 설계해야 한다.
도시 개발 과정에서 주민 의견 수렴 절차를 강화해야 한다.
방치된 공터는 안전을 위해 신속히 녹지로 조성해야 한다.
청소년을 위한 전용 문화 공간을 도시 곳곳에 마련해야 한다.
items.exp: Planners should therefore resist the urge to fill every gap 이하에서 용도가 정해지지 않은 공간을 일부러 남겨 두는 것이 도시를 살아 있게 한다고 주장해요. ②는 필자가 비판하는 방식이고, ⑤는 예시 일부만 확대한 내용이에요.

items.passage: Histories of technology usually tell the story of invention as a series of lonely breakthroughs, each credited to a single brilliant mind. Yet the record is crowded with cases in which two or more people, working independently and often unaware of one another, arrived at nearly the same device or idea within a few years or even months. The telephone, calculus, and the theory of evolution by natural selection all have more than one claimant. Such coincidences become less mysterious once we notice what each inventor depended on: materials that had recently become cheap, instruments that had only just been refined, and problems that a whole generation was discussing at once. An idea that would have been unthinkable fifty years earlier becomes, at a particular moment, the next obvious step for anyone standing in the right place. In that sense, the inventor does not so much break a passage through a solid wall as walk through a door that [the times had already left ajar]. Genius still matters, but it decides who reaches the door first, not whether the door exists.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the times had already left ajar]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: geniuses can see possibilities that remain hidden from everyone else
inventors often copy the unpublished work of their rivals
the conditions needed for the invention were already in place
most inventions are discovered by accident rather than by design
new devices are accepted only after old ones have stopped working
items.exp: 값싸진 재료, 막 개선된 도구, 한 세대가 함께 고민하던 문제 덕분에 어떤 발명이 '다음 단계'가 되었다고 했으므로, 시대가 이미 발명의 조건을 갖춰 두었다는 뜻이에요. ①은 천재가 남이 못 보는 것을 본다는 통념으로 글의 주장과 반대이고, ②는 서로 모른 채 독립적으로 발명했다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Many animals survive the winter by storing food in autumn, and some of them do so in a surprisingly scattered way. Instead of keeping all their acorns or pine seeds in one place, jays and squirrels bury them one or a few at a time in hundreds or even thousands of separate spots across the forest floor. This strategy protects the store from thieves, since no single discovery can wipe it out. It also has a consequence the animals never intend. However good their memory, hoarders fail to recover a portion of what they hide, either because they forget a site, find enough food elsewhere, or die before spring. The forgotten seeds are already planted at just the right depth, often far from the parent tree and away from its shade. For several species of oak and pine, these abandoned stores are the main way new trees become established. In a sense, the forest depends on the imperfect memory of its smallest residents, turning their private losses into its own future.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: methods squirrels use to locate buried food in winter
competition between birds and rodents over limited seeds
reasons trees produce large seed crops only in some years
risks that hoarding animals pose to young forests
the unintended contribution of forgetful hoarders to forest renewal
items.exp: 흩어 저장하는 동물이 일부 씨앗을 되찾지 못하면, 그 씨앗이 알맞은 깊이에 심겨 숲이 새로 자라는 주요 경로가 된다는 내용이에요. ①은 기억을 언급한 일부에 그치고, ④는 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: For online shoppers, free returns have become an expected part of the deal. A customer can order three sizes of the same jacket, keep the one that fits, and send the others back at no apparent cost. Yet the word "free" hides a long chain of expenses. Each returned item must be shipped, inspected, cleaned, repackaged, and entered back into inventory, and this handling often costs more than the item's profit margin. Clothing that has gone out of season may never be sold at full price again, and a significant share of returns is simply thrown away or sent to landfills because processing it is not worth the effort. The trucks carrying returned parcels also add to traffic and carbon emissions. Retailers do not absorb these costs out of generosity; they spread them across all their prices, so that customers who rarely return anything help pay for those who return a great deal. A service that seems to cost nothing is, in reality, paid for by everyone, including the environment.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Online Shopping: Why Prices Keep Falling
How Returns Make Customers More Loyal
Smart Packaging That Cuts Shipping Costs
Why Stores Are Refusing to Accept Returns
items.exp: 무료 반품 뒤에 운송·검수·폐기·탄소 배출 같은 비용이 숨어 있고, 결국 모든 소비자와 환경이 그 값을 치른다는 내용이므로 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 가격이 오히려 반품 비용을 떠안는다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Ingrid Solberg (1884–1957) was a Norwegian engineer known for her work on lifeboat design. Born in a small fishing village near Bergen, she grew up watching boats leave the harbor in all kinds of weather. When she was twelve, her father, a fisherman, was lost at sea, and she became determined to make small boats safer. Because few engineering schools admitted women at the time, she taught herself mathematics and later worked as a draftsman at a shipyard in Trondheim. In 1912, she designed a lifeboat with sealed air chambers along its sides, which allowed it to turn itself upright after capsizing. Shipping companies were at first unwilling to adopt it because of its high cost, but after one of her boats saved the entire crew of a cargo ship in 1921, orders increased rapidly. Solberg never patented the design, saying that a safer boat should belong to everyone. She spent her later years teaching navigation to young fishermen.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 어린 시절 항구에서 배들이 떠나는 것을 보며 자랐다.
열두 살 때 어부였던 아버지를 바다에서 잃었다.
그녀가 설계한 구명보트는 처음부터 해운 회사들에게 널리 채택되었다.
자신의 설계에 대해 특허를 내지 않았다.
items.exp: 해운 회사들은 처음에 높은 비용 때문에 채택을 꺼렸고, 1921년 화물선 선원을 구한 뒤에야 주문이 늘었어요. 따라서 처음부터 널리 채택되었다는 ④가 일치하지 않아요.

items.passage: In the 1870s, the most fashionable bicycle in Europe had a front wheel that could be taller than a grown man. Because the pedals were attached directly to that wheel, a larger wheel ①[meant] a greater distance covered with each turn of the pedals, and speed-loving riders demanded ever bigger ones. The design, however, placed the rider high above the ground and almost directly over the front axle, so that a stone or a sudden stop could throw him headfirst over the handlebars. Such falls were common enough ②[to earn] their own nickname, "taking a header." Young men who enjoyed the risk ③[considering] the machine a test of courage, but older people and most women, whose long skirts made mounting nearly impossible, were largely excluded. The solution came in the 1880s with the so-called safety bicycle, ④[whose] two wheels were of similar size and whose rear wheel was driven by a chain. Gearing now did the work that sheer wheel size had done before, and riders could keep their feet close to the ground. Within a decade, cycling had become a pastime open to millions, ⑤[changing] how ordinary people traveled to work and to the countryside.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③은 주어 Young men who enjoyed the risk 뒤에 오는 문장의 본동사 자리이므로 considering이 아니라 considered로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 주어 a larger wheel의 동사, ②는 enough to부정사, ④는 the safety bicycle을 받는 소유격 관계대명사, ⑤는 결과를 나타내는 분사구문이라 맞아요.

items.passage: When we think about events that are far away in time, we tend to picture them in abstract terms, focusing on why we would do something rather than how. A trip planned for next year is about "relaxing" or "seeing new places"; the same trip next week is about packing, tickets, and taxis. This shift helps explain a familiar pattern. Commitments made for the distant future feel ①[attractive] because we judge them by their broad value, while the practical difficulties remain ②[invisible]. As the date approaches, those details come into sharp focus, and we often ③[regret] promises we made so easily months earlier. The same principle can be turned to our advantage. When facing a difficult decision about the near future, deliberately imagining it from a distance, as if advising a friend or looking back from a year later, can ④[loosen] the grip of immediate worries and bring our deeper goals back into view. Conversely, a plan for the distant future becomes more realistic when we ⑤[ignore] its concrete steps from the start.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 먼 미래의 계획은 추상적으로만 생각해서 비현실적이 되기 쉬우므로, 처음부터 구체적인 단계를 따져 볼 때 더 현실적이 돼요. 따라서 ⑤ ignore는 specify나 consider 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: When hiring managers explain why they chose one candidate over another, a phrase they often reach for is "cultural fit." The idea sounds reasonable: a new employee who shares a team's values is likely to cooperate smoothly and to stay longer. In practice, however, fit is rarely measured against any stated set of values. Interviewers tend instead to judge it by whether a candidate shares their hobbies, their sense of humor, or their educational background, so that fit comes to mean little more than resemblance to the people already in the room. An organization that hires this way gradually loses the variety of perspectives that helps it notice its own errors and imagine alternatives. Teams of similar people feel comfortable, but that comfort can mislead; research on group decision-making indicates that diverse groups, though they experience more friction, examine evidence more carefully because their members cannot simply assume agreement. A company that rewards fit too heavily may thus purchase short-term harmony at the cost of long-term ___, ending up with a workforce that agrees easily precisely because it sees the world in the same way.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 문화적 적합성으로 비슷한 사람만 뽑으면 실수를 알아차리고 대안을 상상하게 해 주는 다양한 관점을 잃는다고 했어요. 따라서 단기적 화합을 얻는 대신 장기적인 적응력(adaptability)을 잃는다는 것이 알맞아요. 비슷한 사람끼리는 오히려 결속력이 강해지므로 ③ cohesion은 잃는 것이 아니에요.

items.passage: How do we know that a thermometer measures temperature correctly? The question sounds trivial until one tries to answer it. Instrument makers in the eighteenth century filled their tubes with mercury, alcohol, or air, and marked the freezing and boiling points of water as fixed reference points. Between those points, however, thermometers using different fluids disagreed, because each fluid expands at a slightly different rate as it warms. To decide which fluid expanded uniformly, one would need to measure its expansion against true temperature, which is exactly what a reliable thermometer was supposed to provide. Investigators were caught in a circle: the standard could be checked only with the very thing it was meant to establish. They escaped it not by finding some vantage point outside measurement, but by ___. In the mid-nineteenth century, physicists built air thermometers of varied construction and compared their readings across a wide range of conditions; the type whose readings stayed most consistent with one another was accepted as the standard. Reliability was not read directly off nature; it was built up step by step.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: trusting the instrument that produced the most dramatic readings
returning to the human sense of warmth and cold as the final judge
defining temperature as whatever the mercury thermometer happened to show
demanding that instruments built in different ways agree with one another
abandoning fixed points and relying on a single master instrument
items.exp: 빈칸 뒤에서 구조가 다른 공기 온도계들을 여러 조건에서 비교해 서로 가장 일치하는 것을 표준으로 삼았다고 했으므로, 다르게 만든 기구들이 서로 일치하기를 요구했다는 ④가 알맞아요. ③은 임의로 하나를 기준으로 정한 것이라 순환을 벗어나는 방법이 아니고, ⑤는 여러 기구를 비교했다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: In many cultures, meals are served on shared plates placed at the center of the table rather than in individual portions. This custom is often explained as a matter of convenience or economy, but it may serve a deeper social purpose. ① Eating this way requires constant small acts of coordination: diners must notice what others have taken, leave enough for latecomers, and offer the best pieces to elders or guests. ② Dishes served this way also tend to cool quickly, so cooks often choose recipes that still taste good at room temperature. ③ Through these quiet negotiations, people practice consideration for one another without saying a word. ④ Researchers studying workplace teams have even found that colleagues who eat from shared dishes cooperate more smoothly in later tasks than those who eat separate meals. ⑤ Sharing food, it seems, is not only about nourishment but also about rehearsing the habits of trust that hold a group together.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 함께 나눠 먹는 식사가 배려와 협력, 신뢰를 연습하게 한다는 사회적 기능에 관한 글이에요. ②는 음식이 빨리 식어 요리법을 고른다는 조리상의 이야기라서 흐름에서 벗어나요. ③의 these quiet negotiations는 ①의 조율 행동을 가리키므로 ①과 ③은 자연스럽게 이어져요.

items.passage:
In medieval Europe, merchants traveling between distant towns faced a serious problem: how could they trade safely with strangers whom they might never meet again?

(A) The great trade fairs of the Champagne region in France offered one solution. Held in a fixed cycle of towns throughout the year, they gathered merchants from Italy, Flanders, and beyond under the protection of local counts, who guaranteed safe passage on the roads leading to them.

(B) Because of this, a good name became a kind of capital. A trader known for fair dealing could buy goods on credit and settle the debt at the next fair, and such promises gradually developed into written documents that allowed value to travel without heavy coins being carried.

(C) Yet safety on the road was only part of the answer. At the fairs themselves, special courts settled disputes within days, and a merchant found guilty of cheating could be barred from all future fairs, a punishment that cost far more than any single dishonest gain.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?

items.passage: Spoken language does not come with spaces between words. When adults talk, the sounds run together in a continuous stream, yet infants somehow learn to pick out individual words from it. ( ① ) One clue lies in the statistics of sound. ( ② ) Within a word, syllables tend to follow one another in a predictable way: in the word "baby," the syllable "ba" is very often followed by "by." Across word boundaries, however, the next syllable is much harder to predict, since "baby" can be followed by almost any word. ( ③ ) In one well-known experiment, researchers played eight-month-old infants a two-minute stream of invented syllables in which some syllables always occurred together while others met only by chance. ( ④ ) Afterward, the infants listened longer to sequences that crossed these chance boundaries than to the "words" they had heard, showing that they could tell the two apart. ( ⑤ ) Remarkably, this skill appears long before children understand what any word means, suggesting that the search for words begins with patterns rather than meanings.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

items.passage: Teachers often assume that the best way to learn problem solving is to solve problems. For beginners, however, this may not be true. A novice facing an unfamiliar problem has to search blindly among possible steps, and this search consumes so much mental capacity that little is left for noticing the underlying pattern. Studies have found that beginners who study fully worked-out examples, with solutions shown step by step, often perform better on later tests than those who spend the same time attempting problems on their own. The advantage, however, does not last. As learners gain experience, the worked examples become unnecessary; reading through steps they already understand wastes effort and can even interfere with their own thinking. For these more advanced students, independent problem solving produces greater gains. The same teaching method, then, can help or hinder depending on who receives it, which means that instruction should change as the learner changes.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Studying worked-out examples benefits learners who are (A) ___, but as their (B) ___ grows, solving problems on their own becomes more effective.
items.exp: 풀이 예제는 초보자(beginners, novice)에게 도움이 되지만, 경험이 쌓이면(As learners gain experience) 스스로 푸는 편이 더 효과적이라고 했어요. 그래서 (A)는 inexperienced, (B)는 expertise가 알맞아요. ⑤는 (A)가 반대예요.

items.passage:
In regions with distinct seasons, a tree adds one ring of new wood each year, and the width of that ring depends on the conditions of the growing season. A warm, wet year produces a broad ring; a year of drought or unusual cold leaves only a thin one. Because the weather varies from year to year across a whole region, trees growing in the same area record the (a)[same] sequence of wide and narrow rings, much like a barcode printed in wood.

This shared pattern allows researchers to do something remarkable. By taking a thin core from a living tree, they can count back from the outermost ring and assign an exact calendar year to every ring inside. They can then compare that sequence with the rings in the beams of an old house. Where the patterns (b)[match], the overlap reveals when the timber was cut, often to the very year. Those beams, in turn, can be matched with even older wood from ruins or from trees preserved in bogs, and so a continuous chronology is built backward, link by overlapping link, sometimes across thousands of years.

The method has transformed archaeology. Before it existed, the age of a wooden structure could usually be estimated only within a range of decades or centuries. Tree rings now allow historians to date a medieval roof, a Viking ship, or a painted wooden panel with a (c)[precision] that few written records can guarantee. They have also served to test other dating techniques: radiocarbon dates, which once contained hidden errors, have been corrected by (d)[ignoring] them against samples of known age taken from tree-ring chronologies.

Beyond dating, the rings preserve a record of past climate. Long runs of narrow rings reveal droughts that no one ever wrote down, and some of these (e)[coincide] with the abandonment of villages or the failure of harvests, offering clues to why communities flourished or declined.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Reading the Years: How Tree Rings Date the Past
Why Trees Grow Faster in Dry Years
Radiocarbon: The Only Clock Archaeologists Trust
Protecting Ancient Forests from Climate Change
The Viking Ship That Changed Archaeology
items.exp: 나이테의 넓고 좁은 패턴을 겹쳐 맞추어 목재의 연대를 해 단위로 알아내고 과거 기후까지 읽어 내는 방법을 설명한 글이에요. ②는 가뭄에 나이테가 좁아진다는 내용과 반대이고, ③은 오히려 방사성 탄소 연대가 나이테로 보정되었다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Emma had been looking forward to Saturday all week. For the first time, her mother had agreed to let her take Biscuit, her four-month-old puppy, to the park by herself. But as they crossed the little bridge over the stream, a delivery truck honked loudly behind them. Biscuit, terrified, jerked backward and slipped free of (a)[her] grip. Before Emma could even shout, the puppy had squeezed under a wooden fence and disappeared into the thick bushes along the water.

(B)
Mrs. Park's garden was full of late autumn flowers, and in the doorway of the shed sat Biscuit, wagging his tail as if nothing had happened. Emma ran to him and buried her face in his fur while he licked her ears. Watching them, Mrs. Park smiled and explained that (b)[she] had left out a bowl of water for the little stranger every night. Emma thanked her again and again. That weekend she came back with a box of homemade cookies, and Biscuit trotted proudly beside her on a brand-new, much stronger leash.

(C)
For over an hour Emma searched, calling Biscuit's name until her voice grew hoarse. She looked under every bench and behind every trash can in the park, but there was no sign of him. When she finally came home in tears, her mother held her for a long time and then suggested they make posters together. That evening they printed fifty copies with Biscuit's photo and their phone number, and Emma insisted on putting up every one (c)[herself], even though it was already getting dark and (d)[her] fingers were stiff with cold.

(D)
Two whole days passed without a single call. Emma could barely eat, and at night she left the back door open a crack, just in case Biscuit found his way home. On the third morning, the phone finally rang. A woman named Mrs. Park, who lived on the far side of the stream, said a small brown dog had been sleeping in her garden shed. "I think he's been eating my cat's food," she added with a laugh. Emma grabbed (e)[her] jacket and was out the door before her mother had even hung up.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 강아지를 잃어버린 (A) 뒤에는 공원을 찾아 헤매고 포스터를 붙이는 (C)가 와요. 이어서 이틀 동안 연락이 없다가 셋째 날 Mrs. Park의 전화를 받는 (D)가 오고, Mrs. Park의 정원에서 Biscuit을 다시 만나는 (B)로 끝나요.

Dear Residents of Hillcrest Apartments,

As many of you know, the building's annual fire safety inspection took place last Tuesday. While most of the results were satisfactory, the inspector raised a serious concern about the stairwells. On several floors, bicycles, strollers, and boxes have been left on the landings, and in some places they block nearly half of the passage. In an emergency, when the elevators cannot be used and the stairs may be filled with smoke, even a single bicycle could cause someone to fall or slow down everyone behind them. We have been given two weeks to correct the problem before a follow-up inspection. We therefore ask all residents to remove any personal belongings from the stairwells by Friday, March 19. Bicycles may be kept in the storage room next to the parking garage, which has recently been fitted with new racks. Thank you for helping us keep everyone in the building safe.

Sincerely,
David Kim
Building Manager

items.passage: Daniel checked the arrivals board for what felt like the hundredth time. His older brother, Chris, had been working overseas for three years, and today he was finally coming home. Daniel had arrived at the airport two hours early, holding a sign he had painted the night before. But the line next to Chris's flight number had just changed from "On Time" to "Delayed." Then, a few minutes later, it simply read "See Agent." Daniel's stomach tightened. He walked to the information desk, but the staff member only said that the plane had been diverted because of a storm and that no further details were available. Daniel sat down, his sign lying face down on his knees, and stared at the floor. Nearly an hour later, his phone buzzed. It was a message from Chris: "Landed safely in another city. Catching the next flight. See you tonight!" Daniel read it three times, laughed out loud, and turned his sign right side up again. He could hardly wait for the evening to come.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Daniel의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 형의 비행기가 지연되고 회항했다는 말만 듣고 걱정하던 Daniel이 안전하게 착륙했다는 메시지를 받고 크게 웃으며 저녁을 손꼽아 기다려요. 따라서 worried → delighted가 알맞아요. 처음부터 기대하던 마음은 있었지만 마지막이 후회가 아니므로 ③은 틀려요.

items.passage: We usually think of a photograph as a record of what was in front of the camera. It is just as much a record of what was not. Every time a photographer raises the camera, a decision is made about where the picture ends, and that edge does far more work than we notice. A picture of a smiling crowd at a festival may leave out the empty streets around it; a dramatic image of a lone tree may exclude the parking lot a few steps to the left. Nothing in the photograph is false, yet the viewer's understanding of the scene can be quietly reshaped. Because the cut is invisible, we rarely ask what lies beyond it. This is why careful viewers of news images, advertisements, and even travel photos learn to look not only at what is shown but at where the picture stops. In photography, [every frame is also a fence]: it draws our attention inward while keeping certain facts firmly outside.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [every frame is also a fence]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: photographs should be protected from unauthorized copying
outdoor scenes are harder to photograph than indoor ones
a photographer must physically approach the subject closely
viewers prefer images with clear borders and strong shapes
choosing what to include also means deciding what to shut out
items.exp: 사진의 가장자리를 정하는 결정이 무엇을 보여 줄지뿐 아니라 무엇을 바깥에 두고 보이지 않게 할지도 정한다는 뜻이에요. ①은 fence를 '보호'로만 읽은 오답이고, ④는 테두리의 시각적 선호를 말해 논지와 관계없어요.

items.passage: When a beach begins to wash away and the sea creeps toward roads and houses, the most natural response is to build a wall. A concrete seawall seems to draw a firm line that the ocean cannot cross, and for the property directly behind it, it often works for a time. Coastal geologists, however, have observed that such walls frequently hasten the loss of the very beach they were meant to protect. A sandy shore survives because it can move: storms carry sand offshore, calmer seasons bring it back, and the beach shifts landward or seaward as conditions change. A hard wall interrupts this exchange. Waves that strike it are reflected rather than absorbed, scouring sand from its base, and the beach in front narrows until it disappears. Neighboring stretches of coast, deprived of sand that once drifted along the shore, may begin to erode faster as well. For this reason, many communities are turning to approaches that work with the shoreline's mobility, such as restoring dunes, adding sand, or gradually moving buildings back from the water.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 해안 침식을 막으려면 방파제를 더 높고 튼튼하게 지어야 한다.
해변의 모래는 폭풍이 지나가면 저절로 원래 자리로 돌아온다.
해안을 고정하는 벽은 오히려 해변을 잃게 하므로 해안의 움직임을 살리는 방식이 낫다.
해안 지역의 건물은 개인보다 지방 정부가 관리해야 한다.
해안 침식은 대부분 인근 해안의 개발 때문에 일어난다.
items.exp: 콘크리트 방파제는 모래의 이동을 막고 파도를 반사해 오히려 해변을 사라지게 하므로, 사구 복원·모래 보충·건물 후퇴처럼 해안의 이동성을 살리는 방식이 낫다는 것이 요지예요. ①은 글이 비판하는 대응이고, ②는 벽이 없을 때의 자연 과정 일부일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: It is natural to assume that antibiotic resistance is a modern problem, created when doctors began prescribing penicillin and its successors in the twentieth century. Investigations of environments untouched by medicine tell a different story. Bacteria recovered from permafrost tens of thousands of years old, and from a sealed cave that had been isolated from the surface for millions of years, carry genes that protect them against many of the drugs used in hospitals today. The explanation lies in where most antibiotics came from in the first place. Many of these compounds were originally produced by soil microbes as weapons against their neighbors, and the neighbors, in turn, evolved defenses long before any human isolated the chemicals. What medicine did was not to invent resistance but to concentrate the pressure, spreading enormous quantities of these old weapons into hospitals and farms, where bacteria carrying ancient defenses had every advantage. Understanding this history helps explain why new antibiotics so often meet resistance surprisingly quickly.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of permafrost in preserving ancient diseases
the deep natural origins of antibiotic resistance
the accidental discovery of penicillin in a laboratory
ways soil microbes improve the fertility of farmland
the decline in the use of antibiotics on modern farms
items.exp: 항생제 내성은 현대 의학이 만든 것이 아니라 토양 미생물 사이의 오랜 싸움에서 비롯되었고, 의학은 그 압력을 키웠을 뿐이라는 내용이에요. ①은 영구 동토층을 예시로만 든 것이고, ③은 글에 나오지 않아요.

items.passage: Investors, it turns out, check their accounts far more often when markets are rising than when they are falling. Researchers who studied login records at several banks found that people looked at their balances eagerly after good news and quietly avoided them after bad news, as though not seeing a loss made it less real. This tendency, nicknamed the ostrich effect after the bird's mythical habit of hiding its head in the sand, appears well beyond finance. Patients postpone medical tests they fear will bring unwelcome results; students leave an exam score unopened for days; homeowners ignore a strange noise in the roof. In each case, avoiding information spares us discomfort in the short term. The cost comes later. A problem that remains unexamined cannot be addressed while it is still small, and the delay often turns a manageable setback into a serious one. Understanding the impulse to look away may be the first step toward resisting it, since what we refuse to see continues to grow whether or not we look.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Investors Should Check Accounts Daily
How Ostriches Protect Themselves from Danger
The Benefits of Ignoring Bad News

Pine Lake Star Night 2027

Join us for an evening under the stars at Pine Lake Nature Park! Local astronomers will guide you through the night sky with professional telescopes.

• When: Saturday, August 14, 2027, 8 p.m. – 11 p.m. (If it is cloudy or rainy, the event will be held on Sunday, August 15.)
• Where: North Meadow, Pine Lake Nature Park
• Fees: Adults $8, Students $5, Children under 7 free

Programs
• 8:00 p.m.: Talk on summer constellations
• 9:00 p.m.: Telescope viewing of Saturn and the Moon

Notes
• Registration is required and must be completed online by August 6.
• Please bring your own blanket or folding chair.
• Flashlights with white light are not allowed; red-light flashlights will be provided at the entrance.
items.q: Pine Lake Star Night 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 날씨가 흐리면 다음 날로 행사가 연기된다.
7세 미만 어린이는 무료로 참가할 수 있다.
참가 등록은 행사 당일 현장에서 한다.

items.passage: For most of its long history, the umbrella was a symbol of rank rather than a shield against rain. In ancient Egypt, Assyria, and China, servants held large parasols over kings and nobles, ①[protecting] them from the sun and announcing their importance to everyone nearby. When the umbrella reached Europe, it was used mainly by women, and a man ②[seen] carrying one in eighteenth-century London risked being mocked as weak or foreign. One traveler, Jonas Hanway, is said to have ignored the laughter and carried an umbrella through the city's wet streets for some thirty years. Coach drivers, who feared losing customers who would otherwise hire a carriage on rainy days, reportedly ③[shouting] insults at him. Gradually, however, the practical value of staying dry won out over pride. By the time Hanway died in 1786, umbrellas ④[had become] a common sight among London gentlemen, and improvements such as steel ribs in the nineteenth century made them lighter and cheaper. An object once reserved for kings had become something that almost anyone could ⑤[afford].
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: 주어 Coach drivers 뒤에 문장의 동사가 와야 하므로 ③ shouting은 shouted로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 동시 동작을 나타내는 분사구문, ②는 a man을 꾸미는 과거분사, ④는 과거 시점 이전에 완료된 일을 나타내는 과거완료, ⑤는 could 뒤의 동사원형으로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: It might seem that businesses would want to locate as far as possible from their competitors, so that customers would have nowhere else to go. Yet in city after city, we find the opposite: furniture stores line the same avenue, and software firms crowd into the same few neighborhoods. Economists explain this pattern by pointing to benefits that ①[outweigh] the costs of competition. When similar firms gather in one place, they share a ②[pool] of skilled workers, who can move from one company to another without relocating. Suppliers of specialized parts and services find it worthwhile to set up nearby, which ③[lowers] costs for everyone. Ideas also travel more easily; engineers who meet at the same cafés exchange information that would never appear in a published report. Customers, too, are ④[drawn] to places where they can compare many options in a single trip. In such clusters, the presence of rivals is not merely tolerated but actually ⑤[threatens] each firm's success, which is why new businesses often choose to open their doors right next to established competitors.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 같은 업종이 모이면 인력·공급업체·정보·고객 측면에서 이익이 생기므로, 경쟁자의 존재가 오히려 각 회사의 성공을 돕는다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 ⑤ threatens는 supports나 contributes to 같은 낱말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Ask an English speaker where a cup is on a table, and you may hear that it is "to the left of the plate." Speakers of some languages would never say this. In Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northern Australia, and in a number of other languages around the world, spatial relations are described almost entirely with fixed compass directions. A cup is "north of the plate," and a person might warn a friend that there is an ant on his "southeast leg." Because these descriptions do not change when the speaker turns around, using the language requires knowing at every moment which way one is facing. Researchers have found that speakers of such languages maintain a remarkable sense of direction, pointing accurately toward distant places even inside unfamiliar buildings. The habit of speaking in this way appears to train a constant, almost automatic awareness of ___ that speakers of English rarely develop.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

items.passage: We like to think of knowledge as something we have earned through our own observation and reasoning. Yet if we examine what we actually know, the picture changes dramatically. Most of us know that the Earth orbits the Sun, that our blood contains cells, and that our country was founded in a certain year, but very few of us have personally checked any of these facts. We believe them because teachers, books, and experts told us so. Some philosophers have treated this dependence as a weakness, a second-rate kind of knowledge to be replaced, whenever possible, by first-hand evidence. But such a demand cannot be met even in principle. A scientist checking one result must rely on instruments built by others, data gathered by others, and theories tested by generations of researchers she has never met. The independent knower, then, is largely a myth. What makes a person reasonable is not that she avoids relying on others, but that ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: she relies wisely, judging whose word deserves her trust
she gradually replaces testimony with personal observation
she accepts only claims that most people already believe
she refuses to form beliefs about matters beyond her expertise
she remembers the original source of every fact she learns

items.passage: A lightning bolt begins long before the flash, in the turbulent interior of a towering storm cloud. ① Strong updrafts carry water droplets high into the cloud, where they freeze, and small ice crystals rising on these currents collide with heavier, softer pellets of ice that are falling. ② In each collision a tiny amount of electric charge is transferred, and because the light crystals tend to gain positive charge while the heavier pellets gain negative charge, the cloud gradually separates into a positive upper region and a negative lower one. ③ As the charge builds, the difference between the two regions, or between the cloud's base and the ground, can reach hundreds of millions of volts, until the air can no longer act as an insulator and a channel of current breaks through. ④ Because light travels much faster than sound, people often count the seconds between the flash and the thunder to judge how far away a storm is. ⑤ The channel heats the air around it to temperatures several times hotter than the surface of the Sun, and that sudden heating makes the air expand explosively, producing the crack and rumble of thunder.

items.passage:
Tardigrades, tiny animals less than a millimeter long, live in moss, soil, and ponds all over the world. Their habitats can dry out completely within hours, a situation that would kill most living things. Yet tardigrades are found again, alive and active, in the very same patches of moss once the rain comes back.

(A) When water returns, the process runs in reverse. Within minutes to hours, the tun absorbs moisture, the protective molecules dissolve, and the animal walks away as though nothing had happened, sometimes after years of waiting.

(B) The secret lies in how they react as their surroundings dry. Instead of dying, a tardigrade responds by pulling in its legs and curling into a dry, barrel-shaped form called a tun. As it does so, it loses nearly all the water in its body.

(C) To survive such extreme drying, its cells produce special proteins that form a glass-like gel. This gel surrounds delicate structures inside the cells and holds them in place, preventing them from breaking apart while the animal's metabolism almost stops.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 건조 뒤에도 살아난다는 주어진 글 뒤에 그 비결로 tun 상태가 되는 과정을 설명하는 (B)가 와요. (C)의 such extreme drying은 (B)에서 몸의 물을 거의 다 잃는 것을 받고, (A)의 the process runs in reverse와 the tun은 앞에서 설명한 건조 과정과 tun을 가리키므로 맨 뒤에 와요.

items.passage: In 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined in a single landmass and had slowly drifted apart. His evidence was striking. ( ① ) The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like neighboring pieces of a puzzle, identical fossils of land reptiles appeared on continents now separated by oceans, and rock layers in Brazil matched those in West Africa. ( ② ) Yet most geologists rejected the idea for decades. ( ③ ) What they could not accept was the lack of a cause: Wegener could not explain what force could push enormous blocks of continental rock through the solid floor of the ocean, and the mechanisms he suggested were shown to be far too weak. ( ④ ) Only in the 1950s and 1960s, when ships mapped the ocean floor and discovered long mountain ridges where new crust is continually formed, did a convincing mechanism appear. ( ⑤ ) The continents, it turned out, do not plow through the seafloor; they ride along with it on moving plates, and Wegener, who had died decades earlier, was finally recognized as having been largely right.

items.passage: It is often argued that shared resources, such as fishing grounds or grazing land, are doomed to be overused. Since each user gains the full benefit of taking more while the cost is spread among everyone, the reasoning goes, the resource will be exhausted unless it is either divided into private property or controlled by the government. Yet researchers studying communities around the world have found many cases that contradict this prediction. Fishing villages, mountain herders, and farming communities sharing water have managed common resources sustainably for centuries. What these groups have in common is not outside control but a set of rules they created themselves: clear boundaries on who may use the resource, limits suited to local conditions, members who watch one another's behavior, and penalties that grow with repeated violations. Because users take part in making and enforcing the rules, they regard them as fair and tend to follow them.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Contrary to the view that shared resources will inevitably be (A) ___, many communities have preserved them through rules that the users themselves (B) ___ and enforce.
items.exp: 공유 자원은 결국 고갈된다(exhausted)는 주장과 달리, 사용자들이 스스로 만든(created themselves) 규칙으로 자원을 지켜 왔다는 내용이에요. 그래서 (A)는 depleted, (B)는 establish가 알맞아요. ③ inherit는 물려받는다는 뜻이라 스스로 만든다는 내용과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
When a new technology first appears, it rarely looks new. The earliest automobiles were called "horseless carriages," and the name was accurate: they had the high wooden bodies, large spoked wheels, and open seats of the vehicles that horses had pulled, and some were even fitted with holders for whips that no driver would ever need. Early electric lamps were often shaped like candle flames, and the first printed books copied the look of handwritten manuscripts, down to the decorated capital letters added by hand.

Such imitation is not simply a failure of imagination. A new device must be (a)[understood] before it can be accepted, and familiar forms tell people what an object is for and how to use it. A machine that looked entirely unfamiliar might have (b)[confused] buyers rather than attracted them. Inventors, too, think with the tools they have, so the old design offers a natural starting point.

The cost of this comfort, however, is that the real (c)[possibilities] of the new technology remain hidden for a time. Because an engine did not tire like a horse, a car had no reason to sit high or to place its passenger behind the power source, yet it took roughly two decades for designers to (d)[abandon] the carriage shape and lower the body for speed and stability. Only when users had grown (e)[unfamiliar] with the device did the old form begin to fall away, and the technology start to take a shape suited to its own nature.

This pattern suggests that judging a new invention by its first appearance can be misleading. What we see at the beginning is often the old world in a new costume.

items.passage:
(A)
Every summer of her childhood, Lily had spent long afternoons in her grandmother's garden, helping her pull weeds and pick ripe tomatoes. So when Grandma Rose broke her hip in early spring and had to stay in the hospital for several weeks, Lily, now fifteen, made a promise. Her parents both worked long hours, and there was no one else to look after the plants. "Don't worry about the garden," she said, holding her grandmother's hand. "I'll take care of everything." Grandma Rose squeezed Lily's fingers and smiled, though Lily could see the worry in (a)[her] eyes.

(B)
When Lily described the rows, Grandma Rose laughed so hard that a nurse looked in to check on her. "Those aren't weeds, dear," she said. "Those are my carrots and beets." Lily felt her face burn. She had pulled out almost an entire bed of young vegetables. But Grandma Rose only shook her head kindly, and then (b)[she] reached over and patted Lily's arm. "Every gardener does something like that once. Now you'll never forget what a carrot looks like." That evening, sitting up in her hospital bed, the old gardener drew Lily a careful map of every bed, with each plant labeled in neat letters.

(C)
With the map in hand, Lily replanted the empty bed and checked every seedling before touching it. She even asked a neighbor to show her how to tie up the bean vines. By the time Grandma Rose came home in June, walking slowly with a cane, the garden was greener than Lily had ever seen it. The old woman stood at the gate for a long time without speaking. Then (c)[she] bent down, pulled a small carrot from the soil, and held it up proudly. "Look at this," she said. "You grew it twice."

(D)
The first weeks went well. Lily watered the beds every morning before school and covered the young plants on cold nights. But one Saturday she noticed rows of thin, feathery green shoots coming up in two of the beds. Sure that (d)[she] had found a weed problem, she spent the whole afternoon pulling them out, filling three buckets. Proud of her hard work, Lily visited the hospital the next day and told her grandmother all about it, expecting (e)[her] to be pleased.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 정원을 맡겠다고 약속한 (A) 뒤에 잡초인 줄 알고 새싹을 뽑은 뒤 할머니께 이야기하러 간 (D)가 와요. 이어서 그것이 당근과 비트였다는 말을 듣고 지도를 받는 (B), 그 지도를 들고 다시 심어 할머니가 퇴원해 정원을 보는 (C)로 끝나요.
