items.exp: (C)에서 Grandma Rose는 지팡이를 짚고 천천히 걸어서 돌아왔다고 했으므로 ③이 적절하지 않아요. 나머지는 (A), (B), (D)의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Howard,

I am writing on behalf of the residents of Building C at Linden Park Apartments. Over the past year, the number of people in our building who commute by bicycle has grown considerably, and many of us now keep our bikes in the narrow hallways or on our small balconies. This is not only inconvenient but, as the fire inspector pointed out during his last visit, potentially dangerous, since bicycles left in corridors can block an escape route in an emergency. We have noticed that the paved area next to the parking lot, behind the recycling bins, is rarely used. It would comfortably hold a covered rack for about twenty bicycles. Several residents have already offered to share the cost, and a local hardware store has given us a reasonable estimate, which I have attached. We would be grateful if the management office could approve the installation of a bicycle rack in that space at its next meeting. Thank you for considering our proposal.

Sincerely,
Daniel Reeves
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 복도에 자전거를 두는 문제를 설명한 뒤, 주차장 옆 빈 공간에 자전거 보관대를 설치하도록 관리사무소가 승인해 달라고 요청하고 있어요. 화재 점검과 재활용품 수거함은 상황 설명에 나온 소재일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Ethan pulled himself out of the pool and sat on the edge, his chest heaving. The last part of the lifeguard certification test was a timed swim: two hundred meters in under four minutes. He had felt strong for the first three lengths, but on the final one his arms had turned to lead, and he had watched the swimmer in the next lane touch the wall well ahead of him. Now the instructor was writing on her clipboard without looking up. Ethan stared at the water and began to rehearse what he would tell his parents. He had trained every morning before school for two months, and it had not been enough. He would have to wait another whole year to try again. Then the instructor called his name and held up the stopwatch. "Three minutes and fifty-one seconds," she said. "Tight, but you made it. And your rescue drill this morning was the cleanest I've seen all day." Ethan blinked at her, then let out a shout that echoed off the tiled walls. He jumped up, nearly slipped on the wet floor, and hugged the startled instructor before he could stop himself.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Ethan의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 마지막 바퀴에서 뒤처져 부모님께 할 말을 미리 생각하며 1년을 더 기다려야 한다고 낙담하다가, 기준 시간 안에 들어왔다는 말을 듣고 소리를 지르며 강사를 껴안아요. 그래서 낙담했다가 몹시 기뻐하는 'discouraged → overjoyed'가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Most residents experience local government the way they experience the weather: as something that simply happens to them. Decisions about which roads are repaved or which parks receive new lighting are made in meetings few people attend, and the results arrive without explanation. It is no surprise, then, that many citizens conclude their voices do not matter and stop paying attention between elections. Cities that want engaged residents should stop merely asking for trust and start handing over real responsibility. A portion of the annual budget, even a modest one, should be set aside for residents to spend directly. Let neighbors propose projects, debate them in open assemblies, and vote on which ones to fund. Critics worry that ordinary people lack the expertise for such choices, but officials can still estimate costs and check whether a project is feasible. What residents contribute is knowledge no report contains: which crossing frightens parents, which corner floods every spring. More importantly, people who have had to choose between a playground and a bus shelter learn what governing actually involves. A city that shares its decisions does not merely spend money better; it produces citizens.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 시는 예산의 일부를 주민이 직접 제안하고 결정하도록 맡겨야 한다.
시 예산은 전문가의 분석에 따라 효율적으로 배분되어야 한다.
주민의 정치 참여를 늘리려면 먼저 선거 투표율을 높여야 한다.
지방 정부는 예산 사용 내역을 주민에게 정기적으로 공개해야 한다.
소규모 공공사업은 주민 단체가 아닌 민간 기업에 맡겨야 한다.
items.exp: 연간 예산의 일부를 떼어 주민이 사업을 제안·토론·투표로 직접 쓰게 하라고 주장해요. ②는 비판론자의 입장에 가깝고, 글은 전문가가 비용 추정만 돕고 결정은 주민이 하라고 해요. ④의 공개는 글이 말하는 '책임을 넘겨주기'에 못 미쳐요.

items.passage: Imagine two drivers who leave the same party, equally tired and equally careless, and who each glance at their phones on the way home. One arrives without incident. The other looks up a second too late as a child steps into the road. The first driver will probably forget the evening; the second will be prosecuted, condemned by neighbors, and haunted for life. Yet nothing in their choices distinguished them. What separated them was the timing of a child's steps, something neither of them controlled. Philosophers call this moral luck, and it exposes a tension in how we judge. We say that people should be held responsible only for what lies within their control, yet our blame, our laws, and even our own guilt follow outcomes that depend on circumstance. Some argue that we should therefore judge the two drivers identically. Others reply that a morality blind to consequences would lose touch with what actually matters to victims. Either way, the case shows that the moral record of a life is [a ledger partly kept by chance]: what we answer for depends not only on what we choose but on how the world happens to respond.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [a ledger partly kept by chance]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a list of good deeds that luck will eventually balance out
a document that courts revise whenever new evidence appears
an account shaped by circumstances beyond our control as well as by our choices
a record that only the person who lived it can fairly judge
a summary of risks that careful people can always avoid
items.exp: 같은 선택을 한 두 운전자가 통제할 수 없는 우연 때문에 전혀 다른 책임을 지게 된다는 예로, 우리가 책임지는 것은 선택뿐 아니라 세상이 우연히 어떻게 반응하는지에도 달려 있다고 했어요. 그래서 ③이 알맞아요. ①은 운이 결국 균형을 맞춘다는 말로 글에 없는 내용이에요.

items.passage: Among the many sounds a bottlenose dolphin produces, one stands apart. Within its first months of life, each calf develops a distinctive whistle, a pattern of rising and falling pitch that differs from those of the other dolphins in its community. This signature whistle appears to function much like a name. Dolphins broadcast their own whistles when they are separated from companions, apparently announcing their identity, and they sometimes copy the signature whistle of a particular individual, which then tends to respond, as though it had been called. In playback experiments, wild dolphins react more strongly to the whistles of close relatives than to those of unfamiliar animals, even when the voice quality of the caller has been artificially removed, which suggests that the information lies in the shape of the whistle rather than in the sound of a particular voice. Such a system makes sense for animals that live in murky water, travel widely, and form alliances that may last for decades: when sight is limited and social life depends on knowing exactly who is who, a learned and stable label for each individual becomes extremely valuable.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of echolocation in hunting in murky water
how dolphin calves learn to imitate their mothers' voices
the difficulty of recording animal sounds in the wild
the lifelong alliances formed among male dolphins
learned whistles that serve dolphins as individual names
items.exp: 돌고래 새끼가 저마다 고유한 휘파람을 만들어 이름처럼 쓰고, 다른 개체의 휘파람을 흉내 내 부르기도 한다는 내용이라 ⑤가 주제예요. ②는 정보가 목소리가 아니라 휘파람의 모양에 있다는 내용과 어긋나고, ④는 그런 체계가 유용한 이유의 일부일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: Look up through the canopy of certain forests and you may notice something strange: the crowns of neighboring trees often stop just short of touching, leaving narrow channels of sky between them, like cracks in a dry riverbed. This pattern, known as crown shyness, has been observed in several species, from some eucalyptus trees to certain pines, and scientists have proposed more than one explanation for it. One idea is mechanical. As trees sway in the wind, their outer branches knock against those of their neighbors, and the tender growing tips are broken off, so a gap gradually forms where the crowns collide. Another explanation points to light. Leaves can detect the changes in light that signal a nearby plant, and branches may stop growing in that direction before contact occurs. The gaps may also bring benefits: they let more light reach the lower leaves and may slow the spread of leaf-eating insects from one tree to the next. Whatever its cause, the pattern shows that even organisms rooted in place respond to their neighbors in subtle ways.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Gaps in the Canopy: Why Some Trees Keep Their Distance
How Wind Decides the Height of Forest Trees
Eucalyptus and Pine: Rivals for the Same Sunlight
Insects That Travel Through the Treetops
Rooted in Place, Trees Cannot Sense Their Neighbors
items.exp: 이웃한 나무의 수관이 서로 닿지 않고 틈을 남기는 현상(crown shyness)과 그 원인·이점을 설명하는 글이므로 ①이 알맞아요. ⑤는 나무가 이웃에 섬세하게 반응한다는 마지막 문장과 반대예요.

items.passage: Mirela Ostrova was born in 1884 in a small fishing town on the Black Sea coast, where her father repaired ships' instruments. As a girl she spent hours in his workshop grinding scraps of glass into lenses, and at sixteen she won a scholarship to study optics in Vienna, one of only two women in her class. After graduating, she joined a firm that manufactured lenses for lighthouses, and within a decade she had designed a lighter, ring-shaped lens that could be produced at half the usual cost. Her design allowed many small harbors, which had never been able to afford a proper light, to install one for the first time. Ostrova refused to patent the lens, saying that a light which saved sailors should belong to everyone. In later life she returned to her hometown and taught physics at the local school until her retirement in 1949. She died in 1957, and a lighthouse at the entrance to her home harbor still bears her name.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 아버지는 선박용 기구를 수리하는 일을 했다.
그녀가 고안한 렌즈는 기존의 절반 비용으로 생산될 수 있었다.
자신이 설계한 렌즈에 대해 특허를 받았다.
은퇴할 때까지 고향의 학교에서 물리를 가르쳤다.
items.exp: Ostrova는 선원을 구하는 빛은 모두의 것이어야 한다며 렌즈의 특허를 내기를 거부했어요(refused to patent). 나머지는 모두 글의 내용과 일치해요.

items.passage: For decades, researchers studying long life focused on diet, exercise, and smoking. More recently, however, a growing body of evidence ①[suggests] that the quality of our relationships may matter just as much. People with strong social ties tend to recover faster from illness, and they are less likely to develop certain chronic conditions. One reason may be stress. When we face a problem alone, the body keeps ②[producing] stress hormones that, over long periods, can damage the heart and weaken the immune system. A friend who listens, or a neighbor who offers help, can reduce that burden. Loneliness, by contrast, seems to keep the body in a state of alert ③[what] it was never designed to sustain. Interestingly, it is not simply the number of contacts that counts. A person surrounded by acquaintances can still feel isolated, while someone with only two or three close friends ④[may feel] deeply supported. What appears to matter is the sense that someone would be there if needed. This is why some doctors now ask patients not only about their habits but also about ⑤[whether] they have someone to call in a crisis.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③ 뒤의 절은 앞의 명사 a state of alert를 꾸미는 관계절이므로 선행사를 포함하는 what이 아니라 that이나 which를 써야 해요. ①은 주어 a growing body에 맞춘 단수 동사, ②는 keep -ing, ⑤는 '~인지'를 뜻하는 명사절 접속사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: For more than a century, public libraries charged small fines for overdue books, assuming that the threat of a penalty would ①[encourage] borrowers to return items on time. In recent years, however, many library systems have abolished these fines, and the results have surprised even their supporters. Return rates did not ②[collapse]; in several cities they stayed nearly the same, and some libraries reported that long-missing books began to come back once borrowers no longer feared a bill at the desk. The fines, it turned out, had ③[discouraged] the very people libraries most wanted to serve. Children and families on tight budgets who owed a few dollars often ④[avoided] the library altogether rather than face the embarrassment of an unpaid debt, and their cards were blocked at exactly the age when reading habits form. Meanwhile, the money collected was small, and staff spent valuable time handling coins and disputes instead of helping readers. Many librarians now regard the old fines as ⑤[necessary], a policy that cost far more in lost trust and lost readers than it ever earned.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 연체료를 없애도 반납률이 유지되었고, 연체료가 오히려 독자를 쫓아냈다는 흐름이므로 사서들은 옛 연체료를 '불필요하거나 역효과를 낸' 정책으로 본다고 해야 해요. ⑤ necessary를 unnecessary나 counterproductive로 바꿔야 해요. ②는 반납률이 무너지지 않았다는 뜻으로 맞아요.

items.passage: Ask people how much their tastes, values, and personalities have changed over the past ten years, and most will describe considerable change. Ask the same people how much they expect to change over the next ten years, and they predict surprisingly little. Studies have found this pattern at every age, from teenagers to the elderly: people readily admit that their past selves were different, yet they imagine that the person they are today is more or less the person they will remain. It is as though each of us regards the present moment as a ___, the point at which our growth has finally come to rest. One reason may be that remembering change is easy, since we can recall old opinions and abandoned hobbies, while imagining change is hard, because we cannot picture preferences we do not yet have. The illusion has practical costs. People commit themselves today, through everything from tattoos to long-term plans, on the assumption that their future selves will want exactly what they want now, and they are often surprised when those future selves disagree.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 사람들은 과거엔 많이 변했다고 인정하면서도 앞으로는 거의 변하지 않을 거라 여겨요. 빈칸 뒤에서 '성장이 마침내 멈춘 지점'이라고 풀어 주므로, 현재를 '종착지'로 본다는 destination이 알맞아요. beginning이나 crossroads는 앞으로의 변화를 전제하므로 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: An audio file compressed into a common streaming format may be a tenth of the size of the original recording, yet most listeners cannot tell the two apart. The trick is not that the compression stores the sound more efficiently in some neutral sense but that it throws a great deal of it away. Engineers have learned that a loud tone masks quieter tones close to it in pitch, and that the ear is far less sensitive to some frequencies than to others; the encoder exploits these facts by discarding whatever the auditory system would fail to register anyway. Judged by the physics of the sound wave, the result is a crude copy, missing much of the information the microphone captured. Judged by the experience of the listener, it is nearly perfect. What this reveals is that faithfulness in reproduction is not a property a copy possesses on its own; it is ___. A format designed for human ears may be hopelessly inaccurate for a bat, and the same file analyzed by a machine could expose losses that no person would ever notice.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a measure of how much of the original data the copy preserves
a technical standard that engineers impose on every listener alike
something that improves steadily as digital storage becomes cheaper
a relation between the copy and the perceiver for whom it is intended
an illusion that disappears once listeners are trained to notice it
items.exp: 압축 파일은 물리적으로는 정보가 많이 빠진 조잡한 복사본이지만, 사람의 귀가 못 느끼는 부분만 버렸기에 듣는 사람에게는 거의 완벽해요. 박쥐나 기계에게는 부정확할 수 있다는 마지막 문장까지 보면, 충실함은 복사본과 그것을 지각하는 대상 사이의 관계라는 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 글이 부정한 물리적 기준이에요.

items.passage: Climbers who tackle short, steep routes known as boulder problems rely on a grading system to describe how hard each problem is, but the numbers they use are less fixed than they appear. ① A grade is first proposed by the person who makes the first ascent, and later climbers either confirm it or argue that it should be raised or lowered. ② Because difficulty depends heavily on body size, reach, and strength, a move that feels impossible to one climber may feel routine to another. ③ Bouldering requires little equipment beyond climbing shoes, a bag of chalk, and a thick pad to cushion falls, which is partly why it has become so popular in cities. ④ As a result, grades are best understood not as precise measurements but as a rough agreement that forms gradually as more people try the problem. ⑤ A newly established problem may shift by a grade or two over its first few years before its rating finally settles.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 볼더링 등급이 고정된 수치가 아니라 여러 사람의 시도로 점차 합의되는 것이라는 흐름이에요. ③은 볼더링에 필요한 장비와 인기 이유를 말하고 있어 등급의 성격이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요. ④의 As a result는 ②의 체격 차이를 이어받아요.

items.passage:
In the early nineteenth century, a screw made in one workshop rarely fit a nut made in another. Each machinist cut threads according to his own habits, choosing the angle, depth, and spacing that suited his tools.

(A) Frustrated by this waste of time, the British engineer Joseph Whitworth gathered screws from workshops across the country and studied their dimensions. In 1841 he proposed a single system, with a fixed thread angle and a set number of threads per inch for each diameter.

(B) His standard was gradually adopted by railway companies and machine builders, and other countries later developed systems of their own. The result was a world in which parts became interchangeable, and a bolt bought in one city could be trusted to fit a machine built in another.

(C) This meant that a broken bolt could not simply be replaced. A new one had to be made to match the old nut, often by the very shop that had produced the original, and repairing a machine far from its maker could take weeks.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 '나사와 너트가 서로 맞지 않는 상황'을 (C)의 This meant가 받아 수리에 몇 주가 걸린다고 해요. 그 낭비를 (A)의 this waste of time이 받아 Whitworth의 제안으로 이어지고, (B)의 His standard가 그 결과를 말해요.

items.passage: A grade is a message. When a teacher records an A on a transcript, she is telling a future reader, such as a university or an employer, something about how a student performed compared with others. ( ① ) For that message to carry information, however, grades must be spread across a range: some students receive A's, others B's, and still others lower marks. ( ② ) In the extreme case, when every student receives an A, the grade tells the reader nothing at all, since it can no longer distinguish the student who mastered the material from the one who barely kept up. ( ③ ) Readers respond to this loss in predictable ways. ( ④ ) Universities and employers begin to rely more heavily on entrance tests, interviews, and the reputation of the school a student attended. ( ⑤ ) Ironically, then, a trend that seems generous to students may end up favoring those from well-known schools, whose A's are trusted, over equally capable students whose A's look exactly like everyone else's.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

When grades drift steadily upward over the years, as they have in many schools, this range gradually narrows.
items.exp: 주어진 문장의 this range는 ② 앞의 '성적이 여러 범위에 퍼져 있어야 한다'는 내용을 가리켜요. 또 범위가 점점 좁아진다는 내용이 있어야 ② 뒤의 In the extreme case(모두가 A를 받는 극단적인 경우)가 자연스럽게 이어져요. ①에는 아직 range가 나오지 않았어요.

items.passage: In many parts of the world, a guest who is offered food or a gift is expected to decline it at first, sometimes two or three times, before finally accepting. To an outsider, this exchange can look puzzling or even insincere: why refuse something you intend to take? Yet the ritual performs a useful social function. By refusing, the guest shows that he or she did not come for the gift and does not wish to impose on the host. By insisting, the host shows that the offer is genuine rather than a polite formality. Each round of refusal and insistence lets both parties display their good intentions without anyone having to state them directly. When the gift is finally accepted, it carries more meaning than it would have if it had been taken immediately, because both sides have publicly confirmed the relationship. Problems arise mainly when people from different traditions meet. A visitor who accepts at once may seem greedy, while a host who offers only once may never learn that the guest actually wanted what was offered.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

The custom of first refusing an offer, though it may appear (A) ___ to outsiders, allows host and guest to (B) ___ their goodwill toward each other without saying so openly.
items.exp: 외부인에게는 이 관습이 insincere(진심이 아닌)하게 보일 수 있으니 (A)는 dishonest, 거절과 권유를 주고받으며 선의를 직접 말하지 않고도 display(보여 준다)하니 (B)는 demonstrate가 알맞아요. conceal은 '숨기다'라서 반대예요.

items.passage:
Immigrant families often follow a pattern so regular that researchers describe it as a three-generation rule. The first generation, who arrive as adults, continue to speak their native language at home and learn the new one only partially. Their children grow up (a)[between] two languages, using the parents' tongue at the kitchen table and the majority language at school and with friends. By the third generation, the grandchildren usually speak only the majority language, and conversations with their grandparents shrink to a few (b)[familiar] phrases.

What drives this rapid shift is rarely a deliberate decision. Few parents choose to let their language disappear; many are (c)[saddened] to discover that their children answer every question in the majority language. The pressure is subtler. School, media, and friendships all reward the majority language, while the heritage language is confined to a narrowing set of situations, mostly conversations with older relatives. A language used only for such (d)[limited] purposes stops feeling useful to a child, and children, practical learners that they are, invest their effort elsewhere.

This explains why the families that do keep their languages alive tend to (e)[shrink] the number of settings in which the language is used. They send children to weekend schools, where it becomes a language of friendship rather than only of obligation. They seek out books, songs, and online communities that make it a language of entertainment. Some arrange long visits to the country of origin, where the language is suddenly necessary for buying snacks or making friends. A language survives not because people are told it is valuable, but because it remains the natural way to do things that matter to them. Heritage languages are lost less through rejection than through the quiet disappearance of the everyday occasions that give a language its reason to be spoken.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Grandparents Refuse to Learn a New Language
Bilingual Schools: The Fastest Route to Assimilation
Parental Choice as the Main Cause of Language Loss
How Children Learn Two Languages Without Confusion

What drives this rapid shift is rarely a deliberate decision. items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 뒤에 주말 학교, 책·노래·온라인 모임, 긴 방문 등 언어를 쓰는 상황을 넓히는 예가 이어지므로, 언어가 쓰이는 환경의 수를 '늘린다'고 해야 해요. (e) shrink를 expand나 multiply로 바꿔야 해요. (d) limited는 나이 든 친척과의 대화로 한정된 쓰임을 가리켜 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Elena had not seen her grandmother in six years, and the phone call saying that the old woman was in the hospital had sent her straight to the station. The night train to the north was nearly empty. In her compartment sat a single passenger, an elderly woman with silver hair pinned neatly behind her head, knitting a long red scarf. Without looking up from her needles, (a)[she] nodded toward the window, where snow was beginning to fall, and remarked that it would be a long night. Then she poured a cup of tea from a thermos and held it out to Elena.

(B)
The clicking stopped. For a moment the woman simply stared at her. 'I was born in Brennick,' she said quietly. 'Who is waiting for you there?' When Elena gave her grandmother's name, Rosa Linde, the woman put a hand to her mouth. Rosa, she explained, had been her closest friend at school. They had promised to write to each other when her family moved to the city, but the letters had grown rare and then stopped, and fifty years had passed. From her purse (b)[she] drew a small, faded photograph of two girls laughing on a riverbank, and Elena recognized her grandmother's smile at once.

(C)
The train reached Brennick just after dawn. As Elena stood to leave, the woman finished the last row of the scarf, tied off the yarn, and pressed it into her hands. Before letting go, she added, 'Red was always Rosa's color. Tell her Margit is sorry for the silence.' At the hospital, Elena found her grandmother pale but awake. When Elena unfolded the scarf and repeated the message, her grandmother's eyes filled with tears. Then (c)[she] asked for a pen and paper, saying there was a letter she should have written long ago.

(D)
Around midnight the train shuddered to a halt. The conductor came through to explain that snow had buried the track ahead and that a plow was on its way. Elena checked her phone again and again, picturing the hospital's visiting hours slipping away. The old woman, however, seemed as calm as if (d)[she] had all the time in the world. As her needles clicked, (e)[she] described the trains of her childhood and asked where Elena was going. 'A little town called Brennick,' Elena said. 'You won't have heard of it.'
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 눈이 내리기 시작한 뒤, (D)에서 기차가 눈 때문에 멈추고 Elena가 Brennick에 간다고 말해요. (B)의 The clicking stopped는 (D)의 바늘 소리를 받고 Brennick 이야기가 이어지며, (C)에서 새벽에 도착해 할머니를 만나요.

items.passage:
Dear Parents and Guardians,

As many of you know, Westfield High School will hold its annual Science Fair on Saturday, March 13, in the main gymnasium. This year more than one hundred and twenty students have registered to present projects, ranging from homemade water filters to computer programs that identify bird songs. That is a wonderful number, but it also means that we need far more judges than our science teachers can provide. We are therefore turning to you. You do not need to be a scientist to serve as a judge. Each judge will receive a simple scoring sheet and a short training session at 8:30 a.m., and will then spend about three hours speaking with students about their projects. What matters most is curiosity and a willingness to ask good questions. If you are able to help, please complete the attached form and return it to the school office by February 26. Your time would give our students a real audience for their hard work.

Warm regards,
Karen Douglas
Science Department Head

과학 교사 연수 프로그램의 일정을 안내하려고

items.passage: At 11:40 p.m., twenty minutes before the deadline, I clicked "Submit" on my application for the summer research program I had wanted for two years. Instead of a confirmation page, the screen turned white and showed a single line: "Service temporarily unavailable." I refreshed the page. Nothing. I tried another browser, then my phone, and the same message appeared each time. My essay, my teacher's recommendation, the transcript I had waited three weeks to receive: all of it seemed to have vanished into the dark. I pictured the program's acceptance list with every name except mine, and my chest tightened until I could barely breathe. At 11:52, I wrote a frantic email to the program office, attaching everything again. Then, at 12:07, my phone buzzed. "Your application has been received. Because of a server error, the deadline has been extended by 24 hours." I read it three times, set the phone down, and let my head fall onto the desk, laughing quietly.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 마감 직전 화면이 멈추고 서류가 모두 사라진 듯해 숨쉬기도 힘들어지는 모습에서 공황 상태가 드러나요. 지원서가 접수되었고 마감이 연장되었다는 메시지를 받고 책상에 고개를 떨군 채 웃었으므로 안도하는 마음으로 바뀌었어요. 그래서 panicked → relieved가 알맞아요.

items.passage: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, collectors traveled through rural villages with notebooks and, later, recording machines, determined to preserve folk songs before modern life swept them away. Their work saved thousands of melodies that would otherwise have vanished. Yet it also changed what a folk song was. In the villages, a song had never existed as a single correct version. Each singer altered the words to suit a local event, slowed the tune for a funeral or quickened it for a wedding, and passed on something slightly different from what she had received. Variation was not a corruption of the song; it was the way the song lived. Once a collector wrote down one performance and published it, however, that version often became the song. Schools taught it, choirs sang it exactly as printed, and singers who changed it were corrected for getting it wrong. In trying to rescue a living tradition, the collectors risked [pressing it flat like a flower in a book], keeping its shape while removing the very growth that had made it alive.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [pressing it flat like a flower in a book]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: recording songs only in the villages where they were first sung
fixing a changing practice into one permanent, approved form
making old songs more popular among young urban audiences
replacing local melodies with songs composed by professionals
losing many songs because of careless note-taking
items.exp: 마을의 민요는 부르는 사람마다 바꾸어 부르며 살아 있었는데, 채집가가 한 번의 공연을 적어 출판하자 그것이 유일한 정답처럼 굳어졌다고 했어요. 따라서 변하던 전통을 하나의 고정된 공인 형태로 굳혀 버린다는 ②가 알맞아요. ⑤는 채집이 오히려 많은 노래를 살렸다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: When people apologize, they often feel an urge to explain. They describe the traffic that made them late, the stress that made them snap, or the confusing instructions that led to the error. These explanations may be perfectly true, and the speaker usually offers them in the hope of being understood. To the person who was hurt, however, they tend to sound quite different. An explanation placed inside an apology shifts attention from the harm that was done to the circumstances of the one who did it, and it suggests, however faintly, that the wrongdoer was not really responsible. The listener then hears less an apology than a defense. Studies of conflict resolution suggest that the apologies people find most convincing share a few features: a clear acknowledgment of what went wrong, an admission of responsibility, and an offer to repair the damage or to act differently in the future. Explanations are not forbidden, but they work better later, once the other person feels that the harm itself has been recognized. An apology that hurries toward its excuses fails at the one thing it is meant to do.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 사과할 때는 잘못이 생긴 상황을 자세히 설명해야 오해를 막을 수 있다.
사과는 상대의 감정이 가라앉은 뒤에 하는 것이 효과적이다.
잘못의 원인이 외부에 있다면 굳이 사과할 필요가 없다.
진정한 사과는 말보다 피해를 보상하는 행동으로 드러난다.
사과할 때는 변명보다 잘못과 책임을 먼저 인정하는 것이 중요하다.
items.exp: 사과 속 변명은 피해에서 가해자의 사정으로 관심을 돌려 방어처럼 들리게 하고, 설득력 있는 사과는 잘못을 인정하고 책임을 받아들이는 데서 시작한다고 했어요. 그래서 ⑤가 요지예요. ①은 글이 경계한 태도이고, ④는 보상이 사과의 한 요소로만 언급되었을 뿐 말보다 행동이라는 내용은 없어요.

items.passage: Why should a serious criminal case be decided by twelve ordinary citizens with no legal training rather than by experienced judges? Critics of the jury system point out that jurors may misunderstand technical evidence, be swayed by emotion, or simply lack the patience for a long trial. These concerns are real. Yet defenders argue that the jury's apparent weakness is also its purpose. A professional judge, however fair, belongs to a small group that shares a training, a vocabulary, and a set of assumptions about how people behave. Jurors bring something different: a range of everyday experience, from running a shop to raising teenagers, which helps them judge whether a witness's story sounds like the way real people act. The jury also links the law to the community it governs. When a verdict must persuade a group of ordinary citizens, the law cannot drift too far from the public's sense of what is fair, and the decision carries a legitimacy that the ruling of an official alone might lack.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the value that ordinary citizens bring to legal judgment
the need for more legal training among jurors
the growing difficulty of understanding scientific evidence
why professional judges make fairer decisions than juries
the history of the jury system in criminal courts
items.exp: 법률 훈련이 없는 시민 배심원이 오히려 다양한 생활 경험으로 증언을 판단하고, 법을 공동체의 공정성 감각과 연결해 판결에 정당성을 준다는 글이에요. 그래서 ①이 주제예요. ②·③은 비판 측 우려를 빌린 보기이고, ④는 글의 주장과 반대예요.

items.passage: Most earthquakes release their energy in seconds, shaking the ground violently enough to topple buildings. In the late 1990s, however, scientists monitoring the Pacific Northwest of North America noticed something odd in their GPS data. Every year or so, the ground near the coast would quietly shift a few millimeters in the opposite direction from its usual slow drift, and the movement would continue for days or even weeks. No one felt it, and no building shook. What they had found was a slow slip event, a kind of earthquake in which the boundary between two tectonic plates slides gently over a long period instead of breaking suddenly. Since then, similar events have been detected in Japan, Mexico, and New Zealand. Slow slips are harmless in themselves, but they matter because they move stress along the fault, sometimes loading the locked portions that produce dangerous earthquakes. Some researchers now hope that monitoring these silent movements could one day help them estimate when and where the next large earthquake is most likely to occur.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Coastal Buildings Survive Large Earthquakes
GPS Satellites Lose Their Signal Near Faults
Earthquakes Without Shaking: The Quiet Slip of Plates
items.exp: 흔들림 없이 판의 경계가 며칠에서 몇 주에 걸쳐 천천히 미끄러지는 '느린 미끄러짐' 지진을 소개하고 그 의미를 설명하므로 ③이 알맞아요. ④는 '언젠가 도움이 되기를 바란다'는 글보다 지나치게 단정적이에요.

items.q: Greenway Pond Dip Day 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 5세 미만 어린이는 무료로 참가할 수 있다.
비가 많이 오면 현미경 실습만 진행된다.
items.exp: 참가자는 방문자 센터의 정문에서 모인다고 안내되어 있어요(meet at the main entrance). 따라서 뒤편에서 모인다는 ①이 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 모두 안내문과 일치해요.

items.passage: Before 1840, sending a letter in Britain was both expensive and confusing. The cost depended on the distance the letter traveled and the number of sheets it contained, and it was usually paid not by the sender but by the person ①[receiving] it. Many recipients, faced with a large charge, simply refused to accept their mail. Some people even developed secret codes, ②[marking] the outside of an envelope with small symbols so that the recipient could read a short message and then hand the letter back unpaid. The reformer Rowland Hill argued that the real cost of the postal service lay not in carrying letters but in the complicated work of calculating and ③[collecting] fees. He proposed a single low price for any letter within the country, paid in advance by the sender. To show that payment ④[had made], the sender would attach a small printed label to the envelope. The result was the world's first adhesive postage stamp, and within a few years the number of letters sent in Britain had more than doubled, ⑤[proving] that a simpler system could also be a far more popular one.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: payment는 '이루어지는' 대상이므로 수동태가 되어야 해요. ④ had made를 had been made로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 the person을 꾸미는 현재분사, ②·⑤는 분사구문, ③은 calculating과 병렬인 동명사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: When we spill coffee on our shirt or wear a slightly ridiculous hat, we tend to assume that everyone around us has noticed. Psychologists call this the spotlight effect: the belief that our appearance and actions are watched far more ①[closely] than they actually are. In one well-known type of study, participants were asked to walk into a room wearing an embarrassing T-shirt and then to estimate how many of the people inside had noticed it. Their guesses were consistently ②[lower] than the true figure; on average, they believed about twice as many people had noticed as really had. The effect arises because each of us is at the center of our own experience. We are intensely ③[aware] of what we are doing and how we look, and we find it hard to set this awareness aside and imagine how little attention others are paying. They, after all, are busy worrying about their own spotlight. Recognizing this bias can be ④[liberating]. A mistake in a presentation or an awkward comment at a party, which may feel unforgettable to us, is usually ⑤[forgotten] by others within minutes, if it was noticed at all.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 스포트라이트 효과는 남들이 자신을 실제보다 더 많이 본다고 믿는 것이므로, 참가자들의 추정치는 실제 수치보다 '높아야' 해요. ② lower를 higher로 바꿔야 해요. 실제 수치의 약 두 배로 추정했다는 흐름과도 맞아요.

items.passage: Walk across almost any university campus or city park and you will find them: narrow strips of worn grass cutting diagonally across lawns, connecting a building entrance to a bus stop or a gate to a café. Planners call them desire paths. They appear wherever the routes people actually want to take differ from the ones that designers laid out in concrete. For a long time, such paths were treated as damage, and grounds staff responded with fences, hedges, and signs asking people to keep off the grass. Some designers, however, have begun to see them differently. Rather than paving every walkway in advance, they open a new space with only a few fixed paths, wait a season or two, and then pave the lines that people's feet have already carved into the ground. In this view, a worn strip of grass is not an act of disobedience but a kind of ___, a record of thousands of small decisions about where people really need to go, offered free of charge to anyone willing to read it.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 닳은 잔디길을 사람들이 실제로 가고 싶은 곳에 대한 수많은 결정의 기록으로 보고, 이를 읽어 길을 포장한다고 했어요. 따라서 사람들의 선호를 조사한 결과 같은 survey가 알맞아요. warning은 과거의 '손상'이라는 관점에 가까워요.

items.passage: Career advice for young people increasingly takes the form of a single command: find work you love. The advice seems generous, freeing workers from the old assumption that a job is merely a means to a paycheck. Yet a growing body of research suggests that the language of passion can quietly change how others treat those who embrace it. In a series of experiments, participants who read about an employee described as passionate about her work were more willing to approve of asking her to stay late without pay, take on unrelated tasks, or give up a weekend than were participants who read about the same employee described in neutral terms. The reasoning, rarely stated aloud, runs roughly as follows: if the work is its own reward, then additional work is not a burden but a gift. Passion, in this view, is treated as a form of payment already received. The consequence is an uncomfortable irony: the very quality that makes a worker valuable to an organization can become the justification for ___. Those who love their jobs most may therefore need, more than anyone, to be clear about where their devotion ends.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: rewarding that worker with greater independence and trust
replacing that worker with someone less emotionally involved
asking that worker to give more while receiving no more in return
encouraging colleagues to discover a similar love for their work
measuring that worker's performance by stricter standards
items.exp: 열정적이라고 소개된 직원에게는 무급 야근이나 관련 없는 업무를 시켜도 된다고 여겼고, 열정을 이미 받은 보수처럼 취급한다고 했어요. 그러므로 조직이 아끼는 열정이 오히려 더 많은 일을 요구하면서 보상은 늘리지 않는 근거가 된다는 ③이 알맞아요. ⑤처럼 평가 기준이 엄격해진다는 내용은 글에 없어요.

items.passage: Any system for arranging books on shelves must decide which subjects belong together and which come first, and these decisions are never neutral. ① A classification scheme designed in the late nineteenth century, for example, might devote dozens of sections to the history and religion of the country where it was created while squeezing the traditions of the rest of the world into a few numbers at the end. ② Because librarians around the world adopted such schemes, the priorities of one time and place were quietly copied into collections far away. ③ A reader browsing the shelves absorbs these priorities without noticing them, learning which topics are treated as central and which as marginal. ④ Many libraries now lend not only books but also musical instruments, tools, and board games, attracting visitors who might never have come in to borrow a novel. ⑤ For this reason, some libraries have begun to revise or replace their inherited systems, recognizing that the order of the shelves shapes the order of a reader's thoughts.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 책을 분류하는 체계에는 만든 시대와 장소의 우선순위가 담겨 있고, 독자는 그것을 모르게 흡수하므로 체계를 고치려는 움직임이 있다는 흐름이에요. ④는 도서관이 악기·공구 등을 빌려주는 새로운 서비스 이야기라 분류 체계의 편향이라는 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
A microwave oven can heat a bowl of soup in two minutes, yet the plate underneath often stays fairly cool. The reason lies in what microwaves actually do to food.

(A) This constant twisting makes the molecules jostle against their neighbors, and the energy of this motion appears as heat. Because ceramic plates and glass contain little water, they absorb little of the energy and warm mainly through contact with the hot food.

(B) Microwaves are a form of electromagnetic radiation, like light or radio waves, and their electric field reverses direction billions of times per second. Water molecules, which carry a slight positive charge at one end and a negative charge at the other, try to line up with this field each time it reverses.

(C) The same principle explains a familiar annoyance. Frozen food often heats unevenly, because ice, whose molecules are locked in a rigid structure, cannot rotate freely and absorbs microwaves poorly, while any melted patches heat rapidly.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 전자레인지가 음식에 무엇을 하는지 묻는 주어진 글 뒤에, 전기장이 방향을 바꿀 때마다 물 분자가 그 방향으로 정렬하려 한다는 (B)가 와요. 이 끊임없는 회전(This constant twisting)이 열이 된다는 (A), 같은 원리로 언 음식이 고르게 데워지지 않는다는 (C)가 이어져요.

items.passage: A bank is, in an important sense, built on a promise it cannot keep all at once. Depositors are told that they may withdraw their money whenever they like. ( ① ) Yet the bank lends out most of the money it receives, keeping only a small fraction in its vaults. ( ② ) On an ordinary day this causes no difficulty, because only a few customers ask for their money at any one time, and new deposits arrive to replace what is withdrawn. ( ③ ) The arrangement becomes dangerous only when depositors begin to doubt it. ( ④ ) As the line outside grows longer, even those who trusted the bank begin to fear that they will arrive too late, and they too rush to withdraw. ( ⑤ ) In this way a bank that was perfectly healthy can be driven to collapse simply because people believe it will fail. To break this cycle, many governments now guarantee deposits up to a certain amount, removing the reason to run.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

If a rumor spreads that a bank is in trouble, people hurry to take out their savings before the money runs out.
items.exp: ③ 뒤에서 예금자들이 의심하기 시작할 때 위험해진다고 한 뒤, 주어진 문장이 그 구체적 상황(소문이 퍼져 사람들이 서둘러 인출함)을 보여 줘요. 그래야 ④ 뒤의 the line outside(밖의 줄)가 자연스럽게 이어져요.

items.passage: Cities are loud places, and much of their noise, from traffic and machinery, is concentrated at low frequencies. For songbirds, which rely on song to defend territories and attract mates, this creates a serious problem: a song that cannot be heard is a song wasted. Researchers comparing populations of the same species in cities and in nearby forests have found a striking pattern. Great tits and several other species sing at noticeably higher pitches in noisy urban areas, lifting their songs above the low rumble that would otherwise drown them out. Some birds also sing louder, and others shift their singing to quieter times of day, beginning before the morning traffic builds. These changes can appear within a few years, suggesting that much of the adjustment comes from flexible behavior rather than slow genetic evolution. The adjustment has limits, however. Higher notes do not travel as far, and females of some species seem to prefer lower songs, so the city bird that makes itself heard may pay a price in attractiveness.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Because urban noise (A) ___ their songs, many city birds (B) ___ the way they sing, although such changes can carry costs.
items.exp: 도시의 낮은 소음이 새의 노래를 묻어 버리므로(drown them out) (A)는 masks, 새들이 음높이·크기·시간대를 바꾼다고 했으니 (B)는 modify가 알맞아요. amplifies는 소음이 노래를 키운다는 반대 의미이고, preserve는 노래를 그대로 지킨다는 뜻이라 맞지 않아요.

items.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the goal of agricultural science was straightforward: grow more food on each hectare of land. Breeders developed high-yielding varieties, and farmers planted vast fields with a single crop, often a single variety, so that every plant could be sown, fertilized, and harvested by the same machines at the same time. The results were (a)[impressive]. Grain yields in many regions doubled or tripled, and the cost of food fell.

Uniformity, however, carries a hidden risk. When every plant in a field shares the same genes, it also shares the same weaknesses. A disease that can attack one plant can attack them all, and nothing in the field slows its (b)[spread]. In 1970, a fungal disease swept through corn fields in the United States, where most of the crop carried the same genetic trait that made it vulnerable. Roughly 15 percent of the national harvest was lost in a single season, and in some southern states the losses were far (c)[smaller].

Diverse fields behave differently. When several varieties or species grow side by side, a pest that thrives on one may find the next plant (d)[unappealing], and its advance is interrupted. Experiments in which farmers planted mixtures of rice varieties instead of a single one have shown sharp reductions in disease, sometimes with little need for chemical sprays. Mixed plantings can also make better use of soil and water, since plants with different root depths draw on different resources.

None of this means that high yields are unimportant. A hungry world needs productive farms. But a system optimized only for the best year may perform terribly in the worst one. Increasingly, agricultural researchers argue that the true measure of a farm is not its peak harvest but its ability to keep producing when conditions turn against it, and that some diversity, even at a small cost in yield, is a (e)[sensible] price to pay for that stability.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: The Fungus That Changed American Corn Forever
Beyond Maximum Yield: Why Diversity Protects Our Crops
Machines and Fertilizers: The Engines of Modern Farming
Rice Mixtures: A Solution to World Hunger
Why Farmers Should Abandon High-Yield Varieties
items.exp: 한 품종만 넓게 심는 획일성은 수확량을 늘렸지만 병에 취약하게 만들었고, 다양성이 안정성을 준다는 글이므로 ②가 알맞아요. ⑤는 높은 수확량이 중요하지 않다는 뜻이 아니라는 마지막 문단과 맞지 않아요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 전국 수확량의 약 15퍼센트가 사라졌고, 일부 남부 주에서는 피해가 그보다 훨씬 '컸다'는 흐름이 되어야 해요. (c) smaller를 greater나 larger로 바꿔야 해요. (d) unappealing은 해충이 다른 식물을 좋아하지 않아 확산이 끊긴다는 뜻으로 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
When the community center asked for a volunteer to coach the Dolphins, an under-ten basketball team that had not won a single game in two seasons, seventeen-year-old Yena raised her hand before she could change her mind. She had played on her school team for years and assumed that teaching children would be easy. The first practice proved her wrong. Ten children ran in every direction, two of them burst into tears after missing shots, and one spent most of the hour lying on the bench. Walking home in the dark, (a)[she] wondered whether she had made a terrible mistake.

(B)
At the second practice, Yena decided to watch before she spoke. She soon noticed that the children were not lazy; they were afraid. Every missed shot drew groans from teammates, so most of them simply avoided the ball. Only one quiet boy, Theo, seemed unafraid of it, yet he never shot at all, passing the ball away the moment it reached him. That evening, (b)[she] threw out her plan of drills and invented a new rule: no one could shoot until every player on the team had touched the ball.

(C)
On the last Saturday of the season, the Dolphins trailed by one point with ten seconds left. Theo dribbled toward the basket, and the crowd expected him to pass as always. Instead he stopped, glanced at the bench, and grinned. Then he bounced the ball to Mia, the smallest player, who had never scored in a game. Her shot rolled around the rim and dropped in. As the buzzer sounded, parents rose and cheered, and (c)[the young coach] found that her eyes were wet. Later, Theo handed her the game ball, saying that (d)[he] wanted her to keep it.

(D)
The new rule changed everything. Because the ball had to move, every child got a chance, and missed shots stopped feeling like disasters. Theo, it turned out, saw the court better than anyone, and he began calling out where his teammates should run. The Dolphins still lost their next four games, but by smaller and smaller margins, and the children left practice laughing. Parents who had once waited in their cars came inside to watch. Yena started keeping a notebook of each player's small improvements, and (e)[she] read a few lines from it at the end of every practice.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 엉망이 된 첫 연습을 그린 (A) 뒤에, 두 번째 연습(At the second practice)에서 아이들의 두려움을 보고 새 규칙을 만드는 (B)가 와요. 그 새 규칙(The new rule)이 팀을 바꾸어 가는 (D), 시즌 마지막 경기에서 Mia의 슛으로 이기는 (C) 순서예요.

choices: Dolphins는 두 시즌 동안 한 경기도 이기지 못했다.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Hartley,

My name is Linh Tran, and I have lived in Maple Grove for eleven years. I read with interest the town's recent announcement about its new emergency alert system, which will send flood, storm, and road-closure warnings to residents by text message and post them on the town website. This is a valuable step, but I noticed that all of the messages will be issued only in English. Our neighborhood is home to more than two hundred Vietnamese-speaking families, many of whom are elderly and read little English. During last spring's flooding, several of my neighbors did not understand the evacuation notice until a relative phoned them hours later. I work as a certified medical interpreter, and I would be glad to translate the town's standard alert messages into Vietnamese free of charge. Two bilingual friends of mine have also agreed to help check the translations and respond quickly whenever new notices are needed. I would welcome the chance to meet with your office to discuss how we might begin.

Sincerely,
Linh Tran
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 긴급 문자 알림 서비스의 가입 방법을 문의하려고
지난봄 홍수 때 늦어진 대피 안내에 항의하려고
재난 알림 문구를 베트남어로 번역하는 봉사를 제안하려고
고령 주민을 위한 영어 교실 개설을 요청하려고
items.exp: 새 재난 알림이 영어로만 나간다는 점을 짚고, 의료 통역사인 자신이 기본 알림 문구를 무료로 베트남어로 번역하겠다고 제안하고 있어요. 지난봄 홍수 이야기는 번역이 필요한 근거로 든 것이지 항의가 아니에요.

items.passage: For the third time that afternoon, Jaemin leaned over his grandfather's shoulder and pointed at the green button on the tablet. "Just tap it once, Grandpa. Once, not three times." The old man nodded seriously, pressed the button with his thick finger, held it far too long, and somehow opened the calendar instead. Jaemin closed his eyes and counted silently to five. His friends were already waiting online for a game he was now going to miss. Why could something so simple take so long? He was about to suggest they try again tomorrow when his grandfather quietly took a folded piece of paper from his shirt pocket. On it, in careful, shaky handwriting, were the steps Jaemin had explained that morning, each one numbered, with small drawings of the buttons beside them. "I practiced after you left," his grandfather said, a little embarrassed. "I want to see your aunt's new baby in Canada before she grows up." Jaemin felt the irritation drain out of him all at once. He sat down beside the old man, his throat suddenly tight, and said softly, "Let's do it together."
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Jaemin의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 같은 설명을 세 번째 하며 눈을 감고 다섯까지 세고, 친구들과의 게임을 놓칠까 답답해했어요. 그러다 할아버지가 손수 적어 연습한 쪽지와 아기를 보고 싶다는 말을 듣고 짜증이 사라지며 목이 메었으므로 ④ frustrated → touched가 알맞아요. 처음부터 들뜬 상태가 아니었으므로 ⑤는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Most young people learn about money through rules handed down by adults: save part of your allowance, never borrow, avoid impulse purchases. Such advice is sound, but advice alone rarely produces good habits, because financial judgment, like most practical skills, develops through experience. A teenager who has never managed a budget has no feel for how quickly small purchases add up or how it feels to run short before the month ends. I believe parents and schools should therefore give adolescents real, if limited, control over money: a monthly sum to cover their own phone bill, transport, and clothing, with the freedom to make mistakes. Some of those mistakes will be painful. A student who spends most of the month's money in the first week will face several uncomfortable weeks. But a lesson learned at sixteen with forty dollars costs far less than the same lesson learned at twenty-five with a credit card. Protecting young people from every financial error simply postpones the education they will eventually need.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 청소년은 부모의 허락 없이 돈을 써서는 안 된다.
청소년에게 실제 돈을 관리할 권한을 주어 경험으로 배우게 해야 한다.
학교는 신용 카드 사용법을 정규 과목으로 가르쳐야 한다.
용돈은 매달 정해진 날짜에 일정하게 주어야 한다.
충동구매를 막기 위해 청소년의 지출을 기록하게 해야 한다.
items.exp: 돈에 관한 판단력은 조언이 아니라 경험으로 길러지므로, 청소년에게 실제 돈을 관리할 권한과 실수할 자유를 주어야 한다고 주장하는 글이에요. 그래서 ②가 알맞아요. ③의 신용 카드는 늦게 배울 때의 비용을 보여 주는 예일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: The body's defenses are usually described in military language of invaders, battles, and attacks, but a more revealing image may be that of a historian. When a microbe enters the body for the first time, the immune system responds slowly, testing and refining its antibodies over several days. Once the threat has been cleared, however, a small population of memory cells remains, each carrying a precise description of an enemy that may never return. Over a lifetime, these cells build up into a detailed record of every infection survived and every vaccine received. This record is not a passive archive. It actively shapes the present: a second encounter with the same microbe is met within hours rather than days, often so quickly that we never feel ill at all. In a sense, [your blood is a library of old illnesses]. The cost of this design is that the past can also mislead. When a virus changes only slightly, the body may respond with antibodies made for the older version, fighting today's battle with yesterday's weapons.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [your blood is a library of old illnesses]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Diseases that a person once had are likely to return later in life.
Blood samples allow doctors to trace a patient's full medical history.
Old illnesses gradually weaken the body's ability to fight new viruses.
The immune system forgets old threats in order to focus on new ones.
The body keeps a record of past infections that guides its later defenses.
items.exp: 면역 기억 세포가 지금까지 이겨 낸 감염의 기록으로 남아 같은 미생물이 다시 오면 훨씬 빨리 대응하게 해 준다는 뜻이에요. 의사가 혈액으로 병력을 알아낸다는 보기는 표현을 글자 그대로 읽은 오답이에요.

items.passage: In many countries, children begin formal reading lessons at five or even four, on the reasoning that an earlier start must produce stronger readers. Yet several education systems, including some that perform well in international comparisons, wait until children are six or seven before formal instruction begins. Studies comparing children taught to read at five with those taught at seven have found that the early starters gain a lead that largely disappears within a few years; by around the age of eleven, the two groups read about equally well, and some evidence suggests the later starters understand what they read slightly better. The explanation may lie in how the early years are used. Time spent on letter drills is time not spent on conversation, storytelling, pretend play, and exploring the world, the very activities that build the vocabulary and background knowledge on which reading comprehension depends. A child who can sound out words but has little to say about them will soon reach a ceiling. Starting later, in other words, is not doing less; it is laying a different and perhaps deeper foundation.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: why delaying formal reading instruction need not harm children's literacy
the benefits of beginning letter drills as early as possible
the difficulty of comparing education systems across countries
the role of parents in teaching children to sound out words
how pretend play can replace reading instruction entirely
items.exp: 읽기 정규 수업을 6~7세로 늦춰도 초기 격차가 몇 년 안에 사라지고, 그 시기에 대화·놀이로 이해력의 바탕을 쌓는다는 내용이에요. ⑤는 놀이가 읽기 수업을 '완전히 대신한다'고 지나치게 넓혔어요.

items.passage: For most of football's history, a goal produced an instant explosion of joy. The ball hit the net, the crowd roared, and the celebration was complete before anyone thought to question it. Video review has quietly changed this sequence. Now, when the ball crosses the line, many fans hesitate, glancing toward the referee and waiting to learn whether a camera somewhere has spotted an offside toe or a handball earlier in the play. The celebration has become provisional, and the joy, when it finally arrives several minutes later, often feels more like relief than delight. Supporters of the technology point out, reasonably, that decisions are now more accurate and that fewer matches are decided by obvious mistakes. Yet accuracy was never the only thing fans came for. Sport offers a rare experience of shared, spontaneous emotion, and that spontaneity depends on outcomes being settled in the moment. A system that improves fairness at the cost of immediacy may be solving one problem while creating another, less visible one.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Video Review Ended Refereeing Errors for Good
Why Fans Distrust Referees More Than Ever
Correct but Delayed: What Video Review Takes from Celebration
The Hidden Cost of Building Bigger Stadiums
Offside Rules Explained for New Supporters
items.exp: 비디오 판독이 판정을 정확하게 해 주었지만, 골 순간의 즉각적인 기쁨을 미루고 줄여 버렸다는 것이 글의 요점이에요. 오심이 완전히 사라졌다는 ①은 글의 일부만 과장했어요.

items.passage: Tomas Elvery was born in 1861 in a fishing village on the coast of Cornwall, England. His father was a boat builder, and as a boy Elvery spent long hours recording wind directions and cloud shapes in a notebook he kept beside his bed. At sixteen he went to sea as a ship's apprentice, and during eight years of voyages he collected more than four thousand weather observations from the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. After leaving the sea, he studied physics in London, where he began comparing his records with those of other sailors. In 1894 he published a chart showing that certain patterns of falling air pressure were followed by storms two days later, a finding that harbor officials soon used to send early warnings to fishermen. Elvery turned down several offers to lead national weather offices, preferring to teach at a small naval college in Plymouth. He died in 1930, and his notebooks are now kept at a maritime museum in Falmouth.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 국가 기상청 책임자 제의를 여러 차례 거절했다.
items.exp: 1894년의 도표는 항만 관리들이 곧바로 어부들에게 조기 경보를 보내는 데 사용했다고 했으니 외면당했다는 ④가 틀려요. 나머지는 지문 내용과 같아요.

items.passage: In the 1860s, steam-powered vehicles were beginning to appear on British roads, and lawmakers, ①[worried] about frightened horses and damaged road surfaces, responded with remarkable caution. The Locomotive Act of 1865 limited such vehicles to four miles per hour in the countryside and two in towns. It also required each vehicle to be preceded by a person on foot carrying a red flag, ②[warn] riders and drivers of its approach. The rule made some sense for slow, noisy machines that shared narrow roads with horses, but the requirement for a person walking ahead remained in force long after its original reasons ③[had faded]. By the time the first petrol-powered cars ④[arrived] in the 1890s, the law was widely blamed for holding back British motoring while builders in France and Germany, ⑤[where] no such limits applied, raced ahead. When the restrictions were finally lifted in 1896, enthusiasts celebrated with a drive from London to Brighton, an event that is still recreated every year. The episode is often cited as a warning about laws written for one technology and left unchanged as the world moves on.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ② 앞 문장의 동사는 required이고, 쉼표 뒤는 붉은 깃발을 든 사람의 목적을 나타내야 하므로 to warn(또는 warning)으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 lawmakers를 꾸미는 분사, ③은 remained보다 앞선 일을 나타내는 과거완료, ④는 과거 시제, ⑤는 France and Germany를 받는 관계부사로 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: We tend to assume that digital information, once saved, will last forever. In fact, digital records may be more ①[fragile] than paper ones. A letter written a century ago can still be read by anyone who picks it up, but a file created twenty years ago may be impossible to open today, not because the data has disappeared but because the software and machines needed to interpret it have become ②[obsolete]. Archivists sometimes call this danger a "digital dark age." Preserving a document therefore requires more than storing its bits; it requires keeping, or ③[recreating], the whole environment in which those bits make sense. Some institutions regularly move files into newer formats, accepting small losses of layout in exchange for continued access. Others maintain emulators, programs that imitate old computers so that original files can be opened in their original form. Both strategies are ④[costly] and demand constant attention. The lesson is that digital permanence is not a property of the medium itself but the result of ongoing effort, and information whose care is ⑤[guaranteed] will quietly slip out of reach.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 디지털 기록의 영속성은 꾸준한 노력의 결과라고 했으니, 손에서 멀어지는 것은 관리가 '보장된' 정보가 아니라 방치된 정보예요. 그래서 ⑤ guaranteed를 neglected 같은 말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: Anyone who has stepped outside after a heavy snowfall knows the strange hush that settles over a neighborhood. Traffic seems distant, footsteps vanish, and even voices sound flat and close. This quiet is not imagined. Freshly fallen snow is mostly air: the delicate crystals pile up loosely, leaving countless tiny pockets between them. When a sound wave enters this maze, it bounces from crystal to crystal, losing a little energy at every turn, until little of it escapes back into the open. A blanket of new snow only a few centimeters deep can thus behave much like the foam panels lining a recording studio. The effect, however, is temporary. As snow settles, melts slightly, and refreezes, its surface becomes hard and smooth, and the pockets close. An icy crust reflects sound rather than trapping it, so a winter street that was hushed at dawn may ring sharply by the following afternoon. What makes fresh snow so quiet, in other words, is its ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 갓 내린 눈은 결정 사이에 작은 공기 틈이 무수히 있어 소리를 가두고, 틈이 닫혀 표면이 단단하고 매끄러워지면 오히려 소리를 반사한다고 했어요. 따라서 조용함의 원인은 ① porousness(구멍이 많음)예요. ⑤ smoothness는 소리를 반사하게 만드는 성질이라 반대예요.

items.passage: When a miner is trapped underground or a child falls into a well, communities will spend almost any amount to bring that one person out alive, and few would call the expense wasteful. Yet the same communities often hesitate to spend a far smaller sum on safety measures that would, over time, prevent many more deaths: better ventilation in mines, covers over wells, guardrails on dangerous curves. Economists describe this as the gap between identified and statistical lives. The trapped miner has a name, a face, and a family waiting at the entrance; the people saved by a guardrail will never know they were saved, and no one can say which drivers they were. Our moral emotions are built to respond to the first kind of life and remain strangely quiet before the second. This is not simply a failure of reasoning, for a society that coldly abandoned a trapped miner because rescue was inefficient would damage something valuable in itself. Still, the imbalance carries a cost that is easy to overlook: ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: rescue efforts should be abandoned whenever their costs exceed their benefits
statistical lives matter less because no one can say who they are
communities that pay for rescues soon have nothing left for anything else
the lives it fails to protect are real, even though they will never appear in any headline
public emotion will correct the imbalance on its own without deliberate effort
items.exp: 이름과 얼굴이 있는 한 사람의 구조에는 큰돈을 쓰면서, 누구인지 알 수 없는 다수를 살릴 안전 대책은 소홀히 한다는 글이에요. 그 불균형의 대가는 '보이지 않지만 실제로 잃는 생명'이므로 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 구조를 포기하는 사회도 소중한 것을 해친다는 글과 맞지 않고, ②는 필자가 아닌 우리 감정의 편향을 사실처럼 말해요.

items.passage: Along the great roads of the Roman Empire stood stone columns known as milestones, placed at intervals of one Roman mile, or about 1.5 kilometers. At first glance they seem to have been nothing more than practical markers for people on the move. ① Each typically recorded the distance to the nearest major town along with the name of the emperor under whom the road had been built or repaired. ② For travelers, they offered useful information that made planning a long journey far easier, much as road signs do today. ③ Roman soldiers, who often marched more than twenty kilometers a day, were also trained to swim and to build fortified camps quickly at the end of each march. ④ For the government, however, the stones served a second purpose: by placing the emperor's name before the eyes of every passing merchant and farmer, they turned the road network into a continuous display of imperial power. ⑤ In this way, a simple tool of measurement also became a means of reminding distant provinces of who ruled them.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 이정표가 여행자에게는 실용적 정보를, 정부에게는 황제의 권위를 보여 주는 수단이었다는 흐름이에요. ③은 로마 병사의 행군 훈련 이야기로 이정표의 두 가지 역할과 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
English spelling is famously unreliable. The letters 'ough' are pronounced differently in 'though,' 'through,' and 'tough,' and silent letters appear in words such as 'knight' and 'knee.' Learners often assume that the system was simply designed badly, but in truth it was hardly designed at all.

(A) Much of the confusion dates from the late fifteenth century, when printing arrived in England. Printers needed fixed forms for words, and the spellings that became standard often reflected pronunciations of earlier times, when the 'k' in 'knight' was still spoken aloud.

(B) The result is a writing system that works less like a guide to modern speech than like a record of its history. Each irregular spelling preserves a trace of how English once sounded, which is why scholars of the language can read in it a kind of map of the past.

(C) At almost the same time, however, the language was in the middle of a major shift in pronunciation, especially in its long vowels. As speech kept changing, the printed forms stayed where they were, so spelling gradually froze around sounds that were disappearing.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: '거의 설계되지 않았다'는 말에 이어 15세기 인쇄술 도입이라는 시점을 처음 꺼내는 (A)가 먼저 와요. 그 시점을 At almost the same time으로 받아 발음 변화를 말하는 (C), 둘의 결과를 The result로 정리하는 (B) 순서예요.

items.passage: Legal and official documents have long been written in a style that ordinary readers find nearly impossible to follow: long sentences, passive constructions, and phrases such as 'notwithstanding the foregoing.' ( ① ) Lawyers have traditionally defended this style as a matter of precision, arguing that familiar legal phrases carry meanings settled by centuries of court decisions. ( ② ) When government agencies and banks have rewritten their forms and contracts in plain language and tested them on real readers, the new versions have usually proved just as legally sound, and sometimes more so, because drafting in simple sentences forced writers to notice ambiguities that dense prose had hidden. ( ③ ) The practical gains are considerable. ( ④ ) Readers make fewer errors when filling out forms, call help lines less often, and are more likely to understand the obligations they are agreeing to. ( ⑤ ) For these reasons, a number of countries now require that documents addressed to the public be written so that their intended readers can understand them on a first reading.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Yet studies of rewritten documents suggest that precision and clarity are rarely in real conflict.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 Yet으로 '정확성 때문에 어려운 문체가 필요하다'는 변호사들의 옹호를 반박하므로 그 바로 뒤인 ②에 와야 해요. 이어지는 '쉬운 말로 고쳐 쓴 문서도 법적으로 똑같이 탄탄했다'는 내용이 그 근거가 돼요. ①에는 아직 precision이 나오지 않았어요.

items.passage: Across cultures, people sing, dance, march, and chant together, often with no obvious practical purpose. Researchers have begun to suspect that such activities do something useful after all. In several experiments, groups of strangers were asked either to walk around a campus in step with one another or to walk normally. Afterward, they played a game in which each person could either put money into a shared pool or keep it. Those who had walked in step contributed more and reported feeling closer to their partners, even though they had met only minutes earlier. Similar effects appeared when participants sang together or tapped along to the same beat. Moving in time with others seems to blur, at least briefly, the boundary between self and group, making it easier to act for the group's benefit. This may help explain why armies drill, why religious communities chant in unison, and why sports fans sing together in the stands: shared rhythm is a low-cost way to turn a collection of individuals into a team.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Engaging in (A) ___ movement or sound with others tends to increase people's willingness to (B) ___ with them.
items.exp: 발맞춰 걷기, 함께 노래하기처럼 남과 박자를 맞춘 활동이 (A)에 해당하고, 그 뒤 공동 기금에 돈을 더 내는 등 집단을 위해 행동했다는 것이 (B)예요. 그래서 synchronized와 cooperate가 맞아요.

items.passage:
When a building is finished, we usually treat it as complete, a fixed object that will remain as its designers intended. Yet buildings that survive for generations rarely stay the way they were built. Owners add rooms, divide halls, and convert factories into apartments and churches into concert halls. A building's long life, in other words, is mostly a life of being (a)[altered] by people its architect never met.

Some buildings handle this well and others badly, and the difference often has little to do with their original beauty. A structure designed tightly around one specific use, with every wall placed for a particular function, tends to (b)[resist] change; when that use disappears, the building becomes expensive to adapt and is often torn down. By contrast, plain buildings with simple frames, high ceilings, and few internal supporting walls can be rearranged again and again. Old warehouses are a well-known example. Built cheaply and without much thought for appearance, they turned out to be remarkably (c)[flexible], housing offices, studios, shops, and homes over the course of a century.

This suggests that the most important quality a building can have may be not perfection but tolerance for future uses that no one can predict. Architects who accept this idea design some parts to be permanent and others to be easily replaced. The structure, which is costly to change, is made strong and simple, while interior walls, wiring, and fittings are treated as temporary layers that later occupants can (d)[preserve] without disturbing the frame. Such buildings are, in a sense, deliberately (e)[unfinished]. They leave room for the people who will live and work in them to complete the design, and in doing so, they last.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Built to Be Changed: Why Adaptable Buildings Endure
The Lost Beauty of Old Warehouses
Why Old Buildings Should Be Kept Unchanged
The Rising Cost of Modern Construction
items.exp: 오래 살아남는 건물은 완벽함보다 예측할 수 없는 미래의 용도를 받아들이는 융통성을 지녔다는 내용이에요. 그래서 '바뀌도록 지어진 건물이 오래간다'는 ①이 제목으로 알맞아요. 창고는 예시일 뿐이고 아름다움은 중요하지 않다고 했어요.

items.q: 밑줄 친 (a)~(e) 중에서 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 구조는 튼튼하게 두고 내부 벽·배선·설비는 나중 사용자가 골조를 건드리지 않고 바꿀 수 있는 임시 층으로 다룬다고 했어요. 그래서 (d) preserve는 replace나 remove로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
When the poster for the city's youth drawing contest appeared on the school bulletin board, Jiho signed up immediately. The theme was "My Neighborhood," and he already knew what he would draw: the great bridge over the river at sunset, its lights reflected on the dark water. Having practiced it many times, (a)[he] was sure it would impress the judges. But when he showed his first sketch to his grandmother, she studied it and asked quietly, "Is this the place you love, or the place you think other people will like?" Jiho did not know how to answer.

(B)
Two weeks later, the results were posted online. Jiho had not won first prize; that went to a beautifully detailed painting of a night market. But next to his name was a special award for "the work that best shows a neighborhood's heart." One judge had added a short comment: "Here is someone the artist has truly looked at." That evening, (b)[he] printed a small copy of the drawing and carried it to the repair booth. Mr. Bae held it under his lamp for a long while in silence. Then he taped it to the wall above his workbench, right where every customer would see it.

(C)
For days, Jiho walked the neighborhood with his sketchbook, trying to see it freshly. On the third afternoon, he stopped in front of a tiny booth at the corner of the market, where Mr. Bae had been repairing shoes for more than forty years. The old man was bent over a worn sneaker, surrounded by tools and scraps of leather. Jiho realized he had passed this booth daily without really seeing it. Shyly, (c)[he] asked if he could draw it. Mr. Bae laughed and said he had never been anyone's model, but he did not send the boy away.

(D)
On contest day, Jiho arrived at the community hall with his sketches of Mr. Bae's booth. Glancing around, he felt his stomach drop. At least five other students were drawing the great bridge, and a boy near the window was already working on a version as polished as a photograph. For a moment, Jiho thought about the old bridge sketch still folded in (d)[his] bag. Then he remembered his grandmother's question. He spread out his sketches of the booth and began to draw, while the boy by the window paused to admire (e)[his] own glowing river.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 할머니의 질문을 받은 지호가 동네를 다니다 배 씨의 구두 수선 부스를 발견하는 (C), 그 스케치를 들고 대회장에 가는 (D), 2주 뒤 결과 발표와 그림을 선물하는 (B) 순서예요. (D)의 Mr. Bae's booth는 (C)에서 처음 소개된 뒤에야 나올 수 있어요.

items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
