배 씨는 40년 넘게 시장 모퉁이에서 신발을 고쳐 왔다.
배 씨는 자신이 누구의 모델이 되어 본 적이 없다고 말했다.
창가 근처의 한 소년은 다리 그림을 그리고 있었다.
items.exp: (B)에서 1등상은 야시장 그림이 받았고 지호는 특별상을 받았다고 했으니 ②가 틀려요.

items.passage:
Dear Parents and Neighbors,

My name is Marcus Delaney, and I coach the under-twelve teams at the Northgate Youth Sports League. Every season, our league welcomes children from families of all backgrounds, and we are proud that no child has ever been turned away because of cost. This year, however, our registration has nearly doubled, and our supply of equipment has not kept up. Many of our newest players arrive at practice without shin guards, proper shoes, or a glove that fits. At the same time, I know that garages and closets throughout our community hold gear that children have simply outgrown. If your family has any clean, usable sports equipment that is no longer needed, I would be grateful if you would consider giving it to the league. Donations can be dropped off at the Northgate Community Center front desk any weekday between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. until March 15. Every item will go directly to a young player who needs it.

Warm regards,
Marcus Delaney
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 사용하지 않는 운동 용품의 기부를 요청하려고
새 운동 용품 구매를 위한 모금 행사를 알리려고
지역 주민 센터의 운영 시간 변경을 공지하려고
items.exp: 등록 인원이 늘어 장비가 부족하니 아이들이 더 쓰지 않는 깨끗한 운동 용품을 리그에 기부해 달라고 부탁하는 글이에요. 주민 센터 운영 시간은 기부 물품을 맡기는 방법으로 나온 것이에요.

items.passage: Seoyeon had been counting the days for a month. Her best friend Yuna, who had moved to Busan the previous spring, was finally coming to visit for the long weekend. Seoyeon had planned everything: the new bubble tea shop near the station, the photo booth where they used to take silly pictures, and a sleepover with the movie they had promised to watch together. On Friday morning, she cleaned her room twice and arranged a pile of snacks on her desk. Every few minutes, she checked the clock and imagined Yuna stepping off the train with her familiar wide grin. At noon, her phone buzzed. It was a message from Yuna: her grandmother had fallen ill, and the family needed to stay home. "I'm so sorry," the message ended. "Maybe next month?" Seoyeon read it three times. Then she sat down slowly on the edge of her bed, looking at the snacks she had arranged so carefully. The room, which had felt so bright that morning, now seemed strangely quiet and empty.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Seoyeon의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 친구의 방문을 손꼽아 기다리며 계획을 세우고 들떠 있다가, 방문이 취소됐다는 메시지를 받고 텅 빈 방을 바라보며 실망해요.

items.passage: When a city burns or is bombed, planners often see a rare chance to start over with broad, straight avenues. Remarkably often, however, the rebuilt city follows the old crooked streets almost exactly. The reason is not simple nostalgia. Beneath every street lie property lines, water pipes, and legal claims that took centuries to accumulate, and redrawing them would require negotiating with thousands of owners at once. As a result, the routes that medieval carts once took between a river crossing and a market square can still determine where a modern bus turns, which corners hold shops, and how wide a sidewalk can be. Decisions made for wooden wheels and walking cattle have hardened into a permanent framework within which every later generation must work. Urban historians sometimes put it this way: in the oldest districts of Europe, [the cart is still steering the traffic]. To understand why a city moves as it does today, then, one must often look not at its current transport plans but at the long-forgotten journeys that first wore its paths into the ground.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the cart is still steering the traffic]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Horse-drawn vehicles remain common in historic city centers.
Old transport routes continue to shape the layout of modern cities.
Modern traffic moves as slowly as carts did in the Middle Ages.
Planners keep old designs because residents miss the past.
Disasters allow cities to replace their crooked streets with new ones.
items.exp: 중세 수레가 다니던 길이 소유권·배관·법적 권리와 얽혀 굳어졌고, 그것이 지금도 버스 노선과 상점 위치, 인도 폭을 정한다고 했어요. 따라서 옛 교통로가 현대 도시의 구조를 여전히 결정한다는 뜻이에요. ④는 향수 때문이 아니라고 한 내용과, ⑤는 옛길을 그대로 따른다는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: Specialized vocabulary is often mocked as jargon, a deliberate fog that experts use to impress or exclude outsiders. The criticism is not entirely unfair, but it overlooks why such vocabulary develops in the first place. Within a community of specialists, a technical term compresses a long, carefully agreed definition into a single word. When one physician tells another that a patient shows a particular sign, or one engineer reports a specific type of fatigue in a metal, the term carries a precise meaning that would otherwise require several sentences and might still be misunderstood. In this setting, jargon is not a barrier but a tool of accuracy and speed. The difficulty arises when the same words travel beyond the group that shares their definitions. To a patient or a client, the compressed term is simply empty, and the precision it offered among colleagues turns into confusion. The responsible use of specialized language therefore depends on the audience: experts should use it freely among themselves, but they owe outsiders the effort of unpacking it into ordinary words.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 전문 용어는 외부인을 배제하려는 의도에서 만들어진다.
전문가들끼리도 전문 용어 대신 일상어를 써야 오해가 줄어든다.
전문 용어는 동료 사이에서는 유용하지만 외부인에게는 풀어 설명해야 한다.
일반인도 전문 분야의 용어를 익혀야 전문가와 소통할 수 있다.
전문 용어의 정의는 시간이 지나면서 점점 모호해진다.
items.exp: 전문 용어는 전문가 집단 안에서 긴 정의를 한 낱말로 압축해 정확하고 빠른 소통을 돕지만, 정의를 공유하지 않는 외부인에게는 빈말이 되니 풀어 말해 줘야 한다는 것이 요지예요. ①은 글이 '완전히 옳지는 않다'고 반박한 통념이고, ②는 동료끼리는 자유롭게 쓰라는 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage: A plant cannot see in the way an animal does, yet it is remarkably sensitive to the presence of its neighbors. Green leaves absorb most of the red light that falls on them but reflect and transmit much of the far-red light, a wavelength just beyond what human eyes can detect. As a result, light that has passed near or through other plants is rich in far-red and poor in red. Special pigments in the plant measure the ratio between these two kinds of light, and a falling ratio signals that competitors are close by, often before they have cast any actual shade. In response, many plants change their growth: they lengthen their stems, raise their leaves higher, and sometimes delay branching, all in an effort to reach the light before their neighbors do. This strategy carries costs, since resources put into height are not available for roots or seeds. Farmers who plant crops close together therefore face a trade-off, because crowded plants may spend energy outgrowing each other rather than producing grain.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: how plants sense and respond to nearby competitors through light
the ways plants defend themselves against animal herbivores
the role of red pigments in giving leaves their color
why far-red light is harmful to most crops
methods farmers use to increase sunlight on their fields
items.exp: 식물이 적색광과 원적색광의 비율로 이웃 식물을 감지해 줄기를 늘이는 등 성장을 바꾼다는 내용이에요. 원적색광이 해롭다는 ④는 글에 없고, 농부 이야기는 마지막에 덧붙인 결과예요.

items.passage: Imagine a gym that offers two memberships: a weekday-only pass for $40 a month and an unlimited pass for $70. Many customers, unsure whether they will really exercise on weekends, choose the cheaper pass. Now suppose the gym adds a third option that almost no one wants: a weekend-only pass for $65. Logically, this should change nothing, since both original options remain available at the same prices. Yet when choices are arranged in this way, noticeably more people tend to pick the unlimited pass. The unattractive option, which marketers call a decoy, succeeds not by being chosen but by making one comparison effortless. Deciding whether unlimited access is worth $30 more than weekday access requires guessing about one's future habits; seeing that it offers far more than the weekend pass for only $5 extra requires no thought at all. Because people find it hard to judge value in absolute terms, they rely on whatever comparisons a menu happens to provide. A seller who understands this need not lower a price to steer customers toward an option; it is enough to place the right companion beside it.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Cheaper Options Always Win Customers
The More Choices, the Harder the Decision
Honest Prices: The Key to Customer Trust
How Gyms Keep Their Members Coming Back
The Option No One Picks: How Decoys Steer Our Choices
items.exp: 거의 아무도 고르지 않는 주말 이용권(미끼)을 추가하면 무제한 이용권과의 비교가 쉬워져 그쪽을 고르는 사람이 늘어난다는 내용이에요. 그래서 '아무도 고르지 않는 선택지가 우리의 선택을 이끈다'는 ⑤가 알맞아요. ①은 싼 이용권을 고르던 사람들이 비싼 쪽으로 옮겨 간다는 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage:

items.q: Hillcrest Junior Robotics Camp 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 로봇 제작 경험이 없어도 참가할 수 있다.
참가자는 개별적으로 로봇을 만들어 대회에 나간다.
items.exp: 4~5일째에는 3명이 한 팀이 되어 로봇을 만들고 금요일 대회에 나간다고 했으니 개별적으로 만든다는 ④가 틀려요.

items.passage: Before the middle of the twentieth century, loading a cargo ship was a slow and costly process. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, and crates of every size, and teams of workers had to lift and arrange each piece by hand, a job ①[that] could keep a ship in port for a week or more. The introduction of the standardized steel container changed all of this. Because every container had the same dimensions and the same fittings at its corners, cranes could lift it directly from a truck or train and ②[place] it onto a ship in minutes. Ports that had once employed thousands of dock workers ③[needed] only a fraction of them, and the cost of moving goods across oceans fell dramatically. Economists still debate how much of the growth in world trade since the 1960s ④[should credit] to the container, but few doubt that it played a major role. Ironically, an invention ⑤[so] simple that it is little more than a large metal box reshaped the global economy more than many complex technologies did.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④는 '성장의 얼마만큼이 컨테이너 덕분으로 여겨져야 하는지'라는 뜻이라 주어 how much와 동사 credit이 수동 관계예요. 그래서 should be credited로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 a job을 받는 관계대명사, ②는 lift와 병렬인 원형, ③은 과거 동사, ⑤는 so ~ that 구문이라 맞아요.

items.passage: Wooden shipwrecks rarely survive long on the seafloor. In most of the world's oceans, a small, worm-like clam called the shipworm bores into sunken timber and can ①[reduce] a hull to fragments within a few decades. The Baltic Sea is a striking exception. Its water is far less salty than the open ocean, and the shipworm, which needs higher salinity to thrive, is largely ②[absent] from its central and northern parts. Cold temperatures and low oxygen levels near the bottom further slow the decay of wood. As a result, the Baltic seafloor holds hundreds of wrecks from the medieval and early modern periods in a state of ③[preservation] that astonishes divers, some with masts still standing and carvings still visible. For archaeologists, these sites reveal what written sources rarely describe: the actual methods by which ships were built, loaded, and repaired. Researchers worry, however, that this protection may be ④[permanent]. As the climate warms and the chemistry of the sea shifts, shipworms have been found farther into the Baltic than before, and wrecks that have lasted for centuries could ⑤[disappear] within a generation.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 연구자들이 걱정하는 내용이고, 뒤에서 배좀벌레가 발트해 안쪽으로 퍼져 난파선이 사라질 수 있다고 했으므로 보호가 '일시적'일 수 있다는 흐름이에요. 따라서 ④ permanent를 temporary로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage: In the second half of the nineteenth century, the electric telegraph allowed a message to cross a continent, and later an ocean, in minutes rather than weeks. But this speed came at a price, and the price was charged by the word. A short international message could cost as much as a laborer earned in several days, so senders learned to strip their language to its bones. Articles, greetings, and polite phrases disappeared; a merchant might write "ARRIVE MONDAY SHIP DELAYED" and trust the reader to supply the rest. Commercial firms went further, buying thick codebooks in which a single invented word stood for an entire sentence such as "Prices have fallen; do not buy until further notice." A whole style of writing, clipped and stripped of every unnecessary syllable, grew directly out of the tariff sheet. Some observers even credited the telegraph with encouraging the plain, compressed prose of journalists who sent their stories over the wire. The cost of each word, in other words, rewarded ___ above every other quality of expression.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 전보 요금이 낱말 수로 매겨져 인사말과 관사를 빼고, 한 낱말로 한 문장을 대신하는 암호책까지 썼다고 했어요. 그러니 낱말당 비용이 '간결함'을 가장 높이 보상했다는 뜻의 brevity가 알맞아요. 암호책이 나오지만 비밀 유지가 아니라 비용 절감이 목적이므로 secrecy는 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: A piano appears to be the most exact of instruments: each key produces a fixed pitch, and a tuner can set every string with electronic precision. Yet almost every interval on a modern piano is, strictly speaking, out of tune. The reason lies in a mathematical inconvenience. Intervals that sound perfectly pure to the ear correspond to simple ratios between frequencies, but these ratios do not fit together neatly; a chain of twelve pure fifths, which ought to return to its starting note several octaves higher, overshoots that note by a small but audible amount. Earlier tuning systems kept certain intervals pure and pushed the leftover error into rarely used keys, which then sounded so harsh that composers avoided them. The system now standard divides the octave into twelve equal steps, spreading the error so evenly that no interval is pure but none is unbearable. What musicians gained in return was the freedom to write in any key and to move between keys at will, a freedom on which much of later Western music depends. The modern piano, then, embodies a deliberate bargain: it ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: preserves the purity of every interval by avoiding the most difficult keys
accepts a slight flaw everywhere in exchange for being usable anywhere
allows each performer to correct the errors of the tuner while playing
sacrifices the freedom to change keys for the beauty of pure sound
proves that mathematical ratios matter less to music than the ear suggests

items.passage: In professional cycling, the rider at the front of a group works much harder than the riders behind. At racing speeds, most of a cyclist's effort goes into pushing air out of the way, and a rider tucked closely behind another can save a large share of that energy. ① This simple physical fact shapes nearly every tactic in a road race. ② Teammates take turns at the front, protecting their leader in the shelter behind them so that he or she will have fresh legs for the final climb or sprint. ③ Riders who break away alone must be considerably stronger than those in the main group, since they face the wind with no one to share the burden. ④ The earliest bicycles had no pedals at all, and riders moved them forward by pushing their feet along the ground. ⑤ For this reason, a lone escape usually succeeds only when the chasing group hesitates or cannot organize itself to share the work of pursuit.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 앞사람 뒤에 붙어 공기 저항을 줄이는 원리가 도로 경주 전술을 좌우한다는 흐름이에요. ④는 초기 자전거에 페달이 없었다는 역사 이야기로 흐름과 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
The satellites that make up a navigation system each carry extremely precise atomic clocks. A receiver on the ground calculates its position by comparing the times at which signals from several satellites arrive, so even tiny errors in those clocks matter.

(A) The two effects work in opposite directions, but they are not equal. Taken together, they cause the satellite clocks to gain about 38 microseconds each day compared with clocks on the ground. That sounds trivial, yet left uncorrected it would cause position errors to grow by roughly ten kilometers every day.

(B) Surprisingly, keeping these clocks accurate requires Einstein's theories of relativity. According to special relativity, a clock moving at high speed runs slightly slower, and the satellites travel at nearly four kilometers per second.

(C) General relativity, however, predicts the opposite effect from gravity. Because the satellites orbit far above the Earth, where gravity is weaker, their clocks run slightly faster than clocks on the surface.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 이 시계들을 정확히 유지하는 데 상대성 이론이 필요하다며 특수 상대성 이론부터 소개하는 (B), however로 반대 효과인 일반 상대성 이론을 말하는 (C), The two effects로 두 효과를 합쳐 결론을 내는 (A) 순서예요.

items.passage: For thousands of years, much of the strength of a horse was wasted in heavy farm work. ( ① ) The harnesses used in the ancient Mediterranean world attached the load to a strap that ran across the animal's throat. ( ② ) When a horse leaned forward to pull, this strap pressed against its windpipe and the large blood vessels of the neck, so the harder it worked, the more it choked. ( ③ ) Oxen, whose bodies were suited to a wooden yoke placed over the shoulders, therefore remained the main plow animals in many regions, despite being much slower. ( ④ ) Because the load now rested on the bony shoulders rather than the soft throat, a horse could throw its full weight into the work and breathe freely while doing so. ( ⑤ ) In parts of northern Europe, where heavy, wet soils demanded great force, the faster horse gradually replaced the ox, allowing a farmer to plow far more land in a single day.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The change came with the padded collar, a stiff ring that fitted around the horse's neck and transferred the pull to its shoulders.
items.exp: ④ 앞까지는 목을 조이는 마구 때문에 말 대신 소가 쓰였다는 내용이고, ④ 뒤는 the load now rested on the bony shoulders로 이미 바뀐 상황을 말해요. 그 사이에 하중을 어깨로 옮기는 패드 달린 목걸이가 등장했다는 주어진 문장이 와야 now가 가리키는 변화가 생겨요.

items.passage: For much of the twentieth century, beavers were treated as pests in many parts of North America, trapped or removed because their dams flooded roads and fields. More recently, scientists studying dry regions have begun to see these animals differently. A beaver dam slows the flow of a stream and spreads water across the surrounding land, creating ponds and wetlands that hold water long after the rains have stopped. Studies comparing streams with and without beavers have found that sections with dams stay green and moist during droughts, while nearby areas without them dry out. When wildfires swept through some western valleys, researchers using satellite images noticed bright green strips of vegetation running through the blackened landscape, exactly where beaver ponds had kept the ground wet. Because a single family of beavers can build and maintain these structures at no cost, some land managers now reintroduce them deliberately, treating them as partners in protecting landscapes from a hotter, drier climate.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

By (A) ___ water in the landscape, beaver dams make surrounding areas more (B) ___ to drought and fire.
items.exp: 댐이 물의 흐름을 늦추고 비가 그친 뒤에도 물을 머금게 하니 (A)는 retaining, 가뭄에도 푸르고 산불 속에서도 녹색 띠로 남았으니 (B)는 resistant예요. ④는 (B)가 글의 내용과 반대예요.

items.passage:
Walk through a hospital's intensive care unit and you will hear a near-constant chorus of beeps. Each patient may be connected to several monitors, and each monitor is designed to sound an alarm whenever a reading crosses a set threshold. On paper, this seems like the safest possible arrangement: no dangerous change should ever go (a)[unnoticed].

In practice, the arrangement often works against its purpose. Studies of intensive care units have found that the large majority of alarms do not require any action. A patient shifts in bed and a sensor slips; a heart rate rises briefly during a cough; a threshold set for an average adult is crossed by a patient for whom the reading is normal. Nurses who hear hundreds of such signals in a single shift learn, quite (b)[reasonably], that most of them mean nothing. They begin to silence alarms automatically, to turn down volumes, or to respond more slowly, and the rare alarm that signals a real emergency is (c)[lost] among the false ones. Safety experts call this alarm fatigue, and it has been linked to cases in which patients were harmed while their monitors were sounding.

The lesson is that a warning system is only as useful as the attention it receives, and attention is a (d)[limited] resource. Every unnecessary alarm draws a little from that supply. Hospitals that have tackled the problem have done so not by adding alarms but by removing them: adjusting thresholds to individual patients, adding short delays so that momentary changes are ignored, and sending only the most serious signals directly to staff. In several cases, the number of alarms fell sharply while patient safety improved. Beyond a certain point, then, each additional warning leaves patients (e)[safer], since it adds to the noise that hides the very dangers alarms were meant to reveal.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Better Sensors: The Key to Safer Hospitals
When Too Many Warnings Make Us Less Safe
Why Nurses Should Respond to Every Alarm
The Rising Cost of Intensive Care Equipment
How Hospitals Train Their Staff to Ignore Noise
items.exp: 병원 경보가 너무 많으면 간호사들이 경보에 둔해져 진짜 위급 신호를 놓치고, 경보를 줄였더니 오히려 환자 안전이 나아졌다는 내용이에요. 그래서 '너무 많은 경고가 우리를 덜 안전하게 만들 때'라는 ②가 알맞아요. ①은 센서 개선이 아니라 경보 수를 줄인 것이 해결책이었다는 글과 맞지 않아요.

items.exp: 경고가 늘어날수록 위험을 가리는 소음이 커진다고 했으니, 어느 지점을 넘으면 경고를 더할 때마다 환자가 덜 안전해진다고 해야 해요. 그래서 (e) safer를 less safe 같은 말로 바꿔야 해요.

items.passage:
(A)
By the second night of the typhoon, the island of Garam had been cut off from the mainland for thirty hours. The power lines were down, the cell tower had gone silent, and the ferry had stopped running. At the village clinic, the nurse was growing worried about Mrs. Baek, an elderly woman whose heart medicine would run out the next morning. Minho, a high school student who had joined his school's amateur radio club only that spring, overheard the nurse talking to his mother and suddenly sat up. (a)[He] knew someone who might help.

(B)
Minho pressed the button and spoke the call sign slowly, just as he had practiced so many times at club meetings. For several minutes there was nothing but static. Then a faint voice answered: a radio operator in the port city on the mainland. With Mr. Hale beside him whispering the proper phrases, Minho explained the situation, spelled out the name of the medicine letter by letter, and repeated the clinic's location twice. The operator promised to contact the coast guard at once, and when the line went quiet, Minho could still feel (b)[his] heart pounding.

(C)
He ran through the rain to the house of Mr. Hale, a retired ship's radio officer who taught the club on weekends. The old man kept a battery-powered transmitter in his study, and within an hour the two of them had stretched a wire antenna between the roof and a pine tree. But when Mr. Hale reached for the microphone, (c)[his] hands were shaking from the cold and from an old illness. He looked at the boy and said quietly, "Your voice is steadier than mine tonight. (d)[You] make the call."

(D)
Shortly after dawn, a coast guard boat appeared through the thinning rain, carrying a box of medicine for Mrs. Baek. That afternoon, Mr. Hale handed Minho a worn notebook in which he had recorded every contact he had made at sea for forty years. On the first empty page, Minho carefully wrote down the details of the night's call, and when (e)[he] signed his name beneath them, the old radio officer smiled and told him the notebook was his to keep.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 도움을 줄 사람을 떠올린 Minho가 Mr. Hale의 집으로 달려가 안테나를 세우는 (C), 직접 무전을 걸어 육지와 연락하는 (B), 다음 날 해안 경비대 배가 약을 싣고 오는 (D) 순서예요. (B)에서 Mr. Hale이 처음 소개 없이 등장하므로 (C) 뒤에 와야 해요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Haddad,

I own Pageturn Books on Merrow Street, one of eleven small shops on the block between Fourth and Sixth Avenue. Last week, we received a notice from your office stating that the sidewalk on our block will be torn up and repaved from November 20 to December 31. We fully support the project; the cracked pavement has caused more than one customer to trip, and we are grateful that the city has finally set aside funds to repair it. However, for most shops on our street, the six weeks before the new year bring in nearly a third of our annual sales. With our entrances blocked by fencing and heavy equipment during that period, many of us fear that we will not survive until spring. I am therefore writing on behalf of the Merrow Street merchants to ask whether the construction could be moved to January and February, when business is usually slow. We would be glad to meet with your staff at any time to discuss a schedule that works for everyone.

Sincerely,
Ruth Calloway
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 보도 보수 공사에 대한 지지를 표명하려고
보도 공사 시기를 비수기로 옮겨 줄 것을 요청하려고
보도에서 넘어진 손님에 대한 보상을 요구하려고
연말 상점가 할인 행사 참여를 권유하려고
공사 관련 상인 설명회 개최를 안내하려고
items.exp: 연말 6주가 연 매출의 3분의 1을 차지하는데 그때 공사로 입구가 막히면 어렵다고 설명한 뒤, 공사를 장사가 한산한 1~2월로 옮길 수 있는지 묻고 있어요. 공사를 지지한다는 말은 요청 앞의 배경일 뿐 목적이 아니에요.

items.passage: On my third night as a volunteer at the animal shelter, I was assigned to a gray dog named Biscuit who had been found tied to a fence two months earlier. The staff warned me that he trusted no one. For an hour I sat on the cold floor outside his kennel, holding out treats and speaking softly, exactly as I had been trained to do. Biscuit stayed pressed against the back wall, his eyes fixed on me, refusing to move even an inch. I checked the clock again and again. Nothing I did seemed to make the slightest difference, and I began to wonder why I had signed up at all. Near the end of my shift, I gave up on the treats and simply sat there with my hand resting on the floor, too tired to try anything else. A few minutes later, I heard the quiet click of claws on concrete. Biscuit crept forward, sniffed my fingers, and slowly lowered his head onto my palm. I held my breath, my eyes suddenly wet, afraid that the smallest movement would break the moment.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 한 시간 동안 아무리 애써도 개가 꼼짝하지 않자 시계만 보며 왜 자원했나 싶어 답답해하다가, 개가 다가와 손바닥에 머리를 얹자 눈물이 맺힐 만큼 감동해요. 그래서 frustrated → moved가 알맞아요. 개가 다가온 뒤 겁에 질린 것은 아니에요.

items.passage: When a student is stuck on a problem, the most natural response for a caring teacher is to step in at once with a clear explanation. The explanation feels efficient, the student looks relieved, and the lesson moves forward. Yet this rescue often comes too early. A learner who has never wrestled with a problem has no sense of where its difficulty lies, so the teacher's elegant solution answers a question the student has not yet learned to ask. By contrast, a student who has spent fifteen minutes trying several approaches, even unsuccessful ones, arrives at the explanation with a set of half-formed ideas that the new knowledge can attach to. The failed attempts are not wasted time; they prepare the ground. This does not mean leaving students alone in frustration for an entire class. It means designing the lesson so that students first face a challenging task with the tools they already have, and only afterward receive the instruction that organizes what they discovered. Teachers should resist the urge to rescue and instead let a period of productive struggle come before explanation.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 교사는 학생이 실패하지 않도록 단계별 안내를 제공해야 한다.
학생의 좌절감을 줄이기 위해 과제의 난이도를 낮춰야 한다.
수업 시간은 효율적인 설명 위주로 운영되어야 한다.
학생 스스로 질문을 만들도록 토론 수업을 늘려야 한다.
교사는 설명에 앞서 학생이 문제와 씨름하는 시간을 주어야 한다.
items.exp: 마지막 문장에서 교사는 곧바로 구해 주려는 충동을 참고 설명 전에 '생산적인 씨름'의 시간을 주어야 한다고 주장해요. ①③은 필자가 비판하는 즉각적인 설명과 같은 방향이라 오답이에요.

items.passage: In many workplaces, effort is easier to see than results. A manager can observe who arrives first and leaves last, who answers messages within minutes, and whose calendar is crowded with meetings, but the value of a well-designed plan or a problem quietly prevented may not become clear for months. Because what is visible gets rewarded, employees learn to display activity: they stay late even when their work is done, copy colleagues on every email, and schedule meetings to show that they are involved. None of this is dishonest, exactly, and much of it feels productive to the people doing it. Yet the signals of work gradually crowd out the work itself. Hours spent looking busy are hours not spent thinking, and the employee who finishes early by working efficiently may appear less committed than the one who struggles slowly. An organization that judges its people this way risks [mistaking the roar of the engine for the speed of the car]. The noise is real, but it reveals how hard the machine is running, not how far it is actually going.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [mistaking the roar of the engine for the speed of the car]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: valuing workers who learn quickly over those with long experience
rewarding results so strictly that cooperation is discouraged
treating visible signs of effort as evidence of real accomplishment
assuming that faster machines will eventually replace slower workers
ignoring the stress that long working hours place on employees
items.exp: 늦게까지 남기, 모든 메일 참조, 회의 잡기처럼 눈에 보이는 활동이 보상받으면서 실제 성과와 혼동된다는 글이에요. 엔진 소리는 얼마나 세게 돌아가는지만 알려 줄 뿐 얼마나 나아갔는지는 아니라는 마지막 문장이 근거라서 ③이 맞아요. ②는 결과를 너무 엄격히 따진다는 말이라 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: Speakers are often taught to eliminate "uh" and "um" from their speech, as if these sounds were nothing more than verbal clutter revealing a lack of preparation. Linguists who study spontaneous conversation, however, have found that such fillers are far from random. Speakers tend to use "uh" before a short pause and "um" before a longer one, and they produce fillers more often just before an unusual word, a complex idea, or a change of topic. Listeners, in turn, appear to make use of these signals. In laboratory studies, people who hear a filler before a word tend to recognize it more quickly when it is unexpected, as though the hesitation had warned them to prepare for something less predictable. Fillers also help manage the flow of turns in conversation: a speaker who says "um" while searching for a word is signaling that she has not finished and should not yet be interrupted. Far from being a failure of communication, then, the humble filler is a small coordinating device that helps speakers and listeners stay in step.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the communicative functions served by hesitation sounds in speech
the need to train speakers to remove fillers from their speech
differences in the use of fillers across languages and cultures
how unexpected words make conversations harder to follow
the reasons listeners interrupt speakers who pause too often
items.exp: 'uh', 'um' 같은 망설임 소리가 쉼의 길이를 알리고, 듣는 사람이 예상 밖의 낱말을 준비하게 하며, 말 차례를 조절하는 역할을 한다는 내용이에요. ②는 글이 반박하는 통념이에요.

items.passage: When shoppers compare two pairs of boots, one priced at forty dollars and the other at one hundred and sixty, the cheaper pair almost always looks like the better deal. The price tag, however, measures only what we pay at the moment of purchase, not what we pay for the service the product provides. If the inexpensive boots fall apart after a single winter while the costly ones, resoled twice, last eight winters, the true cost per season of the "expensive" pair is half that of the "bargain." Economists sometimes describe this as the difference between purchase price and lifetime cost, and the gap can be surprisingly large for anything we use repeatedly, from kitchen knives to washing machines. People with limited incomes are hit hardest, since they often cannot afford the higher initial payment and are forced to buy the cheaper item again and again, spending more over time than wealthier buyers do. In this way, being unable to pay more at the start can make a person pay more in the end.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Expensive Goods Are Always Worth the Money
Shopping Habits That Separate the Rich from the Poor
How Repairs Keep Old Products on the Market
The Price Tag Trap: Why Consumers Prefer Discounts
Cheap Today, Costly Tomorrow: The Real Price of Durability
items.exp: 구입 가격보다 오래 쓰는 동안 드는 비용이 진짜 가격이며, 싼 물건이 결국 더 비쌀 수 있다는 내용이라 ⑤가 알맞아요. ①은 'Always'가 지나친 일반화이고, ②는 소득 이야기가 일부에만 나와요.

items.passage: Lucienne Gardel (1872–1950) was a French cook and teacher who transformed the way cooking was taught in schools. Born in a village near Lyon, she learned to cook in her grandmother's inn, where recipes were passed on by memory and measured by handfuls. At nineteen she moved to Lyon to work in a restaurant kitchen, but she grew frustrated that apprentices were expected to learn simply by watching and were rarely told why a dish succeeded or failed. In 1903 she opened a small evening school where working women could study cooking free of charge, and she required every student to write down each step and weigh every ingredient. Her book Cooking Explained, published in 1911, was written in plain language and gave the reasons behind each technique rather than instructions alone. Although several Paris publishers offered large sums for the rights, she sold the book cheaply so that schools could afford it. During the First World War she organized kitchens that fed thousands of refugees, and her methods were later adopted by schools across the country.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 1911년에 출간된 책에는 각 기술의 이유가 담겼다.
제1차 세계 대전 중 피란민을 먹이는 주방을 조직했다.
items.exp: 1903년에 연 저녁 학교는 일하는 여성들이 free of charge, 즉 무료로 요리를 배울 수 있는 곳이었으므로 ③이 틀려요. 나머지는 grandmother's inn, At nineteen, the reasons behind each technique, fed thousands of refugees와 일치해요.

items.passage: Long before the telegraph, empires faced a basic problem: news could travel no faster than a horse. The Romans addressed this with a state relay system ①[known] as the cursus publicus, in which official messengers changed horses at stations placed along the major roads. A messenger ②[who] rode at full speed for a single stage could hand his dispatch to a fresh rider, so the message itself never had to rest. Under good conditions, important news could cover well over a hundred kilometers in a day. The system, however, was expensive to maintain, and the costs fell heavily on the towns ③[through which] the roads passed, since they were required to supply animals, food, and lodging. Complaints about officials who used the stations for private travel ④[was] common, and several emperors issued orders limiting who could carry the permits that granted access. Even so, the network remained in use for centuries, ⑤[allowing] a vast state to govern provinces that lay weeks away from its capital by ordinary travel.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ④의 주어는 복수 명사 Complaints이므로 was를 were로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 system을 꾸미는 과거분사, ③은 the roads passed through the towns 구조의 '전치사+관계대명사', ⑤는 결과를 나타내는 분사구문이라 맞아요.

items.passage: Tall buildings are designed to move. A skyscraper that tried to stand perfectly rigid against strong winds would need enormous amounts of steel and concrete, and even then the forces might ①[crack] its frame. Engineers instead allow the structure to bend slightly, so that the top of a very tall tower may sway by a meter or more during a storm. The building itself is in no danger, but its occupants are another matter. Humans are surprisingly ②[insensitive] to slow, repeated motion, and office workers on upper floors may feel dizzy or even seasick long before the structure is at any risk. To ③[reduce] this effect, many towers contain a tuned mass damper: a huge weight, sometimes hundreds of tons, hung or mounted near the top of the building. When the wind pushes the tower in one direction, the damper's inertia makes it lag behind and move ④[opposite] to the building, pulling against the sway and gradually draining its energy. The damper is carefully adjusted so that its natural rhythm ⑤[matches] that of the building; only then does it absorb the motion efficiently rather than adding to it.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 건물이 위험해지기 훨씬 전에 위층 사람들이 어지럼이나 멀미를 느낀다고 했으므로 사람은 느리고 반복되는 흔들림에 민감한 거예요. 따라서 ②의 insensitive를 sensitive로 바꿔야 해요. ④는 댐퍼가 관성 때문에 건물과 반대로 움직여 흔들림을 잡는다는 내용과 맞아요.

items.passage: Why do experienced athletes sometimes fail at the very moment their skills matter most? One explanation focuses on where attention goes under pressure. A beginner learning to putt in golf must think through each step, including the grip, the stance, and the angle of the club, and performance depends on this careful attention. With years of practice, however, the movement becomes ___, run by routines that operate largely outside conscious awareness. When the stakes rise, an expert may begin to worry about making a mistake and, in an effort to be careful, start monitoring the movement step by step, as a novice would. This well-intentioned attention interferes with a process that works best when left alone, and the smooth action breaks down into a series of awkward, separate parts. Some coaches therefore encourage athletes in high-pressure moments to focus on a single external target or even to hum a simple tune, keeping the conscious mind occupied so that the practiced skill can run on its own.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 빈칸 뒤 '의식 밖에서 작동하는 루틴에 의해 움직인다'와 마지막 문장의 '연습된 기술이 저절로 돌아가게'로 보아 동작이 자동화된다는 뜻의 automatic이 알맞아요. deliberate는 초보자의 단계별 주의에 해당해 반대예요.

items.passage: We tend to imagine that a perfect memory would preserve everything, and that every act of discarding is a small defeat in the struggle against time. Archivists know otherwise. An archive that kept every receipt, draft, and passing note would not be a richer record of the past but an unusable one, because significance can only emerge against a background of what has been set aside. To decide that one letter matters is already to decide that a thousand others matter less, and this judgment is not an unfortunate limitation on the archive but the very act that gives it a shape. The same is true of individual memory. A person who could recall every moment of every day with equal vividness would have no way to tell which experiences had defined her, since nothing would stand out from anything else. Remembering, in this sense, is less like storing and more like editing. What an archive or a mind preserves is meaningful only because of ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the accuracy with which it records each event
the technology that allows it to store more data
the effort it makes to resist the passage of time
the people who consult it long after it was made
the countless things it has chosen to let go
items.exp: 의미는 버려진 것들을 배경으로만 드러나고, 기억은 저장이 아니라 편집에 가깝다고 했어요. 그러니 보존된 것이 의미를 갖는 것은 버리기로 한 수많은 것들 덕분이에요. ①③은 글이 부정하는 '모두 보존하기' 통념에 가까워요.

items.passage: A woodpecker may strike a tree trunk around twenty times a second, its head stopping abruptly with each blow, yet the bird shows no sign of the brain injuries that such impacts would cause in a human. ① For a long time, scientists assumed that the bird's skull worked like a helmet, with spongy bone and other special structures absorbing the shock before it reached the brain. ② More recent studies using high-speed video, however, found that the head barely cushions the blow at all; the beak and skull slow down almost as sharply as a rigid hammer would. ③ Woodpeckers also play an important role in forest ecosystems, since the holes they carve later serve as nests for owls, squirrels, and many other animals. ④ The real protection appears to come from size: because a woodpecker's brain is tiny and tightly packed within the skull, it experiences far less strain from the same sudden stop than a large human brain would. ⑤ This also explains why evolution never favored a softer skull, since any cushioning would waste the energy the bird needs to drive its beak into the wood.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 딱따구리가 머리를 세게 부딪쳐도 뇌가 다치지 않는 이유를 다루는 글인데, ③은 딱따구리 구멍이 다른 동물의 둥지가 된다는 생태계 역할을 말해 흐름에서 벗어나요. ①의 기존 가설을 ②가 however로 반박하고, ④가 진짜 이유, ⑤가 그 결과를 이어 가요.

items.passage:
Leaf-cutter ants can be seen marching in long lines through tropical forests, each carrying a piece of leaf many times larger than its own head. It would be natural to assume that the ants are carrying food home to eat.

(A) On this paste grows a particular fungus, and it is the fungus, not the leaves, that feeds the colony. The ants weed out competing molds, add their own waste as fertilizer, and even carry pieces of the fungus with them when a new queen leaves to found a colony.

(B) This partnership is so old and so close that neither partner could now easily survive without the other. The fungus no longer lives freely in the wild, and the ants depend on it entirely, an arrangement that humans, with the invention of agriculture, reached only some ten thousand years ago.

(C) In fact, they cannot digest the leaves at all. Instead, the fragments are brought deep underground, where smaller workers chew them into a soft paste and spread it over carefully tended chambers.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 개미가 먹이를 나른다는 추측을 (C)의 In fact가 뒤집고 잎을 반죽(paste)으로 만든다고 해요. (A)의 this paste가 그 반죽을 받고, (B)의 This partnership은 (A)에서 설명한 개미와 균류의 관계를 가리켜요. 그래서 (C)-(A)-(B)예요.

items.passage: Among the earliest photographs of a city street is a view of a Paris boulevard taken from an upper window in 1838. ( ① ) At first glance, the image shows a strangely quiet scene: rows of buildings, a line of bare trees, and a wide road with no one on it. ( ② ) Historians know, however, that the boulevard at that hour of the day would have been crowded with carriages, horses, street vendors, and people on foot hurrying to work or to market. ( ③ ) Where, then, did they all go? ( ④ ) Anything that moved through the frame during that time left too faint a trace to register on the plate, and so the busy traffic simply vanished from the picture. ( ⑤ ) The only exception is a tiny figure near a street corner: a man who stood still long enough to have his boots polished, and who thereby became one of the first people ever to appear in a photograph.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The answer lies in the length of the exposure, which lasted for several minutes.
items.exp: ④ 앞의 'Where, then, did they all go?'라는 질문에 주어진 문장의 The answer가 답하고, ④ 뒤의 during that time은 주어진 문장의 노출 시간(several minutes)을 가리켜요. 다른 자리에는 질문도, that time이 가리킬 대상도 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Hotel room attendants spend their days lifting mattresses, pushing heavy carts, and climbing stairs, yet when researchers asked a group of them how much exercise they got, most answered that they hardly exercised at all. The researchers then divided the workers into two groups. One group was given a short presentation explaining that their daily work met official recommendations for an active lifestyle, along with examples of how many calories each task burned. The other group received no such information. Neither group changed its workload, and a follow-up check found no meaningful difference in what they ate or did outside work. Four weeks later, however, the informed workers had lost weight, lowered their blood pressure, and reduced their body fat, while the other group showed no comparable change. The researchers suggested that how people interpret their activity may influence its effects on the body, possibly by altering stress levels or the small ways they move during the day. What we believe about our effort, it seems, is not entirely separate from what that effort does.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

When workers came to (A) ___ their ordinary labor as exercise, they showed (B) ___ health improvements despite no change in their routines.
items.exp: 일상 업무가 운동 권장량을 충족한다는 설명을 들은 노동자들은 자신의 일을 운동으로 여기게(regard) 되었어요. 생활은 그대로였는데도 체중과 혈압, 체지방이 실제로 줄었으므로 (B)는 measurable이 알맞아요.

items.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, forest managers in many countries treated every wildfire as an enemy to be defeated as quickly as possible. The policy seemed obviously sensible: fire destroys trees, threatens homes, and kills wildlife. Yet in many dry forests, decades of successful firefighting produced exactly the outcome the policy was meant to (a)[prevent]. Before suppression, these forests had burned frequently but lightly. Low fires moved along the ground every few years, consuming fallen needles, dead branches, and young shrubs while leaving most mature trees, protected by thick bark, (b)[unharmed]. Such fires acted as a kind of natural maintenance, keeping the forest floor relatively clear and the stands of trees open.

When these small fires were stopped, the material they would have consumed began to (c)[accumulate]. Dense thickets of young trees filled the gaps between older ones, and their lower branches formed what foresters call ladder fuels, which allow flames to climb from the ground into the tops of the tallest trees. When a fire finally escaped control, as some inevitably did during a hot, windy summer, it found a forest packed with fuel. Instead of creeping along the ground, it raced through the crowns, killing even the oldest trees and heating the soil so intensely that the seeds stored there could not survive. The very (d)[success] of suppression had transformed a forest that once tolerated fire into one that fire could destroy.

Many agencies now use prescribed burning, deliberately setting low fires under carefully chosen conditions to restore the old pattern. The approach requires accepting some smoke and short-term damage in exchange for long-term stability. It reflects a broader ecological lesson: a disturbance that looks purely destructive at one scale may be exactly what keeps a system (e)[fragile] at another.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: How Firefighters Protect Homes from Forest Fires
When Protecting Forests from Fire Makes Them Burn Worse
Why Old Trees Survive Fires Better Than Young Ones
Prescribed Burning: A Dangerous Experiment That Failed
The Role of Wind and Heat in Spreading Wildfires
items.exp: 작은 산불까지 모두 막은 결과 연료가 쌓여 오히려 숲 전체를 태우는 대형 산불이 생겼다는 내용이라 ②가 알맞아요. ④는 처방 화입이 실패했다고 해 글과 반대예요.

items.passage:
(A)
Every Saturday that summer, Jamie woke at four to help Mrs. Alvarez load crates of tomatoes, peaches, and sweet corn into her old pickup truck. The farmers' market opened at seven, and by then the stall had to be set up perfectly: the peaches stacked in neat pyramids, the price cards written in careful chalk, the scale checked twice. Mrs. Alvarez had sold at the same corner for thirty-one years, and Jamie quickly learned that she had firm opinions about everything, especially about the woman who ran the stall across the aisle. "Mrs. Pratt sells pretty fruit," (a)[she] said one morning, lowering her voice, "but pretty is not the same as good."

(B)
Instead, she picked up the last bruised peach, cut it in half with her pocketknife, and handed him a piece. It was sweet and warm, far better than anything that gleamed across the aisle. "Firm fruit travels well," she said. "Ripe fruit tastes well. You never need to apologize for selling something ripe." The next Saturday, she set out a small chalkboard beside the peaches that read "Picked yesterday. Eat today." By ten o'clock there was a line, and Jamie, standing proudly behind the scale, noticed the woman from the week before waiting near the front. When (b)[he] handed her a bag, she smiled and said she had come back for "the soft ones."

(C)
One hot morning in late July, Mrs. Alvarez left early for a doctor's appointment, and for the first time Jamie was in charge of the stall alone. Around noon, a woman picked up a peach, pressed it gently, and put it back with a sigh. "Soft," she said. "Mrs. Pratt's are firmer." Jamie glanced across the aisle at the rival stall, where the fruit gleamed in the sun, and (c)[he] felt a sudden urge to defend Mrs. Alvarez. Without thinking, he offered the woman two peaches for the price of one.

(D)
The woman bought them, but the moment she left, Jamie realized he had no idea whether Mrs. Alvarez would approve. For the rest of the afternoon (d)[he] kept giving discounts to anyone who hesitated, and by closing time only one bruised peach was left but the cash box held far less than usual. When Mrs. Alvarez returned and counted the money, she said nothing for a long while. Jamie stared at (e)[his] shoes, preparing for the scolding he was sure would come.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 시장과 경쟁 가판대를 소개한 뒤, (C)에서 Jamie가 혼자 가판대를 맡아 복숭아를 할인해 주고, (D)의 The woman bought them으로 이어져 꾸중을 각오하며, (B)의 Instead로 꾸중 대신 복숭아를 건네는 장면이 와요. 그래서 (C)-(D)-(B)예요.

The farmers' market opened at seven, and by then the stall had to be set up perfectly: the peaches stacked in neat pyramids, the price cards written in careful chalk, the scale checked twice. Mrs. Alvarez had sold at the same corner for thirty-one years, and Jamie quickly learned that she had firm opinions about everything, especially about the woman who ran the stall across the aisle. "Mrs. Pratt sells pretty fruit," (a)[she] said one morning, lowering her voice, "but pretty is not the same as good."

(B)
Instead, she picked up the last bruised peach, cut it in half with her pocketknife, and handed him a piece. It was sweet and warm, far better than anything that gleamed across the aisle. "Firm fruit travels well," she said. "Ripe fruit tastes well. You never need to apologize for selling something ripe." The next Saturday, she set out a small chalkboard beside the peaches that read "Picked yesterday. Eat today." By ten o'clock there was a line, and Jamie, standing proudly behind the scale, noticed the woman from the week before waiting near the front. When (b)[he] handed her a bag, she smiled and said she had come back for "the soft ones."

(C)
One hot morning in late July, Mrs. Alvarez left early for a doctor's appointment, and for the first time Jamie was in charge of the stall alone. Around noon, a woman picked up a peach, pressed it gently, and put it back with a sigh. "Soft," she said. "Mrs. Pratt's are firmer." Jamie glanced across the aisle at the rival stall, where the fruit gleamed in the sun, and (c)[he] felt a sudden urge to defend Mrs. Alvarez. Without thinking, he offered the woman two peaches for the price of one.

(D)
The woman bought them, but the moment she left, Jamie realized he had no idea whether Mrs. Alvarez would approve. For the rest of the afternoon (d)[he] kept giving discounts to anyone who hesitated, and by closing time only one bruised peach was left but the cash box held far less than usual. When Mrs. Alvarez returned and counted the money, she said nothing for a long while. Jamie stared at (e)[his] shoes, preparing for the scolding he was sure would come.
items.q: 윗글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: Jamie는 새벽 4시에 일어나 농산물 싣는 일을 도왔다.
Mrs. Alvarez는 같은 자리에서 21년 동안 장사를 해 왔다.
Mrs. Alvarez는 복숭아 옆에 작은 칠판을 놓았다.
Mrs. Alvarez는 병원 진료 때문에 일찍 자리를 떠났다.
Jamie는 망설이는 손님들에게 계속 할인을 해 주었다.
items.exp: (A)에서 Mrs. Alvarez는 같은 자리에서 thirty-one years, 즉 31년 동안 장사했다고 했으므로 21년은 틀려요. 나머지는 woke at four, small chalkboard, doctor's appointment, kept giving discounts와 일치해요.

items.passage:
Dear Members of Eastbrook Aquatic Center,

Thank you for your continued support of our pool programs over the past year. As many of you know, the heating system that warms the main pool is now more than twenty years old, and our engineers have warned that it may fail during the coming winter. To avoid a sudden closure in the cold months, we have decided to replace the system this autumn. The work will take place from October 4 to October 22, and during this period the main pool will be closed. The smaller training pool will remain open, but only for lessons and for members over sixty-five, as it cannot safely hold more swimmers at once. We understand that this will be an inconvenience, especially for those who swim every morning before work. To make up for the closure, every member will receive a three-week extension of their membership at no extra charge. We appreciate your patience and look forward to welcoming you back to a warmer pool.

Best regards,
Laura Pennington
Facility Manager
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 난방 시스템 고장에 대한 회원들의 불만에 사과하려고
고령 회원을 위한 새 수영 강좌를 홍보하려고
공사로 인한 주 수영장의 임시 휴장을 알리려고
아침 수영 시간대의 운영 확대를 안내하려고
items.exp: 오래된 난방 시스템 교체 공사로 10월 4일부터 22일까지 주 수영장을 닫는다는 안내가 중심이에요. 회원권 3주 연장은 휴장에 대한 보상일 뿐 가격 인상과는 관계없고, 고령 회원 이야기는 소형 풀 이용 조건이에요.

items.passage: The bus had stopped at an old quarry outside town, and Sora could not imagine a worse way to spend a Friday. Her earth science teacher was handing out small hammers and safety goggles while explaining, for the third time, that the gray cliff in front of them had once been the bottom of a lake. Sora kicked at a pile of loose slabs and checked the time. Two more hours. Her friends had gone to the city art museum, and she had chosen this trip only because the form was due before she could change her mind. Without much interest, she picked up a flat piece of stone, set her chisel along its edge the way the teacher had shown them, and tapped. The slab split cleanly in two. Pressed into the inner surface was a perfect leaf, every vein visible, its outline as sharp as if it had fallen yesterday. Sora stared at it. Then she grabbed another slab, and another, calling to her teacher and asking how old the leaf was and what kind of tree had dropped it.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Sora의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 채석장 견학을 최악의 금요일로 여기며 시간만 확인하던 Sora가, 돌을 쪼개 잎 화석을 발견한 뒤 계속 돌을 쪼개며 선생님께 질문을 쏟아내요. 그래서 bored → fascinated가 알맞아요.

items.passage: Modern medical imaging and screening tests can find abnormalities far smaller and earlier than doctors could detect a generation ago. At first glance, this seems to be pure progress: the earlier a disease is found, the better the patient's chances. The picture becomes more complicated, however, when we look at what these tests actually find. Autopsy studies of people who died of unrelated causes have revealed that many carried small tumors that had never caused symptoms and, in all likelihood, never would have. Some of these growths remain unchanged for decades; others shrink and vanish on their own. When a highly sensitive test detects such a growth in a living patient, however, no one can be certain which kind it is, and so it is usually treated, with surgery, radiation, or drugs that carry real risks. The patient is counted as a survivor of a disease that would never have harmed him. In such cases, the screening program is [putting out fires that would never have spread], and the cost of extinguishing them is borne by healthy people who become patients.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [putting out fires that would never have spread]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: preventing serious diseases before they become dangerous
treating harmless conditions as if they were threats
missing small diseases that later turn fatal
discovering new illnesses that were unknown before
items.exp: 증상을 일으키지 않고 해도 끼치지 않았을 작은 종양까지 찾아내 위험이 있는 치료를 한다는 내용이므로, 밑줄은 해롭지 않은 상태를 위협처럼 치료하는 것을 뜻해요. ①은 글이 문제 삼는 '조기 발견은 무조건 진보'라는 시각이에요.

items.passage: Few scientific goals have attracted as much hope, or produced as much disappointment, as the effort to predict earthquakes. For more than a century, researchers have searched for reliable warning signs: unusual animal behavior, changes in groundwater, bursts of small tremors, shifts in radon gas. Each promising signal has eventually failed the test of repeated observation, appearing before some large earthquakes but not others, and often appearing when nothing followed at all. Most seismologists now accept that, with present knowledge, no method can say when and where a damaging earthquake will strike with enough precision to justify evacuating a city. What they can say, with considerable confidence, is which regions are likely to experience strong shaking over the coming decades. That knowledge is enough to act on. Building codes that require flexible frames, programs that strengthen old schools and hospitals, and drills that teach people what to do in the first seconds of shaking have saved far more lives than any forecast. Communities waiting for a precise prediction may wait forever; those that prepare for the shaking they know will come are protected whenever it arrives.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 지진 예측 기술은 동물의 행동을 관찰하면 크게 향상될 수 있다.
지진 위험 지역의 주민은 다른 지역으로 이주하는 것이 바람직하다.
지진 연구는 예측보다 발생 원리 규명에 집중해야 한다.
정확한 지진 예측을 기다리기보다 예상되는 흔들림에 대비하는 것이 효과적이다.
지진 대피 훈련은 학교와 병원을 중심으로 이루어져야 한다.
items.exp: 지진의 시점과 장소를 정확히 예측하는 방법은 아직 없지만 어느 지역이 강하게 흔들릴지는 알 수 있으므로, 내진 설계·건물 보강·훈련 같은 대비가 생명을 더 많이 구한다는 것이 요지예요. ①은 실패한 예측 신호의 한 예이고, ⑤는 대비책 중 일부만 말해요.

items.passage: In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted in one of the largest volcanic explosions of recorded history. The immediate destruction was terrible, but the eruption's most surprising effects appeared the following year, thousands of kilometers away. Across parts of Europe and North America, 1816 became known as "the year without a summer." Snow fell in New England in June, frosts killed crops in July, and cold, rainy weather ruined harvests across much of Europe, contributing to food shortages and rising grain prices. The cause lay high in the atmosphere. Large eruptions inject sulfur gases into the stratosphere, well above the level where rain can wash them out. There the gases form tiny droplets that spread around the globe and reflect a portion of incoming sunlight back into space. Because these droplets can remain aloft for a year or more, a single eruption can lower average global temperatures by a fraction of a degree, enough to shorten growing seasons in vulnerable regions. Scientists still study such events today to understand how sensitive the climate is to changes in the sunlight that reaches the surface.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the warning signs that come before major volcanic eruptions
the destruction caused near volcanoes by flowing lava
why sulfur gases are quickly removed from the air by rain
the role of grain prices in ending food shortages
how a large eruption can cool the climate far from the volcano
items.exp: 탐보라 화산 분화 뒤 성층권에 퍼진 황 성분 방울이 햇빛을 반사해 멀리 떨어진 유럽·북미에 '여름 없는 해'를 가져온 과정을 설명하므로 ⑤가 주제예요. ③은 비가 닿지 않는 높이에 머문다는 내용과 반대이고, ④는 결과의 한 부분일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: For centuries, sailors told stories of enormous waves that rose without warning from a moderate sea, towering over everything around them before vanishing. Scientists tended to dismiss these accounts. According to the accepted models of ocean waves, a wave more than twice the height of the surrounding waves should occur only once in thousands of years, so reports of such monsters were treated as exaggerations by frightened crews. That view changed on January 1, 1995, when instruments on the Draupner gas platform in the North Sea recorded a single wave about 26 meters high in a sea where most waves were around 12 meters. Because the measurement came from a laser device rather than from a human witness, it could not be explained away. Researchers began to search satellite images and found that such waves were far more common than theory had allowed. They now believe that, under certain conditions, wave energy can become concentrated in one spot, as smaller waves overlap and borrow energy from their neighbors. Ship and platform designers have since had to plan for waves that, until recently, officially did not exist.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Sailors Exaggerate the Dangers of the Sea
How Satellites Changed the Way Ships Navigate
Calm Seas: The Hidden Benefit of Ocean Platforms
From Sailors' Tale to Measured Fact: The Rogue Wave
items.exp: 과학자들이 과장으로 여기던 선원들의 거대 파도 이야기가 1995년 드라우프너 플랫폼의 측정으로 사실로 확인되고, 이후 설계 기준까지 바꾸었다는 글이므로 ④가 알맞아요. ①은 글이 결국 뒤집은 과거의 시각이고, ⑤는 레이저 장비라는 세부만 빌린 오답이에요.

items.passage:

items.q: Riverton Youth Debate Tournament 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 참가비에 모든 팀원의 점심 식사가 포함된다.
각 팀은 예선에서 찬성과 반대 입장을 모두 맡는다.
토론 중에는 휴대 전화를 사용할 수 없다.
items.exp: 고등학생들이 3명씩 팀을 이루어(in teams of three) 참가한다고 했으므로 ①이 안내문과 일치하지 않아요. 나머지는 참가비의 점심 포함, 찬반 예선, 주제 공지일, 휴대 전화 사용 금지와 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: Vampire bats live on a diet that leaves little room for error: a bat that fails to find blood for two or three nights in a row may starve to death. Yet colonies survive because well-fed individuals regularly ①[share] part of their meal with hungry roostmates by bringing up blood. Researchers studying captive colonies found that this sharing is not distributed at random. Bats were more likely to feed those that had fed them in the past, and a bat ②[whose] network of donors was wide was better protected than one that depended on a single relative. Remarkably, when a bat's usual partner was removed, those that had previously built relationships with many non-relatives ③[received] more help than those that had not. The bats also groom one another, and grooming seems ④[to serve] as a way of testing and strengthening a bond before larger investments are made. Seen this way, sharing is less an act of pure kindness than an insurance policy, ⑤[which] costs paid in good times are repaid in bad ones.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ⑤ 뒤에 costs ... are repaid라는 완전한 절이 오므로 관계대명사 which가 아니라 in which로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 복수 주어 individuals의 동사, ②는 network를 이끄는 소유격 관계대명사, ③은 those의 과거 동사, ④는 seem 뒤의 to부정사로 맞아요.

items.passage: For centuries, farmers in many parts of the world have avoided planting the same crop in the same field year after year. Growing a single crop continuously tends to ①[deplete] the particular nutrients that crop needs most, leaving the soil poorer each season. It also allows pests and diseases that specialize in that crop to ②[build up], since they find a fresh supply of their favorite host waiting every spring. Crop rotation addresses both problems. By alternating, for example, wheat with beans and then with a root vegetable, a farmer ③[prolongs] the cycle of pests that depend on a single plant, because the insects hatch into a field with nothing they can eat. Beans and other legumes offer an additional benefit: bacteria living in their roots capture nitrogen from the air and ④[enrich] the soil for the crops that follow. Modern fertilizers and pesticides made it possible for a time to ignore these old lessons, but rising costs and concerns about pollution have led many farms to ⑤[rediscover] rotation as a practical tool.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 해충이 먹을 것이 없는 밭에서 깨어난다고 했으므로 윤작은 해충의 순환을 '끊는' 것이에요. 따라서 ③의 prolongs를 breaks나 interrupts로 바꿔야 해요. ①은 양분 고갈, ②는 해충이 늘어나는 것, ④는 질소로 흙을 비옥하게 하는 것으로 맞아요.

items.passage: A thermometer describes the air, but it says surprisingly little about what our bodies experience. Our skin does not sense temperature directly; it senses the rate at which heat flows into or out of it. That is why a metal railing and a wooden bench left outside on the same winter night, though they are exactly the same temperature, feel so different to the touch: metal draws heat away from the hand far faster than wood. The same principle explains why a windy day at five degrees can feel colder than a calm day at zero. Moving air constantly sweeps away the thin layer of warmth that clings to the skin, so the body loses heat more quickly, and we interpret that rapid loss as cold. Humidity, sunshine, clothing, and even whether we are standing still or walking all change the rate in similar ways. The sensation of cold, then, is ___: it reflects not a property of the air alone but an exchange between the air and a particular body under particular conditions. This is why weather services often report a "feels like" temperature alongside the measured one.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 빈칸 뒤 콜론 이하에서 추위의 감각은 공기만의 성질이 아니라 공기와 특정한 몸 사이의 교환을 반영한다고 하므로 relational(관계적인)이 알맞아요. constant는 바람·습도 등으로 달라진다는 내용과 반대이고, misleading은 감각이 틀렸다는 것이 아니라 관계를 반영한다는 글의 요점과 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: To a nonmathematician, the purpose of a proof seems obvious: it establishes, beyond all doubt, that a statement is true. Yet mathematicians often behave in ways that this view cannot explain. They publish new proofs of theorems that were proved centuries ago and whose truth no one questions. They sometimes feel dissatisfied with a proof that is perfectly valid, such as one produced by a computer checking millions of separate cases, and continue searching for a different one. If certainty were the only goal, these efforts would be pointless, since a result cannot become more certain than certain. The explanation is that a good proof does more than settle a question; it reveals the structure that makes the answer inevitable, connecting the result to other ideas and suggesting where similar results might be found. A proof by exhaustive calculation may confirm a fact while leaving its reasons completely hidden. What mathematicians value in a proof, then, is not only that it shows a result to be true but that ___.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: it can be checked quickly by a computer
it removes every remaining doubt about the result
it was discovered before any competing proof
it makes clear why the result has to hold
it requires as few calculations as possible
items.exp: 좋은 증명은 답이 필연적일 수밖에 없는 구조를 드러내고, 계산만으로 된 증명은 이유를 감춘다고 했어요. 따라서 결과가 '왜' 성립해야 하는지 밝힌다는 ④가 알맞아요. ②는 확실성 자체로, 'not only that it shows a result to be true'와 겹치는 내용이에요.

items.passage: When a museum label credits a Renaissance altarpiece to a famous master, visitors tend to imagine the painter working alone before the panel, applying every stroke himself. ① In reality, most such works were produced in busy workshops, where the master directed a team of assistants and apprentices much as an architect directs builders. ② Apprentices ground pigments, prepared wooden panels, and copied drawings for years before they were trusted to paint anything that would be seen. ③ More experienced assistants often painted backgrounds, drapery, and minor figures, while the master reserved the faces and the most visible passages for his own hand. ④ Contracts of the period sometimes specified exactly which parts the master was obliged to paint personally, showing that patrons understood and accepted this division of labor. ⑤ Ultramarine, the most costly blue of the age, was made by grinding a semiprecious stone that had to be imported from distant mines, and it was often reserved for the robes of holy figures.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 르네상스 제단화가 거장 혼자가 아니라 공방의 분업으로 만들어졌다는 글인데, ⑤는 울트라마린 안료가 비쌌다는 내용이라 분업의 흐름에서 벗어나요. ②의 안료 갈기는 견습생의 역할로, ④의 계약은 분업을 받아들였다는 근거로 이어져요.

items.passage:
Most planets that orbit stars other than the Sun have never been seen directly. Their stars are millions of times brighter than they are, and the faint light reflected from a planet is lost in the glare.

(A) This dip in brightness is astonishingly small. For a planet the size of Earth crossing a star like the Sun, the light falls by less than one hundredth of one percent, a change that can be measured only by extremely stable telescopes, many of them placed in space above the flickering atmosphere.

(B) Instead, astronomers find them indirectly, by studying their effects on the stars. One widely used method relies on a simple fact: when a planet passes between its star and our telescopes, it blocks a tiny portion of the starlight.

(C) Yet such measurements reveal far more than the planet's existence. Because a larger planet blocks more light, the depth of the dip indicates its size, and the time between one crossing and the next shows how long the planet takes to complete an orbit.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 직접 볼 수 없다는 주어진 글 뒤에 (B)의 Instead로 간접 관측법(빛을 가리는 현상)이 나와요. (A)의 This dip은 (B)에서 빛이 일부 가려지는 현상을 받고, (C)의 such measurements는 (A)의 정밀한 측정을 가리켜요. 그래서 (B)-(A)-(C)예요.

items.passage: Anyone who has driven across a long bridge has probably felt a series of small bumps passing beneath the tires at regular intervals. ( ① ) These bumps come from expansion joints, gaps deliberately built into the road surface and often covered by interlocking metal plates shaped like the teeth of a comb. ( ② ) The joints exist because the materials of a bridge are never truly still. ( ③ ) As a result, a steel bridge several hundred meters long can grow by tens of centimeters between a freezing winter night and a hot summer afternoon. ( ④ ) Without room to move, this growth would push against the bridge's supports with enormous force, cracking concrete, bending beams, and loosening the bolts that hold the structure together. ( ⑤ ) The joints absorb this movement, opening slightly in the cold and closing again in the heat, so that the structure can breathe with the seasons rather than fight against them. A bump under the tires, then, is a small reminder of the engineering that keeps the crossing safe.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Like almost all solids, steel and concrete expand when they warm and contract when they cool.

items.passage: Brainstorming sessions, in which a team gathers to call out as many ideas as possible, remain a popular tool in workplaces. The assumption is that ideas spark other ideas, so a group should produce more than the same people working alone. Repeated experiments, however, have found the opposite. When researchers compare the total number of ideas produced by a brainstorming group with the number produced by the same number of individuals working separately, the individuals usually come out ahead, often by a wide margin. Two factors seem largely responsible. First, only one person can speak at a time, so others must hold their ideas while waiting for a turn, and many of those ideas are forgotten or abandoned by the time the chance to speak arrives. Second, people in a group, especially in the presence of a manager, worry about appearing foolish and quietly hold back unusual suggestions. Some organizations now ask employees to write down ideas independently before meeting, using the group session only to combine and develop what individuals have already produced.

items.passage:
Anthropologists have traditionally traveled far from home to study ways of life that seemed strange to them. Over time, however, many came to recognize that the distance was not only geographic. What made fieldwork (a)[productive] was the outsider's inability to take anything for granted. A visitor who does not know the local customs must ask why people greet each other in a particular order, why certain foods are eaten only on certain days, why one seat at the table is always left empty. Questions that a local resident would never think to ask become, for the stranger, the obvious place to begin.

This insight eventually turned anthropology's attention back toward the researchers' own societies. The challenge there is the reverse of the traditional one: instead of making the strange familiar, the anthropologist must make the familiar strange. Consider the ordinary supermarket checkout line. To most shoppers it is (b)[unremarkable], simply a way of getting through the store. Yet an observer who watches it as if seeing it for the first time will notice an elaborate set of unspoken rules. Strangers stand at a carefully judged distance; a plastic divider placed on the belt marks where one person's property ends and another's begins; someone who tries to cut in is met with glances that (c)[enforce] the order more effectively than any written sign.

None of these rules is taught in school, and few people could state them if asked, yet nearly everyone follows them and immediately notices when they are broken. Such patterns are (d)[easy] to see from the inside precisely because they work so smoothly. The task of the anthropologist at home is therefore to cultivate a deliberate (e)[estrangement], to look at the daily routines of one's own community with the same puzzled curiosity that a traveler brings to a distant village.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Making the Familiar Strange: Anthropology Turns Homeward
Why Supermarkets Need Clearer Written Rules
The Dangers of Fieldwork in Distant Villages
How Travel Changes the Customs of Local People
Learning Local Languages: The Key to Fieldwork
items.exp: 낯선 곳에서 모든 것을 당연하게 여기지 않던 인류학의 시선을, 이제 자기 사회로 돌려 익숙한 것을 낯설게 보아야 한다는 내용이라 ①이 알맞아요. 슈퍼마켓 줄은 그 예시일 뿐이에요.

(A)
The Song family's noodle restaurant had stood on the same narrow street for twenty-six years, and in all that time the menu on the wall had barely changed: three kinds of noodle soup, two kinds of dumplings, and a cold noodle dish served only in summer. Minjun, who had grown up doing his homework at the corner table, thought the menu was hopelessly old-fashioned. When the café across the street began drawing long lines with colorful fusion dishes, (a)[he] spread a page of new recipe ideas in front of his father. Mr. Song glanced at it, folded it in half, and went back to skimming fat from the broth.

(B)
For the next three days, Minjun arrived before dawn and stood beside the stove as his father, sitting on a stool with his arm in a sling, explained every step: which bones to roast, when to lower the heat, how to tell by smell that the broth was ready. When the regulars returned that weekend, they ate in contented silence. A month later, the menu on the wall had one new line, a spicy cold noodle dish that (b)[he] had developed and his father had tasted eleven times before approving. It sold out on the first day.

(C)
Mrs. Kang, who had eaten lunch at the restaurant every Tuesday since it opened, put down her spoon after one sip. "Your father's broth takes two days," she said gently. "He started making it the week your mother was in the hospital before you were born. He said he wanted something in his life that he could not rush." (c)[She] patted Minjun's hand and left the bowl half full. That night, Minjun sat for a long time in the empty kitchen, and before closing (d)[he] called his father to ask whether he would teach him how to make the broth properly.

(D)
Then, in early spring, Mr. Song slipped on the wet kitchen floor and broke his wrist. The doctor ordered him to rest for two weeks, and Minjun, now seventeen, insisted that he could run the kitchen alone. On the first day, he quietly replaced the slow-simmered broth with a quicker version from a cooking video and added two of his fusion dishes to the menu. Several customers tried them politely, but the regulars frowned, and by Tuesday (e)[his] confidence had begun to fade.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Minjun의 새 메뉴 제안이 거절된 뒤, (D)에서 아버지가 다쳐 Minjun이 혼자 주방을 맡아 국물을 바꾸고, 화요일 손님인 Mrs. Kang이 등장하는 (C)를 거쳐, 아버지에게 국물을 배우고 새 메뉴를 내는 (B)로 이어져요. 그래서 (D)-(C)-(B)예요.

items.passage:
Dear Mr. Whitfield,

I am the art teacher at Linden Park High School, and I am writing on behalf of the twenty students in our advanced painting class. For the past semester, these students have been studying how public art can change the character of a neighborhood, and they now hope to put what they have learned into practice. During our walks around the area, they were repeatedly drawn to the long brick wall on the east side of your hardware store, which faces the bus stop on Carver Street. At present the wall is bare and, as I am sure you know, has been marked with graffiti several times. My students have designed a mural depicting the history of the street, from its early market days to the present, and they would be honored to paint it on that wall. We would cover all costs for paint and materials, work only on weekends so as not to disturb your business, and take responsibility for maintaining the mural for five years. I have attached the students' sketches for your review. Would you kindly allow us to use the wall for this project?

Sincerely,
Helen Moriarty

items.passage: On the morning of his seventy-fifth birthday, Mr. Kessler ate breakfast alone, as he had every morning since his wife passed away. His daughter lived overseas and had sent a short message the night before, and the phone had not rung since. He washed his single cup, wiped the table twice, and sat by the window, watching the bus he had driven for thirty-two years pass at its usual time. No one would think of him today, he told himself; that was simply how things went when one grew old. In the afternoon, a knock came at the door. He opened it to find a crowd of grown men and women on his steps, some holding flowers, one carrying a cake shaped like a bus. "Route 14, front seat," said a woman in a nurse's uniform, smiling. "You waited for me every morning when I was late for school." One by one, the others told him their own stories. Mr. Kessler tried to answer, but his voice would not come, and he could only press his hand to his chest.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 Mr. Kessler의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 생일 아침 혼자 식사하며 아무도 자신을 기억하지 않을 거라 여기던 Mr. Kessler가, 예전에 버스로 태워 주던 학생들이 찾아와 이야기를 들려주자 말을 잇지 못하고 가슴에 손을 얹어요. 그래서 lonely → touched가 알맞아요. 화가 나 있던 장면은 없어요.

items.passage: Walk through many modern city centers and you will notice benches divided by metal armrests, ledges covered in small spikes, and plazas with no place to sit at all. These features are usually justified as ways of keeping public spaces orderly, discouraging people from lingering too long or sleeping outdoors. Yet their effects reach far beyond the groups they are meant to exclude. The elderly woman who needs to rest between bus stops, the parent with a tired child, and the office worker hoping to eat lunch in the sun are all quietly told that the space is for passing through, not for staying. A city in which people cannot pause is a city in which strangers rarely meet, conversations rarely begin, and the street gradually loses its role as a shared living room. Problems such as homelessness will not disappear because a bench has been made uncomfortable; they will simply move elsewhere. Planners and officials should therefore design public spaces that invite people to sit, rest, and remain, treating comfort not as a risk to be managed but as a basic purpose of the public realm.
items.q: 다음 글에서 필자가 주장하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 도시의 공공장소는 사람들이 머물고 쉴 수 있도록 설계되어야 한다.
