items.passage: Imagine a surgeon who also happens to be the fastest typist in her hospital. She can enter patient records twice as quickly as the clerk who does it for her, and yet it would be foolish for her to take over the job. Every hour she spends typing is an hour not spent operating, and the value of an hour of surgery is far greater than the time she would save at the keyboard. What matters, economists point out, is not who is better at a task in absolute terms but what each person gives up by doing it. This principle, known as comparative advantage, explains why trade benefits even a party that is more productive at everything: by concentrating on what it does relatively best and exchanging for the rest, it obtains more than it could produce alone. The same logic applies within teams and households. A manager who insists on handling every task personally because no one else does it as well may feel admirably capable, but [the best typist in the building should not be typing]. Being able to do something well is not, by itself, a reason to do it.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [the best typist in the building should not be typing]가 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: skilled workers should pass their abilities on to less experienced colleagues
speed matters less than accuracy in routine office work
excelling at a task does not justify doing it if more valuable work is given up
routine tasks should be automated so that experts can focus on their specialty
even talented people must keep practicing basic skills to stay competent
items.exp: 누가 더 잘하느냐보다 그 일을 하느라 무엇을 포기하느냐가 중요하다는 비교 우위의 원리를 말하는 글이에요. 타자를 가장 잘하는 사람이라도 더 가치 있는 일을 포기하게 되면 타자를 치지 말아야 한다는 뜻이라서 ③이 맞아요. ④의 자동화 이야기는 글에 없어요.

items.passage: Does a fly experience a second the same way we do? One way scientists approach this question is by measuring how rapidly an animal's eyes can register changes in light. When a light flickers faster than a certain rate, it appears to an observer as a steady glow, and the point at which this happens differs widely among species. Humans typically stop seeing flicker at around sixty flashes per second, but many flying insects can detect flickers several times faster. Small, quick animals tend to have higher thresholds, while large, slow-moving ones tend to have lower thresholds. This pattern makes ecological sense. A fly that must escape a swatting hand, or a bird that must catch an insect in mid-air, benefits from slicing time into finer pieces, so that a fast-moving threat or prey seems to move more slowly. For a large animal with fewer split-second demands, processing visual information at such a high rate would consume energy without offering much advantage. In this sense, each species may inhabit its own temporal world, perceiving the flow of events at a speed shaped by its body and way of life.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: methods for reducing flicker in artificial lighting
the evolutionary origins of insect flight
why large animals live longer than small animals
the role of energy efficiency in human vision
differences among species in how finely they perceive time
items.exp: 깜빡임을 구별하는 속도가 종마다 다르고, 작고 빠른 동물일수록 시간을 더 잘게 나누어 지각한다는 내용이에요. 마지막 문장도 종마다 자기만의 시간 세계에 산다고 정리하므로 ⑤가 주제예요. ④의 에너지 이야기는 큰 동물을 설명하는 근거일 뿐이에요.

items.passage: In a few mountainous regions of the world, from the Canary Islands to parts of Turkey and Mexico, people have long communicated across valleys by whistling. These whistled forms of speech are not simple codes with a handful of fixed signals, like those a shepherd might use with a dog. Instead, they are versions of the local spoken language transferred into whistles: speakers reproduce the melody and rhythm of words, or the patterns that vowels and consonants create in sound, so that a listener who knows the language can understand entirely new sentences. Because a whistle carries much farther than a shout and loses less clarity in the open air, the practice made sense in landscapes where walking to a neighbor could take an hour. Researchers find whistled speech fascinating for another reason: it shows that the brain can decode language even when much of the usual sound information has been stripped away. Sadly, roads and mobile phones have reduced the need for whistling, and several of these traditions now survive mainly among older speakers, although some communities have begun teaching them in schools.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Speaking Without Words: Language Carried on a Whistle
Mountain Roads That Changed Rural Communication
How the Brain Separates Music from Speech
The Hidden Dangers of Losing Local Dialects
items.exp: 산간 지역에서 지역 언어를 휘파람으로 옮겨 새로운 문장까지 전달하는 휘파람 언어를 설명하는 글이라 ②가 제목으로 알맞아요. 양치기 신호는 휘파람 언어와 다르다고 비교한 예일 뿐이고, 뇌 이야기도 음악과 말을 구분하는 내용이 아니에요.

items.passage: Margit Ellander was born in 1868 in a textile town in western Sweden, the eldest of six children of a mill foreman. Her family owned only two books, a hymnal and an almanac, and she later recalled reading the almanac so often that she could recite its weather tables by heart. At thirteen she left school to work at the mill, but she continued to study at night by borrowing books from a local pastor. In 1894 she published her first collection of stories for children, written in the plain language spoken by working families rather than the formal style then common in children's books. The collection sold slowly at first, but its popularity grew steadily after teachers began reading it aloud in classrooms. With the income from her later books, she opened a free reading room for mill workers and their families in 1905, which stayed open late in the evening so that people could visit after their shifts. By 1920, similar reading rooms had been established in eleven other towns. Ellander continued writing until her death in 1946, leaving behind more than thirty books.
items.q: 다음 글에 관한 내용으로 적절하지 않은 것은?
choices: 1894년에 어린이를 위한 첫 이야기 모음집을 출간했다.
첫 이야기 모음집은 출간 직후부터 큰 인기를 얻었다.
1905년에 공장 노동자와 가족을 위한 무료 열람실을 열었다.
items.exp: 첫 모음집은 처음에는 천천히 팔렸고, 교사들이 교실에서 읽어 주기 시작한 뒤에야 인기가 꾸준히 높아졌다고 했어요. 그래서 ④가 글과 맞지 않아요. 나머지는 책 두 권, 13세에 공장 취업, 1894년 출간, 1905년 무료 열람실 내용과 모두 일치해요.

items.passage: Many people apply sunscreen only on bright summer days, assuming that clouds offer reliable protection. In fact, a thin layer of cloud may let through most of the ultraviolet radiation ①[that] reaches the ground on a clear day, and under certain conditions, light scattered from the edges of clouds can even increase it. Because ultraviolet rays cannot be felt as warmth, people sitting outdoors on a cool, overcast afternoon receive no signal ②[warning] them of the danger. Windows present a similar trap. Ordinary glass blocks most of the rays responsible for sunburn, but it ③[allow] much of the longer-wavelength radiation to pass through, a type of ultraviolet light ④[associated] with wrinkles and the gradual aging of the skin. This is why drivers who spend long hours on the road sometimes show more skin damage on the side of the face ⑤[closer] to the window. The absence of heat or redness, in other words, says little about whether the skin is being harmed.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③의 주어는 단수 대명사 it(= ordinary glass)이므로 allows로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 radiation을 꾸미는 관계대명사, ②는 signal을 뒤에서 꾸미는 현재분사, ④는 '~와 관련된'이라는 과거분사, ⑤는 the side of the face를 뒤에서 꾸미는 형용사 비교급이라 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: Peatlands cover only about three percent of the Earth's land surface, yet they store more carbon than all the world's forests combined. Their secret is water. In a waterlogged bog, oxygen is ①[abundant], so the microbes that would normally break down dead plants work extremely slowly. Instead of decaying, layers of moss and roots ②[accumulate] over thousands of years, locking away the carbon they absorbed while alive. For centuries, however, people drained peatlands to create farmland or to dig peat for fuel. Once the water table drops, air reaches the buried material, and decomposition ③[accelerates], releasing carbon dioxide that has been stored for millennia. Drained peat can also catch fire and smolder underground for months, which makes such fires extremely difficult to ④[extinguish]. For these reasons, a growing number of conservation projects now block old drainage ditches in order to rewet damaged bogs. Restoration is slow, and a rewetted peatland may take decades to begin storing carbon again, but simply stopping its losses is already a ⑤[significant] gain for the climate.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 물에 잠긴 습지에서 미생물이 아주 느리게 일한다고 했고, 물이 빠져 공기가 닿으면 분해가 빨라진다고 했으므로 습지 속 산소는 부족한 거예요. 따라서 ①의 abundant를 scarce로 바꿔야 해요. 식물층이 쌓이고, 분해가 빨라지고, 불을 끄기 어렵다는 나머지는 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: When people recall events from their past, the emotions attached to those memories do not remain constant. Researchers who asked participants to keep diaries of daily events and rate their feelings, and then asked them months later how they felt when remembering the same events, discovered a consistent pattern. The intensity of feelings about both pleasant and unpleasant events declined over time, but the decline was not equal: the sting of unpleasant memories faded considerably faster than the warmth of pleasant ones. An embarrassing mistake that once made someone's face burn might later be recalled with mild amusement, while a happy afternoon with friends keeps much of its glow. This tendency appears across many cultures and age groups, and it is weaker among people suffering from depression, which suggests that it plays a role in healthy emotional functioning. In effect, memory acts as a ___ editor, quietly trimming the pain from our personal history while preserving its pleasures, and allowing most of us to look back on our lives with more satisfaction than the original moments might justify.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 불쾌한 기억의 감정은 빨리 옅어지고 즐거운 기억은 오래 남아, 실제보다 더 만족스럽게 삶을 돌아보게 한다고 했어요. 고통은 잘라 내고 기쁨은 남기는 편집자이니 generous(너그러운)가 알맞아요. 두 감정이 똑같이 줄지 않는다고 했으니 neutral은 맞지 않아요.

items.passage: Historians face a peculiar difficulty that readers of their books rarely appreciate: they know how the story ends. When we read about a war, an economic collapse, or a revolution, we already know which side prevailed, which warnings proved accurate, and which hopes were disappointed. This knowledge silently reorganizes the past. The signs that pointed toward the eventual outcome appear bright and obvious, while the many signs that pointed elsewhere fade into irrelevance. The people who lived through those events, however, enjoyed no such clarity. They faced a future that was genuinely open, crowded with competing possibilities, each of which seemed plausible at the time. To condemn them as foolish for failing to foresee what now looks inevitable is to commit an error of perspective rather than to reach a sound verdict. For this reason, the most careful historians try to ___, reconstructing the range of futures that seemed possible from within a given moment before explaining why only one of them came to pass. Only then can the decisions of the past be understood as genuine choices rather than as steps toward a fixed destination.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: identify the single cause that made each outcome unavoidable
rely on the testimony of those who correctly predicted events
describe the past using only the vocabulary of its own era
set aside what they know of the ending and recover the uncertainty of the time
focus on long-term trends rather than on individual decisions
items.exp: 결말을 아는 것이 과거를 재구성해 버리고, 당시 사람들은 열린 미래를 마주했다고 했어요. 빈칸 뒤에서도 그 순간에 가능해 보였던 여러 미래를 되살린다고 하므로 결말에 대한 지식을 내려놓고 당시의 불확실성을 회복한다는 ④가 맞아요. ①은 결과를 필연으로 보는, 글이 비판하는 태도예요.

items.passage: Between early 2008 and late 2009, competitive swimming witnessed an extraordinary wave of world records, many of them set by athletes wearing newly developed full-body suits made partly or entirely of polyurethane. ① These suits compressed the swimmer's body into a more streamlined shape and trapped air that increased buoyancy, reducing drag in ways that no amount of training could match. ② Swimming is also one of the few sports that exercises nearly every major muscle group while placing relatively little stress on the joints. ③ Critics soon argued that the records were measuring the quality of the fabric rather than the ability of the athlete, and that wealthier national teams with access to the latest suits enjoyed an unfair advantage. ④ In response, the sport's international governing body introduced rules from 2010 limiting the materials and the body coverage allowed in competition swimwear. ⑤ The episode raised a lasting question for every sport that depends on equipment: at what point does technological improvement stop enhancing human performance and begin to replace it?
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 첨단 수영복이 기록을 끌어올리자 비판이 일고 규제가 생겼으며, 장비와 인간 능력의 경계라는 질문을 남겼다는 흐름이에요. ②는 수영이 관절 부담이 적은 전신 운동이라는 건강상 장점을 말해 흐름에서 벗어나요.

items.passage:
When automated teller machines spread through banks in the 1970s and 1980s, many observers predicted the end of the bank teller. A machine could hand out cash and accept deposits at any hour, and it never needed a lunch break.

(A) The prediction seemed reasonable, yet the number of tellers did not collapse in the decades that followed. In many places it actually grew for a time, and the reason lay in the economics of running a branch.

(B) What these tellers did all day, however, changed considerably. Freed from counting cash, they spent more of their time explaining loans, recommending services, and solving problems that no machine could handle, so that the job became less about handling money and more about handling customers.

(C) Since the machines took over routine withdrawals, the average branch could operate with fewer tellers, which made each branch cheaper to run. Banks responded by opening more branches to compete for customers, and the total number of teller jobs rose.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 주어진 글의 은행원이 사라질 거라는 예측을 (A)가 The prediction으로 받아 실제로는 줄지 않았고 그 이유가 지점 운영의 경제학에 있다고 해요. (C)가 그 이유로 지점이 늘어 일자리가 늘었다고 설명하고, (B)가 however로 그 은행원들의 하는 일은 크게 바뀌었다고 마무리해요.

items.passage: Architects designing concert halls have long known that the shape of a room matters as much as its size. ( ① ) Much of what an audience hears does not travel directly from the stage but arrives after bouncing off walls, ceilings, and balconies. ( ② ) Of these many reflections, those arriving from the sides appear to be especially valuable. ( ③ ) Side reflections, however, reach the left and right ears at slightly different moments, creating a sense of being surrounded by the music that listeners consistently rate as one of the most pleasing qualities of a performance. ( ④ ) Narrow, rectangular halls built in the nineteenth century, often called shoeboxes, supply such reflections naturally, because their side walls stand close to every seat. ( ⑤ ) Many modern halls, which wrap terraces of seating around the stage, therefore include angled wall panels designed to send sound toward listeners from the side. In this way, acoustic engineers try to recreate the intimacy of older halls within much larger spaces.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

Reflections from the ceiling, by contrast, reach both ears at nearly the same moment and therefore add loudness but little sense of space.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 천장 반사음은 두 귀에 거의 동시에 도달해 공간감을 주지 못한다는 내용이에요. ③ 뒤의 Side reflections, however가 바로 이 천장 반사음과 대조하는 말이므로 ③에 들어가야 해요. ②에 넣으면 by contrast가 대조할 대상이 없어요.

items.passage: Anyone who has tried to reproduce a grandparent's signature dish from a written recipe knows the frustration. The ingredients are listed and the steps are numbered, yet the result somehow tastes wrong. Part of the problem is that experienced cooks rarely measure. They add flour "until the dough feels right" or cook onions "until they smell sweet," relying on judgments of texture, aroma, and sound that they themselves could not fully put into words. Such knowledge is not hidden deliberately; it simply lives in the hands and senses rather than in sentences. For this reason, it has traditionally passed from one generation to the next not through written instructions but through years of cooking side by side, as a child watches, imitates, and is gently corrected. When families scatter and this shared time in the kitchen disappears, recipes may survive on paper while the skill that gave them meaning quietly vanishes. Some food historians therefore argue that preserving culinary traditions requires filming cooks at work and, better still, bringing learners into the kitchen with them.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Much of a skilled cook's knowledge is (A) ___ in nature, so it has been handed down mainly through (B) ___ rather than through written recipes.
items.exp: 숙련된 요리사의 지식은 말로 다 표현할 수 없는 감각의 판단이라 (A)는 unspoken, 그 지식은 글이 아니라 곁에서 함께 요리하며 전해졌으므로 (B)는 shared practice예요. 일부러 숨긴 것이 아니라고 했으니 secret은 틀려요.

items.passage:
Seawater tastes of salt, but the rivers that feed the oceans taste almost fresh. This apparent puzzle has a simple explanation: river water is not entirely pure. As rain falls through the air, it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic, and as it flows over the land it slowly (a)[dissolves] minerals from the rocks it touches. Every river therefore carries a faint load of dissolved salts to the sea, too small to taste but enormous when added up over millions of years.

Once in the ocean, these salts have nowhere to go. The sun evaporates vast quantities of seawater every day, but evaporation removes only pure water, so the salts become steadily more (b)[diluted] in what remains. The water itself returns to the land as rain, ready to wear away more rock, while the salts stay behind in the sea. Over time, this cycle has turned the oceans into an immense storehouse of dissolved stone.

If salts were only ever added, however, the sea would grow saltier without limit. Yet geological evidence suggests that its saltiness has remained fairly (c)[stable] for hundreds of millions of years. The reason is that the ocean also loses salts. Some are locked into sediments on the seafloor; others react with hot rock where new crust forms along mid-ocean ridges; and in shallow, enclosed seas that dry out, thick layers of salt are (d)[deposited] and eventually buried. Input and output have reached a rough balance, much like a bathtub whose drain removes water as fast as the tap adds it. The saltiness of the sea, then, is not a fixed property but the (e)[outcome] of a slow and continuing exchange between rock, water, and time.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Rivers Are Slowly Becoming Saltier Than the Sea
How Evaporation Turns Seawater into Fresh Water
The Hidden Dangers of Salt in Coastal Farmland
Mid-Ocean Ridges: Where New Seafloor Is Born
From Rock to Sea: How the Ocean Gains and Balances Its Salt
items.exp: 강물이 바위의 광물을 녹여 바다로 소금을 나르고, 증발로 소금이 바다에 남으며, 해저 퇴적 등으로 소금이 빠져나가 균형을 이룬다는 글이에요. 그래서 ⑤가 제목으로 알맞아요. ①은 강이 바다보다 짜진다는 말이라 글과 다르고, ④의 해령은 소금이 빠져나가는 한 예일 뿐이에요.

items.exp: 증발은 순수한 물만 없애므로 남은 바닷물 속 소금은 점점 진해져요. 따라서 (b)의 diluted를 concentrated로 바꿔야 해요. 광물을 녹임(dissolves), 염도가 안정됨(stable), 소금층이 쌓임(deposited), 교환의 결과(outcome)는 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Daniel had been captain of the Westbrook High School chess club for two years, and he took the role seriously. Every Wednesday he arrived early to set up the boards, and every Wednesday a quiet freshman named Leo was already waiting at the door. Leo clearly loved the game, but he lost almost every match. He moved quickly, almost nervously, as though thinking for too long might reveal how little he knew. One afternoon, after watching Leo lose three games in a row, Daniel decided that (a)[he] could no longer simply stand by.

(B)
On the day of the tournament, Westbrook's match came down to the final game, which was Leo's. Daniel, having already finished (b)[his] own game with a draw, stood quietly at the edge of the hall. Leo's opponent offered a quick trade of queens, the kind of offer Leo once would have accepted without a second thought. This time Leo paused, folded his hands, and studied the board for several minutes. Then he declined, and twenty moves later his opponent resigned. As the team burst into cheers, Leo looked across the hall and found Daniel, who was clapping harder than anyone.

(C)
When the others had left, Daniel sat down across from Leo and set up the pieces. "Let's play one game," he said, "but with a rule. Before every move, you have to tell me what you think I'm planning." Leo looked puzzled but agreed. The game took nearly an hour. Again and again, Leo began to reach for a piece, stopped, and explained his reasoning aloud, and more than once he spotted a trap just in time. He still lost, but at the end Daniel smiled. "That was the best you've ever played," (c)[he] said.

(D)
From then on, the two of them met every Wednesday after the club meeting. Daniel never told Leo which move to make; instead, (d)[he] kept asking questions until Leo found the answer himself. Slowly, Leo's games grew longer and his losses fewer. In March, the club entered the regional team tournament, and Daniel surprised everyone by placing Leo on the fourth board. Some members complained that Leo was not ready. Leo himself looked terrified, but when (e)[he] saw Daniel's calm nod, he took a deep breath and accepted the place.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Daniel이 더는 지켜만 보지 않기로 하자 (C)에서 다른 사람들이 떠난 뒤 Leo와 규칙을 둔 대국을 해요. (D)는 From then on으로 그 뒤의 연습과 대회 출전 결정을, (B)는 대회 당일 결과를 다루므로 (C)-(D)-(B)예요.

Daniel은 Leo를 네 번째 보드에 배치했다.
Leo는 대표 선수 자리를 끝내 거절했다.
items.exp: (D)의 마지막에서 Leo는 겁에 질렸지만 Daniel의 끄덕임을 보고 심호흡을 한 뒤 자리를 받아들였어요. 그래서 ⑤가 글과 맞지 않아요. Daniel이 무승부로 경기를 마친 것은 (B)에 나와요.

items.passage:
Dear Ms. Delgado,

I am the activities coordinator at Sunnyvale Senior Residence, and I would like to thank you for confirming our group booking of thirty-two tickets for your company's production of "The Lighthouse Keeper" on Friday, May 14. Our residents have been looking forward to the performance for weeks, and several of them have already read the novel on which the play is based. Since making the booking, however, I have learned that the Friday performance begins at 8 p.m. and ends close to eleven. For many of our residents, a late return creates real difficulties: some need to take medication at fixed times in the evening, and our driver is not permitted to operate the residence bus after 10 p.m. I noticed on your website that there is also a matinee performance on Saturday, May 15, at 2 p.m. I would be very grateful if our booking could be moved to that performance. We are happy to pay any fee involved in exchanging the tickets. Please let me know whether this change is possible.

Warm regards,
Patricia Owens
items.q: 다음 글의 목적으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 공연 단체 관람의 할인 혜택을 문의하려고
입주자들을 위한 공연 관람 일정을 안내하려고
단체 예매한 공연을 낮 공연으로 바꿔 달라고 요청하려고
공연이 늦게 끝나는 것에 대해 항의하려고
items.exp: 금요일 저녁 공연은 너무 늦게 끝나 입주자들에게 어려움이 있으니 토요일 오후 2시 낮 공연으로 예매를 옮겨 달라고 부탁하고 있어요. 그래서 ③이 목적이에요. 늦게 끝나는 사정을 설명할 뿐 항의하는 글은 아니에요.

items.passage: The Ferris wheel had just begun its slow descent when I turned to point it out to my brother and found only empty air beside me. A moment earlier, Minho had been holding the sleeve of my jacket, his face sticky with cotton candy. Now there was nothing but a river of strangers flowing past the ticket booths. I called his name, first quietly and then so loudly that people stared. My heart pounded against my ribs, and every small boy in a red cap seemed, for one terrible second, to be him and then not him. I pictured the parking lot, the busy road beyond the gates, the look on my mother's face. My hands would not stop shaking as I pushed toward the information booth. Then, over the crackle of the loudspeaker, I heard a familiar laugh. There he was, perched on a counter beside a smiling staff member, happily licking a free lollipop. I lifted him into my arms and held him so tightly that he complained. The knot in my chest finally loosened, and I let out a long breath I had not realized I was holding.
items.q: 다음 글에 드러난 I의 심경 변화로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 동생이 사라지자 심장이 쿵쾅거리고 손이 떨릴 만큼 당황했다가, 안내소에서 사탕을 먹고 있는 동생을 찾고 가슴의 응어리가 풀리며 긴 숨을 내쉬었어요. 그래서 ① panicked → relieved가 알맞아요. 처음부터 다급했으므로 ②나 ⑤처럼 무관심·지루함에서 시작한 것이 아니에요.

items.passage: Every organization contains rules and routines whose purpose no one can remember. A form must be signed by two managers rather than one; a meeting is held every Monday even when there seems to be nothing to discuss. To a newcomer eager to make things more efficient, such practices look like obstacles left behind by people who did not know better, and the temptation is to sweep them away at once. Sometimes that is exactly the right decision. Often, however, the practice turns out to have been a quiet solution to a problem that has simply stopped appearing because the practice was there. The second signature may have been introduced after a costly fraud; the Monday meeting may be the only place where two departments that never otherwise speak discover that their plans conflict. Remove the practice, and the old problem returns, usually after the reformer has moved on. The sensible course, then, is not to defend every tradition but to [ask why the fence was built before tearing it down]. If a good reason is found and no longer applies, the reformer can proceed with confidence; if none can be found, investigation, not demolition, is the next step.
items.q: 밑줄 친 [ask why the fence was built before tearing it down]이 다음 글에서 의미하는 바로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: replace old rules gradually rather than all at once
understand the purpose of an existing practice before removing it
protect traditions because they reflect the wisdom of the past
consult newcomers who can see problems more clearly
build new rules that prevent fraud in advance
items.exp: 관습이 지금은 보이지 않는 문제를 조용히 막고 있을 수 있으니, 모든 전통을 지키라는 것이 아니라 없애기 전에 그것이 왜 생겼는지 먼저 알아보라는 뜻이에요. 그래서 ②가 맞아요. 글은 모든 전통을 옹호하지 말라고 했으니 ③은 틀려요.

items.passage: For much of the twentieth century, many architects regarded ornament as a waste. Carved cornices, decorative tiles, and patterned brickwork were seen as leftovers from a less rational age, and the clean, unadorned surface became a sign of honest, modern design. Yet ordinary people have often responded to such buildings with indifference or even dislike, and research on how we experience streets helps explain why. Detail gives the eye something to rest on. A facade with varied textures and patterns rewards a passerby moving at walking speed, offering something new to notice every few steps, while a long blank wall makes the same distance feel longer and duller. Ornament also helps people find their way: a distinctive doorway or a carved figure above an entrance is far easier to remember than one glass box among many. Perhaps most important, buildings with visible craft and character tend to attract affection, and buildings that people are fond of are more likely to be repaired and preserved than torn down. Seen this way, decoration is not an extravagance added to architecture but part of how a building does its work for the people who live among it.
items.q: 다음 글의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: 건물의 장식은 건축비를 늘리므로 최소화해야 한다.
현대 건축은 전통 양식을 그대로 복원해야 한다.
길을 찾기 쉬운 도시를 만들려면 표지판을 늘려야 한다.
건물의 장식은 사람들이 공간을 즐기고 아끼게 하는 실질적 기능을 한다.
건물의 가치는 건축가의 의도보다 시민의 평가로 정해져야 한다.
items.exp: 장식은 걷는 사람의 눈을 즐겁게 하고, 길 찾기를 돕고, 애정을 끌어내 건물이 보존되게 한다고 하며 마지막 문장에서 장식은 사치가 아니라 건물이 하는 일의 일부라고 정리했어요. 그래서 ④가 요지예요. ①은 글이 반박하는 20세기 건축가들의 생각이에요.

items.passage: A hummingbird lives at the edge of what a warm-blooded body can afford. To hover in front of a flower, it beats its wings dozens of times per second, and its heart may race at more than a thousand beats per minute. Such an engine demands constant fuel, and during the day the bird feeds almost continuously on nectar. Night presents a serious problem, since a small bird that cannot eat for ten or twelve hours could burn through its reserves before dawn. Many species solve this by entering a state called torpor. As darkness falls, the bird allows its body temperature to drop sharply, sometimes by more than twenty degrees, and its heart rate and breathing slow dramatically. In this condition it may use only a small fraction of the energy it would need to stay fully warm. The cost is that a torpid bird is nearly helpless, unable to fly or respond quickly to danger. Before sunrise it begins to shiver, rewarming its muscles over the better part of an hour until it is ready to fly off in search of its first meal.
items.q: 다음 글의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: the role of hummingbirds in pollinating flowers
how hummingbirds defend their feeding territories
the effect of cold climates on bird migration
why small birds sing most actively at dawn
the way hummingbirds save energy by slowing their bodies at night
items.exp: 에너지를 많이 쓰는 벌새가 밤에 먹지 못하는 문제를 체온과 심박을 크게 낮추는 torpor 상태로 해결한다는 글이므로 ⑤가 주제예요. ①은 꽃과 꿀이라는 낱말만 빌린 오답이고, 철새 이동이나 새벽 노래는 다루지 않아요.

items.passage: For centuries, the pockets in men's and women's clothing developed along very different lines. From the seventeenth century onward, men's coats, waistcoats, and trousers increasingly had pockets sewn directly into them, giving their wearers a convenient place for coins, letters, keys, and small tools. Women, by contrast, usually wore a separate pair of fabric pouches tied around the waist beneath their wide skirts, reached through slits in the outer garment. These tie-on pockets could be large and held a surprising variety of possessions, from sewing kits to snacks to small books. Around 1800, however, fashion shifted toward narrow, high-waisted dresses that left no room for bulky pouches underneath. Women began carrying small handbags instead, which had to be held in the hand and could easily be lost, forgotten, or stolen. Some historians argue that this change was more than a matter of style. A person with pockets can move through the world with hands free and belongings secure, and the long argument over whether women's clothing should include practical pockets has often been tied to wider debates about independence.
items.q: 다음 글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Handbags Became Fashion's Most Expensive Item
Sewing Through the Centuries: A Tailor's Guide
Hidden in the Seams: Pockets and the Question of Freedom
How Narrow Dresses Improved Women's Health
The Tools Men Carried in the Seventeenth Century
items.exp: 남성복에는 주머니가 붙었지만 여성은 따로 맨 주머니를 쓰다가 좁은 드레스 유행 뒤 손가방을 들게 되었고, 주머니가 손의 자유와 독립 문제와 이어진다고 했어요. 그래서 ③이 제목으로 알맞아요. ①의 가격이나 ④의 건강 이야기는 글에 없어요.

items.passage:
Maple Grove Bookbinding Workshop 2027

Learn to sew and bind your own hardcover notebook by hand in this one-day workshop for beginners!

• When: Saturday, May 15, 10 a.m. – 3 p.m. (lunch break 12:00 – 1:00)
• Where: Maple Grove Public Library, Craft Room (2nd floor)
• Fee: $25 per person (all paper, thread, and tools provided)

Program
• Morning: Folding pages and hand-sewing the book block
• Afternoon: Making and decorating the hard cover
• Each participant takes home one finished notebook.

Notes
• Open to ages 14 and up. Participants under 16 must come with an adult.
• Registration is online only and closes on Monday, May 10. Limited to 15 people.
• Please bring your own lunch. Drinks will be provided.
items.q: Maple Grove Bookbinding Workshop 2027에 관한 다음 안내문의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?
choices: 참가비에 종이와 실, 도구가 포함되어 있다.
참가자는 각자 완성한 공책 두 권을 가져간다.
16세 미만 참가자는 성인과 함께 와야 한다.
items.exp: 참가자마다 완성한 공책 한 권(one finished notebook)을 가져간다고 했으니 두 권이라는 ③이 안내문과 맞지 않아요. 날짜와 시작 시각, 재료·도구 포함, 16세 미만 보호자 동반, 점심 지참은 모두 맞아요.

items.passage: In a few deserts around the world, travelers have reported a strange sound rising from the sand: a deep, steady hum, sometimes compared to a distant airplane or a low note on a cello. These so-called singing dunes ①[produce] their sound when dry sand slides down the steep face of a dune in an avalanche, whether triggered by wind or by a person sliding down the slope. What makes the phenomenon puzzling is that most sand ②[does] not sing at all. Researchers who have studied the dunes report that the sand grains must be very dry, fairly round, and remarkably similar in size, conditions ③[what] allow millions of grains to move together in a synchronized way. When this happens, the sliding layer vibrates like the skin of a drum, and the surface of the dune ④[acts] as a giant loudspeaker. The resulting sound can last for several minutes and may be heard several kilometers away. Interestingly, if a sample of singing sand is carried to a laboratory and ⑤[mixed] with even a small amount of ordinary sand, it often loses its voice.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?
items.exp: ③ 뒤에 allow의 주어가 빠진 불완전한 절이 conditions를 꾸미므로 관계대명사 which나 that으로 고쳐야 해요. ①은 복수 주어 dunes, ②와 ④는 단수 주어 sand, surface와 맞고, ⑤는 is carried와 병렬된 수동태 과거분사라 맞아요.

items.passage: When people are protected from the consequences of a risk, they may begin to take more of it. Economists call this tendency moral hazard, and insurance offers the clearest examples. A driver whose car is fully insured has slightly less reason to ①[avoid] parking on a dark street, and a homeowner whose losses will be covered may feel less ②[urgency] about fixing a faulty wire. None of this requires dishonesty; the protection simply weakens the incentive to be careful. Insurers have developed several tools to ③[counter] the problem. Deductibles require customers to pay the first part of any loss themselves, so that they keep a personal stake in preventing it. Premiums that rise after a claim ④[reward] careful customers relative to careless ones. The same logic applies far beyond insurance. When a large bank expects the government to rescue it in a crisis, its managers may pursue riskier investments, knowing that the losses will be shared while the profits stay private. The challenge for policy makers is therefore to provide protection without ⑤[strengthening] people's sense of responsibility for their own choices.
items.q: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 부분 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?
items.exp: 보호를 제공하면서도 자기 선택에 책임지려는 마음을 '없애지' 않아야 한다는 흐름이므로 ⑤ strengthening은 weakening이나 removing으로 바꿔야 해요. 나머지는 피하다, 긴박감, 대응하다, 보상하다로 모두 문맥에 맞아요.

items.passage: Lullabies sung in different parts of the world differ in language, melody, and instruments, yet listeners seem to recognize them almost instantly. In one large study, people from dozens of countries heard short recordings of songs from cultures they had never encountered and were asked to guess each song's purpose. They identified lullabies with remarkable accuracy, more reliably than love songs or healing songs. The reason appears to lie in features that lullabies share across societies: slow tempos, smooth and repetitive melodies, a narrow range of pitch, and soft, falling contours. Infants themselves respond to these qualities. When researchers played unfamiliar lullabies to babies, their heart rates slowed, their pupils shrank, and their restless movements decreased, even though the songs came from places the infants and their parents had never heard of. Such findings suggest that lullabies are not simply local traditions passed down within each family but draw on a ___ connection between certain sound patterns and calm, one that seems to be built into human perception.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: 서로 다른 문화의 자장가가 느린 박자와 반복적인 선율 같은 공통 특징을 지니고, 처음 들어 본 자장가에도 아기들이 진정되었다고 했어요. 따라서 자장가는 인간의 지각에 새겨진 보편적인(universal) 연결에 바탕을 둔다는 ②가 알맞아요. ③ learned는 가족 안에서 전해지는 전통이라는, 글이 부정하는 생각과 같은 뜻이에요.

items.passage: A translator working on a poem faces a set of demands that cannot all be met at once. The original may rely on rhyme, on the rhythm of its lines, on a pun that works only in its own language, or on an image that carries a particular association for its first readers. A word-for-word rendering may preserve the literal meaning while destroying the music; a version that keeps the rhyme may have to replace the original image with a different one; an explanation of the pun may preserve the joke's content while killing its surprise. Because no rendering can preserve everything, every translator must decide which features of the original are essential and which can be sacrificed. Two skilled translators working from the same poem may therefore produce versions that differ greatly, not because one of them has made errors, but because they have ranked the poem's qualities differently. Seen in this light, a translation is less a copy than an interpretation: whether or not the translator says so, every finished version amounts to ___. Readers who compare several translations of the same work are, in effect, listening to a debate about the original.
items.q: 다음 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: a faithful reproduction of every element of the original
evidence that poetry is impossible to translate
a claim about what matters most in the original
a correction of the weaknesses of the original poem
proof that literal meaning is more important than sound
items.exp: 번역에서는 모든 것을 살릴 수 없어 무엇이 핵심인지 선택해야 하고, 그 순위 매김 때문에 번역본이 달라진다고 했어요. 마지막 문장도 여러 번역이 원작에 대한 논쟁이라고 하므로 원작에서 가장 중요한 것이 무엇인지에 대한 주장이라는 ③이 맞아요. ①은 모든 것을 보존할 수 없다는 글과 반대예요.

items.passage: Adolescents are often described as reckless, but laboratory studies suggest that their risk-taking depends heavily on who is watching. ① In one experiment, teenagers and adults played a driving video game in which they could save time by running yellow lights at the risk of crashing. ② When playing alone, the teenagers took about as many risks as the adults, but when two friends watched from the next room, their risky choices nearly doubled, while the adults' behavior barely changed. ③ Brain scans revealed that the presence of peers heightened activity in reward-related regions of the teenage brain, making the potential payoff of a gamble feel more attractive. ④ Driving simulators are also used by professional racing teams, which rely on them to test new tracks without the expense of real cars. ⑤ These findings have practical implications: some regions now limit the number of young passengers a newly licensed teenage driver may carry, recognizing that a car full of friends changes the decisions made behind the wheel.
items.q: 다음 글에서 전체 흐름과 관계 없는 문장은?
items.exp: 또래가 지켜볼 때 청소년의 위험 행동이 늘어난다는 연구와 그 정책적 의미를 다루는 글이에요. ④는 운전 시뮬레이터가 레이싱 팀에서도 쓰인다는 내용으로, 또래와 위험 감수라는 흐름과 관계가 없어요.

items.passage:
Today it seems obvious that every house should have a number, so that letters, visitors, and deliveries can find it. Yet in most European cities before the eighteenth century, buildings were identified by descriptions rather than numbers.

(A) The motive behind the first large-scale numbering, however, had little to do with mail. In several eighteenth-century states, officials numbered houses so that they could count residents, collect taxes, and locate young men for military service.

(B) Because the numbers made people easier to find, they were not always welcomed. In some cities residents removed or painted over the plates on their doors, and authorities had to threaten fines to keep them in place.

(C) A merchant might live 'at the sign of the golden lion' or 'opposite the old well,' and finding an address often meant asking neighbors along the way. Such descriptions worked reasonably well in small communities where everyone knew one another.
items.q: 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (C)는 주어진 글의 '숫자 대신 묘사'의 예를 들어요. (A)는 however로 흐름을 바꿔 첫 번호 매기기의 동기가 우편이 아닌 세금·징병이었다고 하고, (B)는 그래서 사람들이 번호를 반기지 않았다고 이어져요. 따라서 (C)-(A)-(B)예요.

items.passage: Many marathon runners describe a sudden collapse in energy somewhere around the thirtieth kilometer, a moment they call hitting the wall. ( ① ) Instead, the explanation lies largely in how the body fuels long efforts. ( ② ) During running, muscles burn a mixture of fat and carbohydrate, and the faster the pace, the more they depend on carbohydrate, which is stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver. ( ③ ) For many runners at race pace, these stores are enough to last roughly thirty kilometers, well short of the full distance. ( ④ ) Fat, by contrast, is stored in amounts large enough to fuel days of activity, but the body can convert it into usable energy only slowly. ( ⑤ ) Once glycogen runs low, the runner is forced to rely more heavily on this slower fuel, and the pace that felt comfortable an hour earlier suddenly becomes impossible to maintain. This is why experienced runners eat carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before a race and take sports drinks or gels during it.
items.q:
글의 흐름으로 보아, 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 적절한 곳은?

The experience is not simply a matter of tired legs or a lack of willpower, as many beginners assume.
items.exp: 주어진 문장은 지친 다리나 의지 부족 탓이 아니라는 내용이라, 벽에 부딪힌다는 현상 소개 바로 뒤, 그리고 진짜 원인이 연료 방식에 있다는 The explanation 문장 앞인 ①에 들어가야 해요. Instead는 앞의 부정 내용을 받으므로 주어진 문장이 바로 앞에 있어야 해요.

items.passage: Studies of museum visitors have repeatedly found that people spend remarkably little time in front of any single work of art, often less than half a minute, and a good part of that time is spent reading the label. Some museums have begun experimenting with a different approach. In programs sometimes called slow looking, participants are invited to sit before one painting for ten or even twenty minutes, without a guide and without their phones, and simply observe. Many describe the first few minutes as uncomfortable or even boring. After that, however, details begin to emerge that they had not noticed at first: a figure half-hidden in the background, a change in the direction of the brushstrokes, a color that seems to shift as the eyes adjust to it. When asked afterward, participants commonly report not only that they remember the painting far better but also that they have come to like it more than works they passed quickly, even ones they had initially preferred. Attention, it seems, does not merely record the value of an artwork; it helps to create it.
items.q:
다음 글의 내용을 한 문장으로 요약하고자 한다. 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

Viewers who (A) ___ the time they spend with a single artwork tend to discover more in it and come to (B) ___ it more.
items.exp: 한 작품 앞에 10~20분 머물게 하자 처음엔 못 본 세부를 발견하고 그 작품을 더 좋아하게 되었다고 했어요. 그래서 (A)는 시간을 늘린다는 extend, (B)는 더 좋아한다는 appreciate가 알맞아요. 작품을 의심하거나 무시하게 되었다는 내용은 없어요.

items.passage:
When people first encounter an unfamiliar website, they usually judge it by what appears on the screen. Does it look professional? Is there an "About" page, a clear logo, a list of references? Researchers who asked students, and even well-educated adults, to evaluate online sources found that most of them did exactly this, reading carefully from the top of the page to the bottom and trusting what looked (a)[polished]. The problem is that these signals are easy to fake. A group funded by an industry with something to sell can build a site that looks just as serious as that of a university research center, complete with charts and footnotes.

The same researchers then studied professional fact-checkers and found that they behaved very differently. Within seconds of landing on an unfamiliar site, the fact-checkers often (b)[left] it, opening new tabs to search for what other sources said about the organization behind it. Rather than reading vertically, down a single page, they read laterally, across many pages. In the time it took students to admire a site's design, the fact-checkers had discovered who funded it and whether independent journalists considered it (c)[reliable].

What makes this finding striking is that the fact-checkers' advantage did not come from greater knowledge of the subject. It came from a different habit: a willingness to (d)[trust] their first impression of a page and to treat the page itself as the least informative place to learn about its credibility. This suggests that media literacy may be less about memorizing checklists of warning signs and more about building a few efficient routines. Teaching students to pause, leave the page, and ask what the rest of the web says about a source may (e)[protect] them more effectively than training them to inspect each site ever more closely.
items.q: 윗글의 제목으로 가장 적절한 것은?
choices: Why Fact-Checkers Know More Than Students
How Website Design Has Changed Over Time
Memorizing the Warning Signs of Fake News
Leave the Page to Judge the Page: Reading Laterally
items.exp: 학생들은 한 페이지를 위에서 아래로 꼼꼼히 읽으며 겉모습을 믿지만, 전문 팩트체커는 바로 페이지를 떠나 다른 출처를 확인하는 수평적 읽기를 한다는 글이에요. 그래서 ⑤가 제목이에요. 팩트체커의 강점은 지식이 아니라 습관에서 왔다고 했으니 ①은 틀려요.

items.exp: 팩트체커는 페이지의 첫인상을 믿지 않고 페이지 자체를 가장 정보가 적은 곳으로 여겼으므로 (d) trust는 distrust나 question으로 바꿔야 해요. 세련된 겉모습(polished), 사이트를 떠남(left), 신뢰할 만함(reliable), 보호(protect)는 모두 맞아요.

items.passage:
(A)
Mina had imagined that volunteering at Riverside Hospital would mean helping nurses or comforting crying children. Instead, on her first Saturday, the volunteer coordinator, Ms. Grant, handed her a cart of magazines and a single instruction: visit Mr. Abbott in Room 412. "He had hip surgery a week ago," (a)[she] explained, "and he hasn't said more than ten words to anyone since he arrived." Mina pushed the cart down the corridor, her stomach tight, wondering what a sixteen-year-old could possibly say to a man who did not want to talk.

(B)
After that, the visits changed completely. Each Saturday Mr. Abbott told Mina stories about the marshes where he had spent forty years watching birds, and she brought him new photographs to identify. When the physical therapist mentioned that he could see a bird feeder from the window at the end of the hall, he began walking there every afternoon with his walker, something he had refused to do before. "Whatever you're doing," Ms. Grant told Mina, "keep doing it." Mina only smiled, because (b)[she] knew she had done nothing more than ask about a bird.

(C)
On the day Mr. Abbott went home, he asked a nurse to call Mina before she started her rounds. When (c)[she] arrived, he handed her a worn book with a faded green cover: his own field guide, its margins filled with notes in small, careful handwriting. "Somebody should keep using it," he said gruffly. Mina thanked him, and later, on the bus home, she read the note he had written on the first page: "To my best student, who reminded me to look out the window."

(D)
Mr. Abbott barely looked up when she entered. Mina offered him magazines, then the newspaper, then a crossword, and each time he shook his head. As (d)[she] was about to leave, she noticed a pair of old binoculars on his bedside table. On the next visit, she showed him a photograph of a small brown bird she had taken in her backyard and asked if he knew what it was. He took her phone, studied the picture, and frowned. "That's not a sparrow," he said. "That's a wren. Look at the tail." Then, to (e)[her] surprise, he kept talking for half an hour.
items.q: 주어진 글 (A)에 이어질 내용을 순서에 맞게 배열한 것으로 가장 적절한 것은?
items.exp: (A)에서 Mina가 Mr. Abbott의 병실로 향하자 (D)에서 처음엔 무엇에도 반응하지 않던 그가 새 사진을 보고 말을 시작해요. (B)는 After that으로 그 뒤 달라진 방문을, (C)는 퇴원하는 날을 다루므로 (D)-(B)-(C)예요.
